fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.s{animation:t 4s ease-in-out infinite;transform-box:fill-box;transform-origin:center}@keyframes t{0%,100%{transform:rotate(-6deg)}50%{transform:rotate(6deg)}}</style><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff8e1'/><g font-size='54' text-anchor='middle'><text class='s' x='80' y='110'>🌞</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:.5s' x='220' y='110'>🐰</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:1s' x='360' y='110'>🐻</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:1.5s' x='500' y='110'>👖</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:2s' x='150' y='210'>🐴</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:2.5s' x='300' y='210'>🍲</text><text class='s' style='animation-delay:3s' x='450' y='210'>🐜</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Can you name the story for each picture?
fig.alt: Swinging emoji pictures: sun, bunny, bear, trousers, donkey, pot, ant

check.q: Which story teaches 'check before you believe'?
check.why: In Funny Bunny everyone ran without checking whether the sky was really falling.

sections.md:
**Opposites:** hot – cold, long – short, big – small, start – stop, remember – forget, work – play, strong – weak, on – off.

**Rhymes:** sun – fun, rain – train, cat – hat, pot – hot, bear – chair.

**Animal sounds:** donkey brays, dog barks, cat mews, rooster crows, frog croaks, duck quacks.

**Size words:** big, bigger, biggest.

**-ing words:** rain – raining, play – playing, cook – cooking.

check.q: What is the opposite of start?
check.why: Stop is the opposite of start, like the words for the magic porridge pot.

sections.h: Who said it? Who did it?
sections.md:
- Who blew hard but lost? **The Wind.**
- Who ran shouting about the sky? **Funny Bunny.**
- Who ate Baby Bear's porridge? **Curlylocks.**
- Who shortened the trousers? **The family, one by one.**
- Who stood on top of the cat? **The rooster.**
- Who forgot the stopping words? **The girl's mother.**
- Who saved food for winter? **The ant.**

check.q: Who stood on top of the pile of animal musicians?
check.why: The rooster was at the top, on the cat, which was on the dog, which was on the donkey.

sections.md:
1. Read the question twice.
2. Answer in a full sentence: *The ant stored food for winter.*
3. Start with a capital letter and end with a full stop.
4. Write neatly and leave space between words.
5. For drawing questions, label your picture.

parts.md: The night before her exam, Riya fell asleep on her English book. Suddenly the pages fluttered and out jumped a tiny ant! "Revise with me," said the ant.
The Sun waved and the Wind puffed. Funny Bunny hopped by shouting, and Riya called, "Check first!" The four musicians sang, and a pot bubbled porridge until Riya shouted, "Stop, little pot!"
Riya woke up smiling — and gave Mummy a smile, which came right back. In the exam she remembered every story, because she had met them all in her dream.

summary: Each unit has a poem and a story.
A Smile: a smile is free and spreads.
The Wind and the Sun: gentleness beats force.
Rain and Storm in the Garden: rain is everywhere; storms pass.
Funny Bunny: check before you believe.
Mr Nobody and Curlylocks: own up to what you do.
Make It Shorter: tell your team what you have done.
The Mumbai Musicians: friends are strong together.
The Magic Porridge Pot: know how to stop.
The Grasshopper and the Ant: plan and save.
Revise opposites, rhymes, animal sounds and size words.
practice: Write the lesson of The Wind and the Sun.
Why did the friends believe Funny Bunny?
What three things did Curlylocks use in the bears' house?
Who are the Mumbai Musicians?
What were the words to stop the magic pot?
Write five pairs of opposites.
Write the sounds of four animals.
Which is your favourite story? Write two lines about it.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-10-strange-tal.title: Strange Talk and The Grasshopper and the Ant
rd-school-c2-english.unit-10-strange-tal.subtitle: Croak, quack, grunt — and why the ant worked all summer

sections.md:
Shh! Close your eyes and listen. If you walk past a pond at night in the monsoon, you hear *croak, croak*. In a village yard you hear *quack, quack* and *cluck, cluck*. The poem **Strange Talk** imagines that each animal is really *talking* — in its own language!

The child in the poem meets little creatures one by one: a frog in the grass, a duck, a pig, and small birds and insects. Each one makes its own sound. The child wonders: *what are they saying to each other?* Is the frog telling a joke? Is the duck calling its babies? To us the words sound strange. But to the animal friends, they surely make perfect sense.

It is a fun poem to read aloud. Make each animal's noise as you read!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.b{animation:p 2s ease-in-out infinite;transform-box:fill-box;transform-origin:center}@keyframes p{0%,100%{transform:scale(.8);opacity:.4}50%{transform:scale(1.1);opacity:1}}</style><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#e0f2f1'/><ellipse cx='120' cy='240' rx='70' ry='20' fill='#4fc3f7'/><ellipse cx='120' cy='215' rx='38' ry='24' fill='#66bb6a'/><circle cx='105' cy='195' r='8' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='135' cy='195' r='8' fill='#fff'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='220' rx='40' ry='26' fill='#fff' stroke='#999'/><circle cx='335' cy='190' r='18' fill='#fff' stroke='#999'/><path d='M350 190 l18 4 l-18 4z' fill='#ffa000'/><ellipse cx='480' cy='220' rx='55' ry='35' fill='#f8bbd0'/><circle cx='530' cy='210' r='14' fill='#f48fb1'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='22'><g class='b'><rect x='60' y='100' width='110' height='45' rx='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#333'/><text x='115' y='130' text-anchor='middle'>croak!</text></g><g class='b' style='animation-delay:.7s'><rect x='245' y='110' width='110' height='45' rx='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#333'/><text x='300' y='140' text-anchor='middle'>quack!</text></g><g class='b' style='animation-delay:1.4s'><rect x='425' y='110' width='110' height='45' rx='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#333'/><text x='480' y='140' text-anchor='middle'>grunt!</text></g></g></svg>
fig.caption: Frog, duck and pig — each speaking its own 'strange' language.
fig.alt: A frog, a duck and a pig with speech bubbles saying croak, quack and grunt

check.q: What sound does a duck make?
check.why: A duck says quack, which is its own way of talking.

sections.md:
The poem was written by a poet whose words are in your Marigold book — read it there (link at the end). Here is what it tells us, part by part:

- **First part:** the child hears a little frog and a duck. Their sounds are not our words, so the child calls their talk *strange*.
- **Middle part:** more creatures join in — small, busy animals with their own squeaks and calls. The world is full of voices!
- **Last part:** the child asks a big question: *What do they say? Do they understand each other?* The poem ends with wonder.

**The big idea:** every animal has its own way to talk. We should listen kindly, even when we do not understand.

**Rhyming words:** poems often end lines with words that sound alike — *talk / walk*, *sing / ring*, *day / say*, *hop / stop*. Can you find rhyming pairs in the poem?

| Animal | Sound |
|---|---|
| frog | croak |
| duck | quack |
| pig | grunt / oink |
| hen | cluck |
| crow | caw |
| cuckoo (koel) | coo-oo |
| snake | hiss |
| bee | buzz |
| dog | bark / woof |
| cat | mew / meow |
| cow | moo |
| lion | roar |

**Did you know?** The koel sings loudly in Indian summers, just before the monsoon.

**Game:** One friend makes a sound, the others guess the animal!

check.q: Which animal says 'buzz'?
check.why: Bees buzz as their wings move very fast.

sections.h: The story: The Grasshopper and the Ant
sections.md:
This is a very old fable, first told long ago by **Aesop**, a storyteller of ancient Greece. Here it is in our own words.

It is a hot, sunny summer. A happy **grasshopper** spends every day jumping, singing and dancing in the green grass.

Nearby, a small **ant** is busy from morning to night. She carries grains of food, one by one, and stores them safely in her home under the ground.

"Why do you work so hard?" laughs the grasshopper. "Come and sing with me!"

"I am storing food for the cold winter," says the ant. "You should do the same." But the grasshopper only laughs and plays on.

Then **winter** comes. Snow covers the ground. There is no grass and no food. The grasshopper is cold and very hungry. He knocks at the ant's door and begs for something to eat.

The ant has plenty, because she planned ahead. In many retellings she shares a little and reminds him to work and save next time. The grasshopper learns his lesson.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='300' height='300' fill='#c8e6c9'/><rect x='300' width='300' height='300' fill='#e3f2fd'/><circle cx='60' cy='50' r='28' fill='#ffd54f'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -40;0 0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><ellipse cx='150' cy='220' rx='35' ry='12' fill='#7cb342'/><path d='M130 225 l-25 25 M170 225 l25 25' stroke='#558b2f' stroke-width='4'/></g><circle cx='90' cy='268' r='4' fill='#ffcc80'><animate attributeName='cx' values='240;60;240' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><g fill='#fff'><circle cx='350' cy='40' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' values='0;300' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='450' cy='20' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' values='0;300' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='540' cy='60' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' values='0;300' dur='3.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><rect x='300' y='250' width='300' height='50' fill='#fff'/><path d='M420 250 a40 40 0 0 1 80 0z' fill='#8d6e63'/><text x='150' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='18' font-family='sans-serif'>Summer: play or work?</text><text x='450' y='130' text-anchor='middle' font-size='18' font-family='sans-serif'>Winter: who has food?</text></svg>
fig.caption: Summer: the grasshopper jumps while the ant carries grain. Winter: snow falls and only the ant has a store.
fig.alt: Split scene of summer and winter

check.q: Why did the ant have food in winter?
check.why: The ant worked hard and saved food during summer, so she had enough for winter.

sections.md:
**The ant**
- hard-working, wise, thinks about tomorrow
- kind — she shares in the end

**The grasshopper**
- happy, playful, carefree
- does not think about the future, but learns his lesson

**Talk about it:** Are you more like the ant or the grasshopper? Is it okay to be a little bit of both?

Is playing bad? No! Play is good for us. The lesson is about **balance** and **planning ahead**.

- Work first, then play.
- Save a little for later — like keeping coins in a gullak (piggy bank).
- Think: *what will I need tomorrow?*

In India, farmers store grain after the harvest so they have food until the next one. That is the ant's wisdom.

check.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
options: Plan ahead and save for later
check.why: The story teaches us to work and save for the future while still enjoying life.

sections.md:
**Seasons:** summer, monsoon, winter, spring.

**Opposites:** work – play, hot – cold, full – empty, busy – lazy, summer – winter, laugh – cry.

**Describing the characters:** the ant is *hard-working* and *wise*; the grasshopper is *carefree* and *playful*.

**Action words:** jump, sing, dance, carry, store, knock, beg, share.

**Fill in:** The ant ____ food. (stores) The grasshopper ____ all day. (sings)

check.q: What is the opposite of 'hot'?
check.why: Cold is the opposite of hot, like winter is the opposite of summer.

parts.md: Tara got two rupees every Sunday from Dada. Her cousin Bunty spent his at once on toffees. Tara spent one rupee and dropped one into her clay gullak.
Bunty laughed. "You are like that ant!" Months went by. Then the Dussehra mela came to town, with a giant wheel and a toy shop.
Tara broke open her gullak — enough for the ride and a kite! She bought a ride for Bunty too. "Next year," said Bunty, "I am getting a gullak." Being an ant, they agreed, was fun after all.

summary: Strange Talk is a poem about animal sounds as animal languages.
Frog croaks, duck quacks, pig grunts, hen clucks, crow caws.
The child wonders what the animals are saying.
The Grasshopper and the Ant is an old fable by Aesop.
In summer, the grasshopper plays and sings all day.
The ant works hard and stores food for winter.
In winter the grasshopper is hungry; the ant has enough.
Lesson: work, save and plan for the future.
Play is good, but balance work and play.
practice: Write the sounds of a frog, a duck and a crow.
What does the child in the poem wonder?
What did the grasshopper do in summer?
What did the ant do in summer?
What happened to the grasshopper in winter?
Who was wise? Why?
Write the opposites: work, hot, busy.
How can you save for later like the ant?

rd-school-c2-english.unit-3-smile-wind-s.title: A Smile and The Wind and the Sun
rd-school-c2-english.unit-3-smile-wind-s.subtitle: Can a smile travel? Who is stronger, the wind or the sun?

sections.h: Have you ever caught a smile?
sections.md:
Think of a morning when your friend smiled at you at the school gate. What did your face do? It smiled back! You did not even try. That is the big idea of the poem **A Smile**.

The poem tells us that a smile is a very special thing:

- It costs **nothing**. You do not need one rupee to give it.
- It is easy to **give**. You only need to turn up the corners of your mouth.
- When you give it away, you **still have it**. Your smile does not get used up.
- It **spreads**. One smile makes another person smile, and that person makes one more person smile.

So a smile is like a little lamp. You light your friend's lamp, and your own lamp keeps shining too.

**Did you know?** Babies start to smile back at people when they are only a few weeks old.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.f{animation:p 3s infinite}.f2{animation:p 3s 1s infinite}.f3{animation:p 3s 2s infinite}@keyframes p{0%,100%{transform:scale(1)}50%{transform:scale(1.12)}}</style><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff8e7'/><g class='f' style='transform-origin:120px 150px'><circle cx='120' cy='150' r='55' fill='#ffd166'/><circle cx='102' cy='135' r='6'/><circle cx='138' cy='135' r='6'/><path d='M95 165 Q120 190 145 165' stroke='#000' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/></g><g class='f2' style='transform-origin:300px 150px'><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='55' fill='#ffb4a2'/><circle cx='282' cy='135' r='6'/><circle cx='318' cy='135' r='6'/><path d='M275 165 Q300 190 325 165' stroke='#000' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/></g><g class='f3' style='transform-origin:480px 150px'><circle cx='480' cy='150' r='55' fill='#a0e7a0'/><circle cx='462' cy='135' r='6'/><circle cx='498' cy='135' r='6'/><path d='M455 165 Q480 190 505 165' stroke='#000' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/></g><path d='M185 150 H230' stroke='#e76f51' stroke-width='6'/><polygon points='230,140 248,150 230,160' fill='#e76f51'/><path d='M365 150 H410' stroke='#e76f51' stroke-width='6'/><polygon points='410,140 428,150 410,160' fill='#e76f51'/><text x='300' y='265' font-size='22' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>One smile makes another smile!</text></svg>
fig.caption: A smile passes from one face to the next.
fig.alt: Three smiling faces with arrows between them

keyTerms: smile — a happy look on your face
give — to let someone have something

check.q: What happens to your smile when you give it to someone?
check.why: A smile is special because when you share it, you keep it too and it spreads to others.

sections.md:
Let us play with some words.

| Word | Meaning | Use it |
|---|---|---|
| free | costs nothing | The smile is free. |
| share | give a part to others | I share my tiffin. |
| spread | go to many places | The news spread fast. |

**Rhyming words** sound the same at the end: *smile – while – mile*, *sun – fun – run*, *day – play – may*.

Try it: say one word that rhymes with **cat**. (hat, mat, bat!)

sections.h: The story: The Wind and the Sun
sections.md:
The second lesson is an old fable, a story that teaches a lesson. The **Wind** and the **Sun** have an argument. Each one says, "I am the stronger one!"

They see a man walking on a road. He is wearing a coat. They make a deal: whoever can make the man take off his coat is the stronger one.

1. The Wind goes first. It blows and blows. Leaves fly, dust swirls. But the man feels cold, so he **holds his coat tighter**.
2. The Wind blows harder still. The man pulls the coat even closer. The Wind gets tired and gives up.
3. Now the Sun takes a turn. It comes out from behind a cloud and shines **gently and warmly**.
4. The man feels warm, then hot. He wipes his face, and then he **takes off his coat**!

The Sun wins. The lesson: **being gentle and kind works better than being rough and forceful.**

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><radialGradient id='s'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#fff3b0'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#f4a261'/></radialGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#cdeffd'/><rect y='250' width='600' height='70' fill='#8fd18f'/><g><circle cx='500' cy='70' r='45' fill='url(#s)'><animate attributeName='r' values='40;50;40' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g stroke='#6c8ebf' stroke-width='5' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M40 90 Q90 70 140 90'><animate attributeName='d' values='M40 90 Q90 70 140 90;M60 90 Q110 110 160 90;M40 90 Q90 70 140 90' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M30 130 Q90 110 150 130'><animate attributeName='d' values='M30 130 Q90 110 150 130;M50 130 Q110 150 170 130;M30 130 Q90 110 150 130' dur='2.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='18' fill='#e9c46a'/><rect x='282' y='170' width='36' height='60' rx='8' fill='#9b2226'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;1;0;0;1' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='288' y='172' width='24' height='56' fill='#457b9d'/><rect x='288' y='228' width='8' height='24' fill='#333'/><rect x='304' y='228' width='8' height='24' fill='#333'/><text x='90' y='175' font-size='20' font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'>Wind</text><text x='500' y='145' font-size='20' font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'>Sun</text><text x='300' y='295' font-size='18' font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'>Warmth wins — the coat comes off</text></svg>
fig.caption: The wind blows; the man holds his coat. The sun shines; the coat comes off.
fig.alt: Wind lines, a sun and a man whose red coat disappears

check.q: Why did the man take off his coat?
options: He felt warm in the sun
check.why: The gentle warm sunshine made him feel hot, so he took the coat off himself.

sections.h: Who is who in the story?
sections.md:
- **The Wind** — proud, noisy, uses force. It thinks shouting and pushing will win.
- **The Sun** — calm and patient. It does not boast. It uses warmth.
- **The man** — he simply does what feels right. Cold makes him hold on; warmth makes him let go.

Think about school. If a friend grabs your pencil, you hold it tight. If a friend asks nicely, you happily share. That is the Wind and the Sun in your classroom!

check.q: Which word best describes the Sun in the story?
check.why: The Sun shone softly and warmly, which shows it was gentle.

sections.md:
Words that tell us more about a thing are **describing words**.

- the **strong** wind
- the **warm** sun
- the **long** road
- a **heavy** coat

Opposites from the story: **hot – cold**, **strong – weak**, **gentle – rough**, **on – off**.

Action words: blow, shine, walk, hold, take off.

check.q: What is the opposite of hot?
check.why: Cold is the opposite of hot, just like the cold wind and the hot sun.

parts.md: Meena was going to Nani's house in Jaipur by train. The coach was full and everyone looked grumpy. An uncle frowned at his phone. A baby was crying. Meena felt a little sad too.

Then she remembered what her teacher said: a smile costs nothing. So Meena smiled at the crying baby. The baby stopped, stared, and gave a big toothless grin! The baby's mother smiled at Meena. The uncle looked up and smiled at the mother.
Soon the whole coach was smiling and sharing peanuts. When Meena got down at Jaipur, she was still smiling. She had given away so many smiles, and she still had her own. "A smile train!" she laughed.

summary: A smile costs nothing and is easy to give.
When you share a smile you still keep it.
Smiles spread from person to person.
The Wind and the Sun argued about who was stronger.
The Wind blew hard, but the man held his coat tighter.
The Sun shone gently and the man took off his coat.
Kindness and gentleness work better than force.
Rhyming words end with the same sound: sun, fun, run.
Describing words tell us more: warm sun, strong wind.
practice: Why is a smile called free?
What did the Wind and the Sun argue about?
What did the man do when the Wind blew hard?
How did the Sun win?
Write two rhyming words for 'day'.
Write the opposites: hot, strong, on.
Draw the Sun and the Wind and write one line about each.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-4-rain-garden.title: Rain and Storm in the Garden
rd-school-c2-english.unit-4-rain-garden.subtitle: Pitter-patter on the roof — and a tiny world caught in a big storm

sections.md:
Dark clouds roll over the sky. The wind smells of wet earth — that lovely smell is called *petrichor*. Then — *pitter-patter, pitter-patter* — the rain begins! The leaves shine, the roads turn into little rivers and the frogs start to sing.

In this unit we read a short rain poem and a story called **Storm in the Garden**, about very small creatures who face a very big storm.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#cfd8dc'/><g fill='#90a4ae'><circle cx='150' cy='60' r='45'/><circle cx='210' cy='50' r='55'/><circle cx='270' cy='65' r='40'/><circle cx='390' cy='60' r='45'/><circle cx='450' cy='50' r='55'/></g><g stroke='#1e88e5' stroke-width='3'><line x1='160' y1='110' x2='155' y2='125'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-10 170' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='220' y1='110' x2='215' y2='125'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-10 170' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='280' y1='110' x2='275' y2='125'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-10 170' dur='.9s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='400' y1='110' x2='395' y2='125'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-10 170' dur='1.1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='460' y1='110' x2='455' y2='125'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-10 170' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g><rect y='260' width='600' height='40' fill='#66bb6a'/><path d='M60 260 v-60 h80 v60z' fill='#ffcc80'/><path d='M50 200 l50 -40 l50 40z' fill='#e57373'/><circle cx='500' cy='240' r='30' fill='#43a047'/><rect x='495' y='240' width='10' height='25' fill='#795548'/></svg>
fig.caption: Clouds, falling raindrops, a house and a tree getting wet.
fig.alt: Rain falling from grey clouds onto a house and a tree

check.q: What do we see in the sky before it rains?
check.why: Dark, heavy clouds carry the water that falls as rain.

sections.md:
This is an old English nursery rhyme. Nobody knows who wrote it, and it is free for everyone to read.

> Rain on the green grass,
> And rain on the tree,
> Rain on the house-top,
> But not on me!

**Line by line**
- *Rain on the green grass* — the rain falls on the grass in the park and the field.
- *And rain on the tree* — the leaves get wet and drip.
- *Rain on the house-top* — the rain drums on the roof: tap, tap, tap!
- *But not on me!* — the child is inside, or under an umbrella, safe and dry. The child is happy and a little bit proud!

**Rhyming words:** *tree – me*.

(Your Marigold book may show a different rain poem; read it there. The idea is the same: rain falls everywhere, and it is fun to watch.)

check.q: In the rhyme, where does the rain NOT fall?
check.why: The last line says 'But not on me', so the child stays dry.

sections.md:
Here is the story in our own words. Read the full story in your Marigold book.

**1. A sunny garden.** In a garden live many tiny creatures — ants, a snail, beetles and other small bugs. For them, a blade of grass is like a tall tree and a puddle is like a lake.

**2. The sky turns dark.** One day black clouds come. The wind blows hard. Then a big storm begins! Huge raindrops crash down. For a little ant, one raindrop is as big as a bucket of water is for us.

**3. Running for shelter.** The little creatures are frightened. They hurry to hide — under a big leaf, a mushroom or a flower pot. They stay close together and help each other.

**4. Waiting.** Thunder booms. Water flows like a river past their hiding place. They wait and wait, and keep each other brave.

**5. The sun comes back.** At last the storm stops. The sun shines. The garden is washed clean and sparkling. The creatures come out, safe and happy.

**What the story teaches:** small friends who stay together are safe. After every storm, the sun comes again.

check.q: What did the tiny creatures do in the storm?
check.why: They ran to a safe place and stayed together until the storm passed.

sections.md:
In the story, everything looks huge to the little creatures. Let us compare:

| For us | For an ant |
|---|---|
| a raindrop | a bucket of water |
| a puddle | a big lake |
| a leaf | a roof |
| a blade of grass | a tall tree |

**Try this:** Lie down in a garden and look up at the grass. How big does it look?

- Carry an umbrella or wear a raincoat.
- Do not stand under a tree when there is thunder and lightning.
- Stay away from deep water and open drains.
- Fun: make paper boats and float them in a puddle! Jump in small puddles with gumboots.

**Did you know?** In India, most rain comes in the **monsoon** months, June to September. Farmers wait for it to grow rice.

check.q: Where should you NOT stand when there is lightning?
check.why: Lightning often strikes tall things like trees, so it is unsafe to stand under them.

sections.md:
**Rain words:** cloud, drop, puddle, thunder, lightning, umbrella, raincoat, rainbow.

**Sound words:** pitter-patter, drip-drop, boom (thunder), whoosh (wind).

**Opposites:** wet – dry, big – small, dark – bright, start – stop.

**Make sentences:** *I see a ______ in the sky.* (rainbow) *My shoes are ______.* (wet)

parts.md: When the first monsoon rain came, Chotu folded a paper boat from an old notebook page. He set it in the stream running beside his lane in Pune.
An ant was floating on a leaf nearby, spinning in the water. Chotu gently let the ant climb onto his boat. The boat sailed along to a dry step.
The ant walked off onto the step. The rain stopped and a rainbow came out. "Even a small boat can save a small friend," smiled Ammi.

summary: Rain falls from dark clouds.
The rhyme 'Rain' says rain falls on grass, trees and roofs, but not on the child.
Rhyming words: tree – me.
In 'Storm in the Garden', tiny creatures face a big storm.
They hide together under shelter and help each other.
After the storm, the sun shines again.
To small creatures, raindrops and puddles look huge.
Stay safe in rain: umbrella, no standing under trees in lightning.
practice: What do you see before it rains?
Where does the rain fall in the rhyme?
Who lives in the garden in the story?
What did the creatures do when the storm came?
What happened after the storm?
Write four rain words.
Write the opposites of wet and big.
Draw a rainy day and write one line about it.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-5-zoo-sky-fall.title: Zoo Manners and Funny Bunny
rd-school-c2-english.unit-5-zoo-sky-fall.subtitle: How to behave at the zoo — and the day the 'sky fell down'

sections.md:
Have you been to a zoo, like the one in Delhi, Mysuru or Kolkata? Lions, elephants, monkeys, peacocks! The poem **Zoo Manners** is a funny poem about how to behave when you visit animals.

The poem gives playful advice: every animal is different, so be careful how you act near each one. You would not tease a big animal, and you would not be rude to a small one either. The poem uses fun rhymes with animal names.

**Good zoo manners:**

1. Do not tease or shout at the animals.
2. Do not throw food or plastic into the cages.
3. Stay behind the railing.
4. Walk slowly and talk softly.
5. Put waste in the dustbin.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fefae0'/><rect y='240' width='600' height='60' fill='#a3b18a'/><g><ellipse cx='170' cy='180' rx='80' ry='55' fill='#9e9e9e'/><circle cx='100' cy='150' r='40' fill='#9e9e9e'/><path d='M70 165 Q50 220 75 235' stroke='#9e9e9e' stroke-width='16' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'><animate attributeName='d' values='M70 165 Q50 220 75 235;M70 165 Q30 200 40 160;M70 165 Q50 220 75 235' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><circle cx='95' cy='140' r='5'/><rect x='120' y='220' width='20' height='30' fill='#9e9e9e'/><rect x='200' y='220' width='20' height='30' fill='#9e9e9e'/></g><g stroke='#6d4c41' stroke-width='6'><line x1='300' y1='170' x2='300' y2='250'/><line x1='360' y1='170' x2='360' y2='250'/><line x1='420' y1='170' x2='420' y2='250'/><line x1='290' y1='190' x2='430' y2='190'/></g><circle cx='510' cy='190' r='20' fill='#ffcc80'/><rect x='495' y='210' width='30' height='40' fill='#1976d2'/><text x='450' y='130' font-size='18' font-family='sans-serif'>Shh… stay behind</text><text x='450' y='152' font-size='18' font-family='sans-serif'>the railing!</text></svg>
fig.caption: A child watches an elephant quietly from behind the railing.
fig.alt: An elephant swinging its trunk, a railing, and a child standing calmly

check.q: Which is good zoo manners?
check.why: Staying behind the railing keeps both you and the animals safe and calm.

sections.md:
| Animal | Lives in | Says |
|---|---|---|
| lion | den | roar |
| bird | nest | chirp/tweet |
| horse | stable | neigh |
| cow | shed | moo |
| bee | hive | buzz |
| rabbit | burrow | squeak |

**Did you know?** A rabbit's long ears can turn to catch sounds from different sides.

Funny Bunny is a little rabbit. One day, while she is sitting under a tree, something falls **plop!** on her head.

"Oh no! The sky is falling!" she cries, and she runs off in a panic.

On the way she meets friend after friend — a hen, a cock, a duck and others. Each one asks, "Where are you running?" Each one hears "The sky is falling!" and joins the run without checking. The line of frightened friends grows longer and longer.

At last they meet someone calm who asks the most important question: **"Did you see it fall?"** They all go back to the tree. And what do they find? Only a small thing that dropped from the tree — not the sky at all! The sky is still up there, blue and safe.

Everyone laughs at themselves. The lesson: **do not believe and spread a story without checking it first.**

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#e0f7fa'/><rect y='220' width='600' height='60' fill='#81c784'/><rect x='40' y='90' width='24' height='130' fill='#795548'/><circle cx='52' cy='80' r='55' fill='#388e3c'/><circle cx='110' cy='120' r='9' fill='#8d6e63'><animate attributeName='cy' values='120;200;200' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;30 0;0 0' dur='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><ellipse cx='170' cy='200' rx='26' ry='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#999'/><ellipse cx='160' cy='170' rx='6' ry='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#999'/><ellipse cx='176' cy='170' rx='6' ry='20' fill='#fff' stroke='#999'/><circle cx='260' cy='200' r='20' fill='#ffb74d'/><circle cx='340' cy='200' r='20' fill='#fff176'/><circle cx='420' cy='200' r='20' fill='#e57373'/></g><text x='380' y='90' font-size='22' font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'>"The sky is falling!"</text><text x='380' y='120' font-size='16' font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'>…but did anyone check?</text></svg>
fig.caption: Something drops from the tree, and a line of friends runs off without checking.
fig.alt: A small fruit drops from a tree; a bunny and three birds run in a line

check.q: What really fell on Funny Bunny?
options: A small thing from the tree
check.why: Only something small from the tree fell on her; the sky was safe where it always is.

sections.md:
Why did all the friends believe the bunny? Because they were scared, and they did not stop to look.

Today people sometimes send messages on phones saying scary things that are not true. The Funny Bunny lesson works there too:

- **Stop.** Do not panic.
- **Look.** Ask: did you see it?
- **Check.** Ask a grown-up you trust.
- Then **share** only what is true.

check.q: What should you do when you hear a scary story?
check.why: Checking first stops a wrong story from spreading and scaring others.

sections.md:
Many old stories give animals rhyming names, like *Funny Bunny*. Make your own!

- Silly + ? → *Silly Billy*
- Happy + ? → *Happy Pappy*
- Lucky + ? → *Lucky Ducky*

**Question words:** who, what, where, why. *Where are you going? What fell? Who saw it?*

parts.md: In a forest near Ranthambore lived Mor, a wise peacock. One morning a squirrel came racing past. "The river has gone! The river has gone!" A deer and two monkeys were running behind her.
Mor spread his tail and stopped them. "Did you see it go?" The squirrel blinked. "A crow told me." "Then let us look," said Mor. Together they walked to the bank.
The river was right there, sparkling. Only the morning fog had hidden it. Everyone laughed. From then on, the forest had a rule: before you run, ask Mor's question — did you see it?

summary: Zoo Manners is a funny poem about how to behave with animals.
At the zoo, do not tease, shout or throw food.
Stay behind the railing and keep the zoo clean.
Animals have homes: den, nest, stable, hive, burrow.
In Funny Bunny, something falls on the rabbit's head.
She thinks the sky is falling and runs in panic.
Friends join her without checking.
They find that only something small had fallen from the tree.
Lesson: check a story before believing or spreading it.
practice: Write three good zoo manners.
Where does a bee live? Where does a lion live?
What did Funny Bunny think was falling?
Name two friends who ran with her.
What question should the friends have asked?
Make two rhyming names like Funny Bunny.
Draw your favourite zoo animal and write what sound it makes.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-6-owning-up.title: Mr Nobody and Curlylocks and the Three Bears
rd-school-c2-english.unit-6-owning-up.subtitle: Who broke the cup? Who ate the porridge? Owning up to what we do

sections.md:
Someone spilled milk on the floor. Someone left the tap running. Someone tore a page from the book. When Mummy asks, "Who did it?", everyone says... **"Nobody!"**

The poem **Mr Nobody** is a funny poem about this. It imagines a strange little man called Mr Nobody who lives quietly in every house. Nobody ever sees him, but he gets blamed for all the mischief:

- cracked plates and broken cups,
- doors left open, buttons pulled off,
- ink spilled, papers scattered,
- muddy footprints on the clean floor.

Of course, there is no real Mr Nobody! The poem is gently laughing at us. When we do not want to own up, we blame 'nobody'. The poem asks us, with a smile: *who really did it?*

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.g{animation:h 4s ease-in-out infinite}@keyframes h{0%,100%{opacity:.15}50%{opacity:.7}}</style><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff3e0'/><rect y='230' width='600' height='70' fill='#d7ccc8'/><g class='g'><circle cx='300' cy='110' r='30' fill='#b0bec5'/><rect x='280' y='140' width='40' height='70' rx='12' fill='#b0bec5'/><text x='300' y='118' text-anchor='middle' font-size='26' font-family='sans-serif'>?</text></g><path d='M90 230 l20 -25 l20 25z' fill='#fff' stroke='#555'/><path d='M100 220 l10 -6' stroke='#c62828' stroke-width='3'/><ellipse cx='450' cy='250' rx='50' ry='10' fill='#fff'/><g fill='#6d4c41'><ellipse cx='180' cy='265' rx='8' ry='12'/><ellipse cx='210' cy='255' rx='8' ry='12'/><ellipse cx='240' cy='265' rx='8' ry='12'/></g><text x='300' y='40' font-size='22' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>"Who did it?" "Nobody!"</text></svg>
fig.caption: A broken cup, spilled milk, muddy footprints — and a ghostly 'Mr Nobody'.
fig.alt: A faint question-mark figure fading in and out over a messy room

check.q: Why does everyone blame Mr Nobody?
options: They do not want to own up
check.why: Mr Nobody is not real; people blame him because they do not want to admit what they did.

sections.md:
**Owning up** means saying, "I did it. I am sorry." It takes courage. But it makes things better:

- People trust you.
- The problem gets fixed faster (someone can mop up the milk!).
- You feel light and happy inside, not worried.

Magic words: **Sorry. Please. Thank you. Excuse me.**

check.q: You broke a glass by mistake. What should you say?
options: I did it, I am sorry
check.why: Saying 'I did it, I am sorry' is honest and helps grown-ups clean up safely.

sections.h: The story: Curlylocks and the Three Bears
sections.md:
In a little house in the forest live three bears: **Father Bear** (big), **Mother Bear** (middle-sized) and **Baby Bear** (small). One morning their porridge is too hot, so they go for a walk while it cools.

A little girl with curly hair, **Curlylocks**, finds the house. The door is open, so she walks in without asking.

1. **Porridge:** She tastes three bowls. One is too hot, one is too cold, and Baby Bear's is just right — she eats it all up!
2. **Chairs:** She tries three chairs. One is too hard, one is too soft, Baby Bear's is just right — but it breaks!
3. **Beds:** She tries three beds. One too high, one too low, Baby Bear's just right — and she falls asleep.

The bears come home. "Someone has been eating my porridge!" says Baby Bear. "And sitting in my chair, and it is broken!" Then they find Curlylocks asleep in Baby Bear's bed. She wakes, gets a fright, and runs away home.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f1f8e9'/><g fill='#8d6e63'><circle cx='120' cy='130' r='55'/><circle cx='80' cy='80' r='16'/><circle cx='160' cy='80' r='16'/><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='42'/><circle cx='270' cy='112' r='13'/><circle cx='330' cy='112' r='13'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><circle cx='460' cy='170' r='30'/><circle cx='440' cy='143' r='10'/><circle cx='480' cy='143' r='10'/></g></g><g fill='#3e2723'><circle cx='105' cy='120' r='5'/><circle cx='135' cy='120' r='5'/><circle cx='288' cy='142' r='4'/><circle cx='312' cy='142' r='4'/><circle cx='450' cy='165' r='4'/><circle cx='470' cy='165' r='4'/></g><g fill='#fff' stroke='#555'><path d='M80 230 h80 a40 25 0 0 1 -80 0z'/><path d='M270 240 h60 a30 20 0 0 1 -60 0z'/><path d='M440 245 h40 a20 14 0 0 1 -40 0z'/></g><text x='120' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-family='sans-serif'>too hot</text><text x='300' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-family='sans-serif'>too cold</text><text x='460' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-family='sans-serif'>just right!</text></svg>
fig.caption: Big, middle-sized and small — three bears and three bowls of porridge.
fig.alt: Three bears of different sizes with three bowls labelled too hot, too cold, just right

check.q: Whose porridge was 'just right'?
check.why: In the story Baby Bear's bowl was just right, so Curlylocks ate it all.

sections.md:
- She went into someone's house **without asking**.
- She ate food that was **not hers**.
- She **broke** a chair and did not say sorry.
- She **ran away** instead of owning up.

What could she have done? Knocked and waited. Asked before eating. Said, "I am sorry I broke your chair. Can I help fix it?" That is how the two lessons of this unit join together: **be honest and own up.**

check.q: What should Curlylocks have done about the broken chair?
options: Say sorry and offer to help
check.why: Owning up and offering to help is the honest and kind thing to do.

sections.md:
Size words: **big – bigger – biggest**, **small – smaller – smallest**.

- Father Bear is **big**. Mother Bear is **smaller**. Baby Bear is the **smallest**.

Opposites from the story: hot – cold, hard – soft, high – low, big – small, asleep – awake.

parts.md: It was Diwali eve. Amma had made a plate of besan ladoos for the neighbours. In the morning, three were missing! "Who ate them?" asked Amma. "Nobody!" said Chintu and Pinky together.
Chintu felt a heavy feeling in his tummy, and it was not the ladoos. He had eaten two in the night. Pinky had eaten one. Neither wanted to say it.

At last Chintu stepped forward. "It was me. Two. I am sorry." Pinky whispered, "One was me." Amma laughed and hugged them. "Thank you for owning up. Now come — let us make more together." The lamps that night felt extra bright.

summary: Mr Nobody is an imaginary man blamed for all the mischief at home.
The poem gently laughs at us for not owning up.
Owning up means saying 'I did it, I am sorry'.
Honesty builds trust and helps fix problems quickly.
Curlylocks entered the bears' house without asking.
She ate Baby Bear's porridge, broke his chair and slept in his bed.
The bears found her and she ran away.
She should have asked first and said sorry.
Size words: big, bigger, biggest; small, smaller, smallest.
practice: Name three things Mr Nobody is blamed for.
Is Mr Nobody a real person? Why do people blame him?
Name the three bears.
What three things did Curlylocks try in the house?
What happened to Baby Bear's chair?
What should you do if you break something by mistake?
Fill in: big, ______, biggest.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-7-draw-short.title: On My Blackboard I Can Draw and Make It Shorter
rd-school-c2-english.unit-7-draw-short.subtitle: Chalk pictures, and the trousers that got far too short

sections.h: A whole world on a blackboard
sections.md:
Give a child a piece of chalk and a blackboard, and what happens? Magic! The poem **On My Blackboard I Can Draw** is about a child who draws all kinds of things with chalk — and then rubs them out to draw again.

What can you draw? Lots of things you love: a house, a tree, the sun, a bird, a boat, your friends. With just a few lines, a whole picture comes alive. And the best part — when you rub it out, the board is ready for a new picture.

Drawing helps us **imagine**. A circle can be a ball, a sun, a face or a wheel. You decide!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.dr{stroke-dasharray:400;stroke-dashoffset:400;animation:d 5s ease infinite}@keyframes d{0%{stroke-dashoffset:400}50%,90%{stroke-dashoffset:0}100%{stroke-dashoffset:400}}</style><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#6d4c41'/><rect x='20' y='20' width='560' height='280' fill='#1b4332'/><g fill='none' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='4' stroke-linecap='round'><path class='dr' d='M80 230 v-70 l50 -40 l50 40 v70 z'/><path class='dr' d='M115 230 v-35 h30 v35'/><circle class='dr' cx='470' cy='80' r='35'/><path class='dr' d='M300 230 v-80'/><circle class='dr' cx='300' cy='120' r='38'/><path class='dr' d='M390 240 h120 l-20 25 h-80z M450 240 v-70 l40 50'/></g><text x='300' y='290' fill='#fff' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>house · tree · sun · boat</text></svg>
fig.caption: Chalk lines draw a house, a tree, the sun and a boat — then fade, ready to draw again.
fig.alt: Animated white chalk lines drawing a house, tree, sun and boat on a green board

check.q: What does a child do in the poem?
check.why: The poem is about a child drawing many things on a blackboard with chalk.

sections.md:
Every drawing is made of simple shapes.

| Shape | Can become |
|---|---|
| circle | sun, ball, face, wheel |
| triangle | roof, mountain, sail |
| square | window, box, house |
| line | stick, road, rain |

**Try it:** a circle + two triangles on top = a cat's face!

check.q: Which shape is best for a roof?
check.why: A triangle has a pointed top, just like the roof of a house.

sections.md:
A man buys a new pair of trousers for a special day. At home he tries them on. Oh dear — they are **too long**! They drag on the floor.

He asks the people in his family, one by one, to make them shorter. Each one is busy and says, "Not now." So the man goes to bed sad.

But later that night, each person feels sorry. Quietly, one after another, each one gets up, takes the trousers and **cuts them a little shorter**, then stitches them neatly. Nobody tells the others!

In the morning the man puts on his trousers. They are now **far too short** — up near his knees! Each helper had shortened them, so together they cut far too much.

The story is funny, but it teaches us: **talk to each other.** When we work in a team, we must tell others what we have done.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#e3f2fd'/><line x1='0' y1='270' x2='600' y2='270' stroke='#555' stroke-width='3'/><g fill='#3949ab'><rect x='270' y='40' width='60' height='30'/><rect x='270' y='70' width='26' height='200'><animate attributeName='height' values='200;200;160;120;80;80;200' keyTimes='0;0.15;0.35;0.55;0.75;0.95;1' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='304' y='70' width='26' height='200'><animate attributeName='height' values='200;200;160;120;80;80;200' keyTimes='0;0.15;0.35;0.55;0.75;0.95;1' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='17'><text x='360' y='110'>snip 1 ✂️</text><text x='360' y='150'>snip 2 ✂️</text><text x='360' y='190'>snip 3 ✂️</text><text x='60' y='140'>Too long…</text><text x='60' y='165'>then too short!</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Three secret snips — and the long trousers end up far too short.
fig.alt: Animated trousers getting shorter in three steps

check.q: Why did the trousers become too short?
options: Each person cut them without telling the others
check.why: Each family member shortened them secretly, so together they cut off far too much.

sections.h: Long and short, more and less
sections.md:
Let us measure with the story.

Suppose the trousers were too long by **one hand-span**. If **three** people each cut one hand-span, how much was cut? **3 hand-spans** — that is 2 hand-spans too many!

**Opposites:** long – short, tall – short, more – less, night – morning, before – after.

**Comparing:** long, long**er**, long**est**; short, short**er**, short**est**.

check.q: What is the opposite of long?
check.why: Short is the opposite of long, like the trousers that became short.

sections.md:
Everyone in the story wanted to help. That was kind! The problem was that nobody **told** anyone. In your class group work:

1. Decide who will do which job.
2. Say when you have finished.
3. Check before doing a job again.

**Did you know?** In a cricket team, fielders shout "Mine!" before catching the ball so two players don't crash into each other.

parts.md: In a Lucknow kitchen, Dadi put a pot of dal on the stove and went to pray. Mummy came in, tasted it, and thought, "No salt!" She added a spoon of salt and went out.
Then Papa came in. "No salt!" he said, and added a spoon. Then big sister Zoya did the same. Nobody said a word to anyone.

At lunch, everyone took a bite and made a funny face. Dal as salty as the sea! Dadi laughed so hard. "Next time," she said, "we put a little paper on the pot: SALT ADDED." And from that day, they always did.

summary: On My Blackboard I Can Draw is about drawing many things with chalk.
Drawing helps us imagine; we can rub out and draw again.
Pictures are made of shapes: circle, triangle, square, line.
In Make It Shorter, a man's new trousers are too long.
Each family member secretly cuts them shorter at night.
In the morning the trousers are far too short.
Lesson: in a team, tell others what you have done.
Opposites: long – short, more – less.
Comparing words: long, longer, longest.
practice: Name four things you can draw on a blackboard.
Which shapes make a house?
What was wrong with the new trousers?
Who cut the trousers? When?
Why were the trousers too short in the morning?
What lesson does the story teach?
Write the opposites: long, more, night.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-8-music-musici.title: I am the Music Man and The Mumbai Musicians
rd-school-c2-english.unit-8-music-musici.subtitle: Pia-pia-piano! — and four animal friends who sang a gang of robbers away

sections.md: Tap a spoon on a steel glass — *ting!* Clap your hands — *clap!* Beat a tiffin box — *dhum dhum!* Music is all around us. In this unit we sing a song about a music man and read a funny story about four animals who want to become musicians in Mumbai.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff8e1'/><rect x='60' y='120' width='200' height='90' fill='#3e2723'/><g fill='#fff'><rect x='70' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='95' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='120' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='145' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='170' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='195' y='170' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='220' y='170' width='20' height='40'/></g><circle cx='420' cy='160' r='50' fill='#ef6c00'/><circle cx='420' cy='160' r='30' fill='#ffe0b2'/><g font-size='34' fill='#6a1b9a' font-family='serif'><text x='150' y='90'>♪<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;20 -60' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='400' y='90'>♫<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-20 -60' dur='2.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0' dur='2.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text></g><text x='100' y='240' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='16'>piano</text><text x='395' y='240' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='16'>drum</text></svg>
fig.caption: A piano and a drum, with musical notes floating up.
fig.alt: A piano and a drum with floating music notes

check.q: Which of these can make music?
check.why: A drum makes a sound when you beat it, so it is a musical instrument.

sections.h: 📜 Song: I am the Music Man (traditional)
sections.md:
This is an old folk song for children. It is sung in a call-and-answer way: one group asks, another group answers. Here is how it goes:

> I am the music man,
> I come from down your way,
> And I can play.
> What can you play?
> I play the piano.
> Pia-pia-piano, piano, piano,
> Pia-pia-piano, pia-piano.

**What it means, line by line**
- *I am the music man* — the singer is a happy musician.
- *I come from down your way* — he lives near you, in your town.
- *And I can play* — he knows how to play music.
- *What can you play?* — the others ask him (the call).
- *I play the piano* — he answers (the response).
- *Pia-pia-piano…* — everyone pretends to play the piano with their fingers and sings the funny sound!

**Make new verses:** change *piano* to *big drum* (*boom-di-boom*), *flute* (*too-too-too*), *tabla* (*dha-dhin-dhin-dha*) and act each one out.

check.q: In the song, what does the music man play first?
check.why: He answers 'I play the piano' and everyone sings 'pia-pia-piano'.

sections.md:
| Instrument | How we play it | Sound |
|---|---|---|
| piano | press keys | plink-plonk |
| drum, dholak | beat | dhum-dhum |
| tabla | tap with fingers | dha-dhin |
| flute, bansuri | blow | too-too |
| guitar, sitar | pluck strings | twang |
| shehnai | blow | used at weddings |
| bells, manjira | shake / strike | ting-ting |

**Did you know?** The sitar, tabla and bansuri are Indian instruments enjoyed all over the world.

sections.h: Story: The Mumbai Musicians (scene by scene)
sections.md:
This story is based on an old German folk tale, *The Town Musicians of Bremen*, retold in your book with Indian names. Here it is in our own words.

**1. The donkey.** A donkey has worked hard for years carrying heavy loads. Now he is old and his master no longer wants him. The donkey has an idea: *I can still sing! I will go to Mumbai and become a musician.*

**2. The dog.** On the road he meets a tired old dog who can no longer guard his master's house. "Come with me," says the donkey. "You can bark the music!"

**3. The cat.** Next they find a sad cat who cannot catch mice any more. "Join our band!" they say. She can mew.

**4. The rooster.** Then they meet a rooster crowing loudly. He too joins the group. Now there are four musicians!

**5. A house in the forest.** Night comes. They see a light in a house. Through the window they spot a gang of **robbers** eating a big feast.

**6. The plan.** The dog climbs on the donkey's back, the cat on the dog, and the rooster on top of the cat. Then — all together — they *bray, bark, mew and crow* as loudly as they can!

**7. The robbers run.** The robbers think a terrible monster has come. They run away into the forest, screaming. The four friends eat the food and stay in the cosy house.

**8. Happy ending.** The robbers never come back. The four friends live happily together and sing every day — they never even reach Mumbai!

fig.alt: Four animals stacked on each other singing loudly at night

check.q: Why did the robbers run away?
check.why: The four animals made all their sounds together, and the robbers thought a monster had come.

sections.md:
- **Old does not mean useless.** Each animal was sent away, but together they did something clever.
- **Teamwork:** one small sound is not scary; four sounds together are very strong.
- **Kindness:** we should care for old animals and old people.

**Who said it?** Match the sound: donkey — *hee-haw* (bray); dog — *woof* (bark); cat — *meow* (mew); rooster — *cock-a-doodle-doo* (crow).

check.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
check.why: The four friends were weak alone, but together they scared away the robbers.

sections.md:
**Animal sounds (action words):** a donkey *brays*, a dog *barks*, a cat *mews*, a rooster *crows*.

**Opposites:** old – young, loud – soft, day – night, happy – sad.

**One and many:** robber – robbers, musician – musicians, donkey – donkeys.

parts.md: On a rainy Sunday in Chennai, the power went off and the TV went quiet. Meena was bored. Paati took out six steel glasses and filled them with different amounts of water.
She tapped them with a spoon. Each glass sang a different note! Meena's brother brought a tiffin box to beat like a drum. Dad whistled like a flute.
Soon the neighbours peeped in and clapped along. "We are the Chennai Musicians!" laughed Meena. When the power came back, nobody wanted the TV on.

summary: 'I am the Music Man' is a traditional call-and-answer song.
The music man plays the piano: pia-pia-piano!
We can make new verses with drum, flute and tabla.
Instruments are played by pressing, beating, blowing or plucking.
The Mumbai Musicians is based on 'The Town Musicians of Bremen'.
An old donkey, dog, cat and rooster set off to be musicians.
They find robbers in a house and stand on each other's backs.
Their loud song scares the robbers away.
Lesson: teamwork, and old friends still have value.
practice: Sing 'I am the Music Man' with a new instrument.
Name four musical instruments.
Why did the donkey leave his master?
Which animals joined the donkey?
What did the animals see in the house?
How did they scare the robbers?
Write the sounds: donkey, dog, cat, rooster.
Write the opposites of old and loud.

rd-school-c2-english.unit-9-granny-porri.title: Granny Granny Please Comb My Hair and The Magic Porridge Pot
rd-school-c2-english.unit-9-granny-porri.subtitle: A loving granny's comb — and a pot that would not stop cooking

sections.md: In the morning rush before school, someone helps you get ready. Maybe it is Amma, Papa, Didi — or Dadi and Nani, who oil your hair, comb it gently and tie a neat plait. This unit has a warm poem about a granny combing a child's hair and a funny magic story about a pot full of porridge.

check.q: What do we use to make our hair neat?
check.why: A comb untangles hair and makes it neat.

sections.h: The poem: Granny Granny Please Comb My Hair
sections.md:
This poem was written by **Grace Nichols**, a poet from Guyana in the Caribbean. Please read it in your Marigold book (link at the end). Here is what it says, part by part, in our own words.

**Part 1 — the child asks Granny.** The child loves it when Granny combs her hair. Granny is patient and gentle. She takes her time, so it never hurts.

**Part 2 — the child compares with Mummy.** When Mummy combs her hair, Mummy is in a hurry! She has so much work. She pulls and tugs quickly, and the child says *ouch*.

**Part 3 — Granny's lap.** With Granny, the child sits comfortably between Granny's knees. Granny talks to her softly, tells her she is lovely, and combs slowly. The child feels loved and calm.

**Part 4 — the big feeling.** The child wishes Granny would comb her hair every day, because Granny's love makes her feel special.

**What it means:** Grandparents often have time and patience to give children. Mummy loves the child too — she is just busy. The poem is about *gentle care*.

**Rhyming words to look for:** *hair – care*, *time – mine*.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fce4ec'/><rect x='180' y='170' width='240' height='100' rx='20' fill='#8d6e63'/><circle cx='300' cy='90' r='40' fill='#d7a77a'/><path d='M260 80 q40 -50 80 0' fill='#e0e0e0'/><rect x='250' y='130' width='100' height='80' rx='20' fill='#7e57c2'/><circle cx='300' cy='200' r='28' fill='#c68a5b'/><path d='M272 195 q28 -45 56 0' fill='#212121'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 25;0 0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='330' y='160' width='40' height='10' fill='#ffb300'/><g stroke='#ffb300' stroke-width='3'><line x1='335' y1='170' x2='335' y2='180'/><line x1='345' y1='170' x2='345' y2='180'/><line x1='355' y1='170' x2='355' y2='180'/><line x1='365' y1='170' x2='365' y2='180'/></g></g><text x='300' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='16'>slow, gentle strokes</text></svg>
fig.caption: Granny gently combs the child's hair as the child sits in front of her.
fig.alt: A grandmother combing a child's hair

check.q: Why does the child like Granny combing her hair?
check.why: Granny takes her time and combs gently, so it does not hurt.

sections.h: Story: The Magic Porridge Pot (scene by scene)
sections.md:
This is an old folk tale collected by the **Brothers Grimm** in Germany about 200 years ago. Here it is in our own words.

**1. A hungry girl.** A poor little girl lives with her mother. One day there is nothing to eat. The girl goes into the forest to look for berries.

**2. The old woman.** In the forest she meets a kind old woman who gives her a little **pot**. "When you are hungry, say *Cook, little pot, cook!* and it will make sweet porridge. When you have enough, say *Stop, little pot, stop!*"

**3. Never hungry again.** The girl takes the pot home. It works! Every day she and her mother eat good porridge.

**4. Mother forgets.** One day the girl goes out. The mother is hungry and says, "Cook, little pot, cook!" The pot cooks. She eats her fill — but she has **forgotten the magic words** to stop it!

**5. Porridge everywhere!** The pot cooks and cooks. Porridge fills the pot, spills over the stove, the kitchen, the house, and flows out into the street. Soon the whole town is covered with porridge! People have to eat their way through it.

**6. The girl returns.** At last the girl comes home and sees the mess. She says, "Stop, little pot, stop!" — and the pot stops at once.

**7. The end.** Anyone who wanted to come back into the town had to eat their way in!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#e3f2fd'/><rect y='250' width='600' height='50' fill='#bcaaa4'/><path d='M230 170 h140 l-15 80 h-110z' fill='#37474f'/><rect x='220' y='160' width='160' height='16' rx='6' fill='#455a64'/><path d='M230 165 q70 -40 140 0 v10 h-140z' fill='#fff3c4'><animate attributeName='d' values='M230 165 q70 -40 140 0 v10 h-140z;M140 250 q160 -160 320 0 v10 h-320z;M30 270 q270 -200 540 0 v10 h-540z' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><text x='300' y='40' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='20'>Cook, little pot, cook!</text></svg>
fig.caption: The magic pot keeps cooking until porridge covers the whole street.
fig.alt: A pot overflowing with porridge that spreads across the floor

check.q: Why did the porridge fill the whole town?
options: The mother forgot the words to stop the pot
check.why: The mother did not know 'Stop, little pot, stop!', so the pot kept cooking.

sections.md:
| Character | What they are like |
|---|---|
| the little girl | kind, careful, remembers the magic words |
| the mother | loving but forgetful |
| the old woman | kind and magical |

**Lessons**
- Listen carefully and remember instructions.
- Too much of even a good thing can be a problem.
- Kindness (the old woman's gift) can change a life.

check.q: Who knew the words to stop the pot?
check.why: The old woman told the girl, and the girl stopped the pot when she came home.

sections.md:
**Kitchen words:** pot, pan, spoon, stove, bowl, porridge (a soft food made by boiling oats or grains in milk or water, like our *daliya* or *kheer*).

**Hair words:** comb, plait, ribbon, oil, tangle.

**Opposites:** start – stop, full – empty, fast – slow, hungry – full, poor – rich.

**Fill in:** Granny combs ______ (slowly). Mummy combs ______ (quickly).

parts.md: Every summer holiday Riya went to Nani's house in Jaipur. Each morning Nani oiled her hair and made two plaits with red ribbons, humming an old song.
When school started, Riya had to comb her own hair. It was tangled and it hurt! She remembered Nani's slow, patient strokes.
On a video call, Nani showed her: start at the ends, go gently, then reach the top. Now Riya combs her little brother's hair the same way — slowly, with love.

summary: The poem is by Grace Nichols; read it in your Marigold book.
The child loves Granny combing her hair because Granny is gentle and patient.
Mummy is busy and combs in a hurry, which hurts.
The poem is about love and care from grandparents.
The Magic Porridge Pot is an old Grimm folk tale.
An old woman gives a poor girl a pot that cooks on command.
'Cook, little pot, cook!' starts it; 'Stop, little pot, stop!' stops it.
The mother forgets the stop words and porridge fills the town.
The girl comes home and stops the pot.
practice: Who combs the child's hair gently?
Why does Mummy comb in a hurry?
Who gave the girl the pot?
What were the magic words to start the pot?
What happened when the mother forgot the words?
How did the porridge stop?
Write the opposites of fast and full.
Who combs your hair? Write two lines.

rd-school-c2-hindi.matra-dohrao.title: मात्राएँ दोहराएँ और बारहखड़ी
rd-school-c2-hindi.matra-dohrao.subtitle: क + आ = का! मात्राओं से अक्षर कैसे बदलते हैं

sections.md:
सोचो, **क** अकेला खड़ा है। उसके पास **आ** आता है — और वह बन जाता है **का**! जैसे *काका*, *कान*।

हिंदी में **स्वर** (अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ) जब किसी **व्यंजन** (क, ख, ग…) के साथ जुड़ते हैं, तो वे अपना पूरा रूप नहीं लिखते। वे एक छोटा-सा चिह्न बन जाते हैं। इसी चिह्न को **मात्रा** कहते हैं।

- **अ** की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती। क में पहले से अ छिपा है: क = क् + अ।
- बाकी हर स्वर की अपनी मात्रा है।

check.q: किस स्वर की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती?
check.why: अ हर व्यंजन में पहले से छिपा रहता है, इसलिए उसकी अलग मात्रा नहीं होती।

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff3e0'/><text x='150' y='150' font-size='110' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1565c0'>क</text><text x='270' y='140' font-size='60' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><text x='370' y='150' font-size='110' text-anchor='middle' fill='#e65100'>ा<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1;0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='500' y='150' font-size='110' text-anchor='middle' fill='#2e7d32'>का<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;1;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='300' y='230' font-size='26' text-anchor='middle'>व्यंजन + मात्रा = नया अक्षर</text></svg>
fig.caption: क में आ की मात्रा (ा) जुड़ते ही का बन जाता है।
fig.alt: क और आ की मात्रा मिलकर का बनाते हुए

check.q: 'फूल' में कौन-सी मात्रा है?
check.why: फूल में फ के नीचे बड़े ऊ की मात्रा (ू) लगी है।

sections.md:
किसी एक व्यंजन के साथ सारी मात्राएँ लगाकर पढ़ने को **बारहखड़ी** कहते हैं। ‘बारह’ इसलिए क्योंकि पुराने समय में बारह रूप गाए जाते थे।

**क की बारहखड़ी:** क का कि की कु कू के कै को कौ कं कः

**म की बारहखड़ी:** म मा मि मी मु मू मे मै मो मौ मं मः

**ल की बारहखड़ी:** ल ला लि ली लु लू ले लै लो लौ लं लः

**र के साथ ध्यान दो:** र + उ = **रु** (रुपया), र + ऊ = **रू** (रूप)। यहाँ मात्रा नीचे नहीं, र के बगल में लगती है!

**खेल:** ताली बजाकर गाओ — *क, का, कि, की…* फिर अपने नाम के पहले अक्षर की बारहखड़ी बनाओ।

check.q: 'र' में 'उ' की मात्रा लगाने पर क्या बनता है?
check.why: र + उ = रु, जैसे रुपया; इसमें मात्रा र के बगल में लगती है।

sections.md:
मात्रा बदली तो **अर्थ** बदल गया! देखो:

| छोटी मात्रा | बड़ी मात्रा |
|---|---|
| दिन (day) | दीन (गरीब) |
| कुल (पूरा) | कूल (किनारा) |
| सुर (संगीत) | सूर (सूरज / सूरदास) |
| मेला | मैला (गंदा) |
| चल | चाल |

इसलिए बोलते समय ध्यान से सुनो — छोटी मात्रा जल्दी, बड़ी मात्रा खींचकर बोली जाती है।

check.q: इनमें से किस शब्द में 'ऐ' की मात्रा है?
check.why: बैल में ब के ऊपर दो तिरछी रेखाएँ (ै) हैं, यही ऐ की मात्रा है।

sections.md:
मात्राओं को याद करने का एक गीत (हमारा अपना):

> आ की मात्रा डंडा सीधा,
> इ की टोपी आगे बैठी।
> ई की टोपी पीछे जाए,
> उ ऊ नीचे पैर हिलाए।
> ए ऐ ऊपर झंडा फहराए,
> ओ औ डंडे संग मुस्काए!

हर पंक्ति बताती है कि मात्रा कहाँ लगती है — आगे, पीछे, ऊपर या नीचे।

parts.md: मीना के स्कूल में मात्रा-मेला लगा। हर बच्चे को एक मात्रा का कार्ड मिला। मीना को मिला ‘ा’।
मीना जिस भी अक्षर के पास खड़ी होती, नया शब्द बन जाता — म के पास ‘मा’, न के पास ‘ना’। सब बच्चे हँसते-हँसते शब्द बनाने लगे: ‘नाना’, ‘राजा’!
आखिर में मैडम बोलीं, “अकेला अक्षर चुप रहता है, मात्रा मिलते ही बोल उठता है।” मीना ने उस दिन बारह नए शब्द बनाए।

summary: स्वर का छोटा चिह्न जो व्यंजन के साथ लगता है, मात्रा कहलाता है।
अ की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती।
छोटी इ अक्षर से पहले लगती है, बड़ी ई बाद में।
एक व्यंजन के साथ सब मात्राएँ लगाना बारहखड़ी है।
र के साथ उ और ऊ की मात्रा बगल में लगती है: रु, रू।
मात्रा बदलने से अर्थ बदल जाता है: दिन–दीन।
चंद्रबिंदु (ँ) नाक से बोला जाता है।
practice: ग की बारहखड़ी लिखो।
ई की मात्रा वाले चार शब्द लिखो।
दिन और दीन में क्या अंतर है?
र + ऊ से क्या बनेगा? एक शब्द लिखो।
इन शब्दों में मात्रा पहचानो: मोर, बैल, झूला।
अपने नाम में कौन-कौन सी मात्राएँ हैं?
अं की मात्रा वाले तीन शब्द लिखो।

rd-school-c2-hindi.sangya.title: संज्ञा: नाम वाले शब्द
rd-school-c2-hindi.sangya.subtitle: हर चीज़ का एक नाम है — और हर नाम एक संज्ञा है!

sections.md:
सुबह उठकर तुम क्या देखते हो? **माँ**, **पापा**, **दूध** का गिलास, खिड़की से **सूरज**, आँगन में **तोता**। ज़रा सोचो, अगर इन चीज़ों के नाम न होते तो हम बात कैसे करते? “वो… वो… वो चीज़ दो!” — कितना मुश्किल होता!

**किसी व्यक्ति, जानवर, वस्तु, स्थान या भाव के नाम को संज्ञा कहते हैं।**

उदाहरण: राम, बिल्ली, किताब, दिल्ली, खुशी।

check.q: इनमें से संज्ञा कौन-सा शब्द है?
check.why: किताब एक वस्तु का नाम है, इसलिए वह संज्ञा है।

sections.md:
नाम वाले शब्द कई तरह के होते हैं। इन्हें पाँच घरों में रखो:

| किसका नाम? | उदाहरण |
|---|---|
| 👧 **व्यक्ति** | मीना, अमर, दादी, डॉक्टर, शिक्षक |
| 🐘 **जानवर / पक्षी** | हाथी, गाय, मोर, कुत्ता, मछली |
| 🎒 **वस्तु** | बस्ता, पेंसिल, गेंद, थाली, पंखा |
| 🏙️ **स्थान** | मुंबई, स्कूल, बाज़ार, गाँव, नदी |
| 😊 **भाव** (जो दिखता नहीं, महसूस होता है) | खुशी, प्यार, डर, गुस्सा, दोस्ती |

भाव वाले नाम छुए नहीं जा सकते, पर हम उन्हें महसूस करते हैं — जैसे जन्मदिन पर **खुशी**!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#e8f5e9'/><g font-family='sans-serif' text-anchor='middle'><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='20' y='80' width='100' height='100' rx='14' fill='#ffcc80'/><text x='70' y='140' font-size='40'>👧</text><text x='70' y='205' font-size='18'>व्यक्ति</text></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='2s' begin='.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='135' y='80' width='100' height='100' rx='14' fill='#a5d6a7'/><text x='185' y='140' font-size='40'>🐘</text><text x='185' y='205' font-size='18'>जानवर</text></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='2s' begin='.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='250' y='80' width='100' height='100' rx='14' fill='#90caf9'/><text x='300' y='140' font-size='40'>🎒</text><text x='300' y='205' font-size='18'>वस्तु</text></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='2s' begin='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='365' y='80' width='100' height='100' rx='14' fill='#ce93d8'/><text x='415' y='140' font-size='40'>🏙️</text><text x='415' y='205' font-size='18'>स्थान</text></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -8;0 0' dur='2s' begin='1.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='480' y='80' width='100' height='100' rx='14' fill='#fff59d'/><text x='530' y='140' font-size='40'>😊</text><text x='530' y='205' font-size='18'>भाव</text></g><text x='300' y='45' font-size='24'>संज्ञा के पाँच घर</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: व्यक्ति, जानवर, वस्तु, स्थान और भाव — सबके नाम संज्ञा हैं।
fig.alt: संज्ञा के पाँच प्रकार के चित्र

check.q: 'खुशी' किस घर में जाएगी?
check.why: खुशी दिखती नहीं, महसूस होती है, इसलिए वह भाव का नाम है।

sections.md:
कुछ नाम **किसी एक खास** व्यक्ति, जगह या चीज़ के होते हैं, कुछ नाम **पूरी जाति** के।

| आम नाम (सबके लिए) | खास नाम (सिर्फ़ एक का) |
|---|---|
| लड़की | मीना |
| शहर | जयपुर |
| नदी | गंगा |
| पर्वत | हिमालय |
| त्योहार | दिवाली |
| कुत्ता | मोती (तुम्हारे कुत्ते का नाम) |

बड़ी कक्षाओं में तुम पढ़ोगे कि खास नाम को **व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा** और आम नाम को **जातिवाचक संज्ञा** कहते हैं, और भाव वाले नाम को **भाववाचक संज्ञा**।

check.q: 'गंगा' कैसा नाम है?
check.why: गंगा एक खास नदी का नाम है, इसलिए यह खास नाम है।

sections.md:
हर वाक्य में संज्ञा छिपी रहती है। उसे ढूँढो:

1. **मीना** **बाज़ार** गई। (व्यक्ति, स्थान)
2. **तोता** **अमरूद** खाता है। (पक्षी, वस्तु)
3. **दादी** ने **कहानी** सुनाई। (व्यक्ति, वस्तु)
4. **अमर** को **डर** लगा। (व्यक्ति, भाव)
5. **बच्चे** **पार्क** में **गेंद** से खेले। (व्यक्ति, स्थान, वस्तु)

**ध्यान दो:** *खाता है, गई, खेले* — ये काम बताने वाले शब्द हैं, संज्ञा नहीं। *सुंदर, लाल, बड़ा* — ये कैसा है बताते हैं, ये भी संज्ञा नहीं।

**सवाल पूछो:** “**कौन?**” या “**क्या?**” — जिसका उत्तर मिले, वही अक्सर संज्ञा होता है।

check.q: 'मोर नाच रहा है।' इस वाक्य में संज्ञा कौन-सी है?
check.why: मोर एक पक्षी का नाम है; 'नाच रहा है' काम बताता है।

sections.md:
यह खेल दोस्तों के साथ खेलो! एक अक्षर चुनो, जैसे **म**। अब जल्दी-जल्दी लिखो:

| नाम | शहर | चीज़ | जानवर |
|---|---|---|---|
| मीना | मुंबई | मेज़ | मोर |
| (क) कबीर | कोलकाता | कलम | कबूतर |
| (ग) गीता | गुवाहाटी | गिलास | गाय |

जिसने सबसे पहले लिखा, उसे अंक मिलेंगे। तुमने देखा? ये सारे शब्द **संज्ञा** हैं!

संज्ञा एक भी हो सकती है और अनेक भी:
- केला → केले
- लड़का → लड़के
- किताब → किताबें
- चिड़िया → चिड़ियाँ
- गाय → गायें

**क्या तुम जानते हो?** ‘संज्ञा’ शब्द का अर्थ ही है — *नाम* या *पहचान*।

parts.md: एक राजा को अजीब बीमारी हुई — वह सब चीज़ों के नाम भूल गया! उसने कहा, “मुझे वो… गोल-गोल… मीठी… चीज़ दो!” मंत्री ने गेंद ला दी।
राजा बोला, “नहीं! खाने वाली!” रसोइया लड्डू लाया। पूरा महल परेशान। तब एक छोटी लड़की आई और हर चीज़ पर उसके नाम की पर्ची चिपका दी — ‘थाली’, ‘गिलास’, ‘कुर्सी’, ‘लड्डू’।
राजा पर्चियाँ पढ़ते-पढ़ते सारे नाम फिर से सीख गया। उसने खुश होकर कहा, “नाम न हों तो बात ही न हो!” उस दिन से राज्य में ‘संज्ञा दिवस’ मनाया जाने लगा।

summary: किसी व्यक्ति, जानवर, वस्तु, स्थान या भाव के नाम को संज्ञा कहते हैं।
व्यक्ति: मीना, दादी; जानवर: गाय, मोर।
वस्तु: पेंसिल, गेंद; स्थान: दिल्ली, स्कूल।
भाव: खुशी, डर, प्यार — ये महसूस होते हैं।
खास नाम एक का होता है (गंगा), आम नाम सबका (नदी)।
‘कौन?’ या ‘क्या?’ पूछकर संज्ञा पहचानो।
काम बताने वाले और ‘कैसा’ बताने वाले शब्द संज्ञा नहीं हैं।
संज्ञा एक और अनेक हो सकती है: केला – केले।
practice: संज्ञा किसे कहते हैं?
पाँच जानवरों के नाम लिखो।
अपनी कक्षा की पाँच वस्तुओं के नाम लिखो।
दो खास नाम और दो आम नाम लिखो।
वाक्य में संज्ञा पर गोला लगाओ: 'राधा ने आम खाया।'
भाव वाले तीन नाम लिखो।
अनेक बनाओ: लड़का, किताब, चिड़िया।

rd-school-c2-hindi.sanyukt-akshar.title: संयुक्त अक्षर और र के रूप
rd-school-c2-hindi.sanyukt-akshar.subtitle: जब दो अक्षर हाथ पकड़ लेते हैं — क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र और र के अनोखे रूप

sections.md:
‘**पक्का**’ बोलो। सुनो — बीच में *क्* की आधी आवाज़ और फिर *का*। जब कोई व्यंजन **आधा** बोला जाता है और अगले व्यंजन से जुड़ जाता है, तो उसे **संयुक्त अक्षर** (या संयुक्त व्यंजन) कहते हैं।

आधा अक्षर बनाने के लिए अक्सर उसका **खड़ा डंडा हटा** देते हैं:
- **क** → क्  (प्यार, पक्का)
- **स** → स्  (स्कूल, नमस्ते)
- **प** → प्  (प्यास, प्याला)
- **न** → न्  (हिन्दी, अन्न)
- **म** → म्  (अम्मा, गुम्मा)

जिन अक्षरों में डंडा नहीं होता (जैसे ट, ड, द), उनके नीचे **हलंत (्)** लगाते हैं: *ट्*, *द्*।

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#e1f5fe'/><g font-size='90' text-anchor='middle'><text x='110' y='140' fill='#1565c0'>स्<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;120 0;120 0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='330' y='140' fill='#c62828'>क</text><text x='520' y='140' fill='#2e7d32'>स्क<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text></g><text x='300' y='215' font-size='24' text-anchor='middle'>स् + क = स्क (स्कूल)</text></svg>
fig.caption: आधा स् आकर क से जुड़ता है और स्क बनता है, जैसे स्कूल में।
fig.alt: आधा स और क मिलकर स्क बनाते हुए

check.q: 'प्यार' में कौन-सा अक्षर आधा है?
check.why: प्यार में प आधा (प्) है और य से जुड़ा है।

sections.md:
हिंदी वर्णमाला के अंत में चार संयुक्त अक्षर आते हैं। ये इतने मिल गए हैं कि नया रूप बन गया:

| संयुक्त अक्षर | किससे बना | शब्द |
|---|---|---|
| **क्ष** | क् + ष | क्षमा, कक्षा, रक्षा, पक्षी |
| **त्र** | त् + र | त्रिशूल, पत्र, मित्र, छात्र |
| **ज्ञ** | ज् + ञ | ज्ञान, विज्ञान, यज्ञ |
| **श्र** | श् + र | श्रम, श्रमिक, आश्रम, श्री |

**बोलने का तरीका:** *ज्ञ* को आमतौर पर ‘ग्य’ जैसा बोला जाता है (ज्ञान = ग्यान)।

check.q: 'त्र' किन दो अक्षरों से मिलकर बना है?
check.why: आधा त और र मिलकर त्र बनाते हैं, जैसे मित्र में।

sections.h: र के रूप: पहला — ऊपर का ‘रेफ़’ (र्)
sections.md:
र बड़ा शरारती अक्षर है! जब **र आधा** होता है और अगले अक्षर से पहले बोला जाता है, तो वह अगले अक्षर के **सिर पर** छोटी-सी टोपी बनकर बैठ जाता है। इसे **रेफ़** कहते हैं।

- क + र् + म = **कर्म**
- ध + र् + म = **धर्म**
- प + र् + व = **पर्व**
- गर्मी, सूर्य, चर्खा, दर्द, कुर्सी, मुर्गा

**पहचान:** बोलकर देखो — *कुर्-सी*। ‘र्’ की आवाज़ पहले आती है, पर टोपी **अगले** अक्षर (स) पर लगती है।

check.q: 'कुर्सी' में रेफ़ (र्) किस अक्षर के ऊपर लगा है?
check.why: र् की आवाज़ 'कु' के बाद आती है, इसलिए उसकी टोपी अगले अक्षर 'सी' पर लगती है।

sections.h: र के रूप: दूसरा और तीसरा — नीचे वाला र
sections.md:
जब **पूरा र** किसी आधे अक्षर के **बाद** आता है, तो र नीचे की ओर तिरछी लकीर बन जाता है।

**(क) डंडे वाले अक्षरों में तिरछी लकीर (्र)**
- प + र = **प्र** — प्रेम, प्रकाश, प्रणाम
- क + र = **क्र** — क्रम, चक्र
- ग + र = **ग्र** — ग्रह, ग्राम
- ब + र = **ब्र** — ब्रश

**(ख) बिना डंडे वाले अक्षरों में नीचे उल्टा ‘^’ (्र)**
- ट + र = **ट्र** — ट्रक, ट्रेन
- ड + र = **ड्र** — ड्रम, ड्रामा

**(ग) र पर उ / ऊ की मात्रा** — र के बगल में: **रु** (रुपया, गुरु), **रू** (रूप, रूमाल)। र में ऋ की मात्रा नहीं लगती।

| रूप | कहाँ | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| र् (रेफ़) | ऊपर | कर्म, सूर्य |
| ्र (तिरछा) | नीचे, डंडे वाले अक्षर | प्रकाश, क्रम |
| ्र (^) | नीचे, बिना डंडे वाले | ट्रक, ड्रम |
| ृ (ऋ मात्रा) | नीचे | कृपा, गृह (यह र नहीं, ऋ है!) |
