fig.caption: A wriggling earthworm, a bird, a cow and an ant — 0, 2, 4 and 6 legs.
fig.alt: Four animals in a row with different numbers of legs.

check.q: How many legs does a spider have?
check.why: Spiders have eight legs, which is one way we know they are not insects.

sections.h: Feathers, fur, scales – ears and tails
sections.md:
Poonam also notices what covers each animal's body.

| Body covering | Animals |
|---|---|
| **Feathers** | crow, sparrow, parrot, duck, peacock |
| **Hair or fur** | dog, cat, squirrel, cow, goat |
| **Scales** | fish, snake, lizard |
| **Smooth, wet skin** | frog, earthworm |
| **Hard shell** | snail, tortoise |

**Ears you can see.** Look at a cow, dog or goat – their ears stick out clearly. Now look at a crow or a lizard – you cannot see ear flaps, though they *can* hear through small openings on the sides of the head.

**Tails.** Many animals have tails, used in different ways: a cow flicks away flies, a squirrel balances while jumping, a fish steers in water, a dog wags to show it is happy, and a bird uses its tail feathers to turn in the air.

**Activity – Animal detective card:** For any animal, fill in: name, home, legs, body covering, ears visible (yes/no), tail (yes/no), food.

check.q: Which animal has feathers?
check.why: Only birds have feathers, and the parrot is a bird.

sections.h: What animals eat, and being kind
sections.md:
Animals eat different foods:

- **Plants and grass:** cow, goat, rabbit, deer.
- **Other animals:** lion, frog (eats insects), lizard.
- **Both:** crow, dog, bear — and people!

Animals feel hunger, thirst, pain and fear, just like us. Poonam's day out teaches her to be gentle. In summer you can keep a bowl of water on your balcony for birds. Never throw stones at dogs or pull a cat's tail. Watch animals quietly — they will show you much more when they are not afraid.

> Did you know? Many Indian homes put out a little grain for sparrows and pigeons every morning — a tiny act of care.
keyTerms: Observe — look carefully and notice details
Nest — a home birds build
Burrow — a hole in the ground where an animal lives

check.q: Which is a kind thing to do for birds in summer?
options: Keep a bowl of water out
check.why: Birds get very thirsty in hot weather, so a bowl of clean water helps them.

story.title: The Lizard Who Lived Behind the Calendar

parts.md: Every evening, when the tube light came on, Meenu saw a little lizard creep out from behind the calendar on the kitchen wall. She squealed the first time. 'Ma! A lizard!' Her mother only smiled. 'Watch what it does,' she said. Meenu watched. The lizard stayed very still, like a stick. A mosquito buzzed close to the light. Snap! The mosquito was gone.

After that, Meenu named the lizard Chhipkali Chachi. She counted: one mosquito, two flies, a moth. 'Chachi eats the insects that bite us,' she told her brother proudly. From then on, nobody in the house chased the lizard. Meenu had learnt the secret of this chapter: when you look closely, even a small creature on the wall has a job, a home and a life of its own.

summary: Animals live all around us — in trees, water, soil, holes and our homes.
On her walk Poonam meets dogs, cats, squirrels, birds, cows, fish, frogs, ants and a lizard.
Birds live in nests; rats and rabbits in burrows; ants in anthills.
Frogs live both in water and on land.
Animals move by flying, walking, hopping, crawling, swimming or slithering.
Some animals move in many ways, like the duck.
Animals come in many sizes and have different numbers of legs.
Insects have 6 legs; spiders have 8.
Bodies are covered with feathers, fur, scales or smooth skin.
Some animals have ears we can see; birds and lizards do not.
Some animals eat plants, some eat other animals, some eat both.
Animals feel pain and fear, so we must be kind to them.

glossary.d: The place where an animal naturally lives
A small animal with six legs
Small hard plates covering fish and snakes
To eat grass in a field

practice: Name three animals that live on trees.
Name two animals that live in holes in the ground.
Write the ways in which a duck can move.
Make a table of five animals and the number of legs each has.
Name two animals with feathers, two with fur and two with scales.
Name two animals whose ears you can see and two whose ears you cannot.
How do different animals use their tails?
Which animals did you see on your way to school today?
Why should we not tease animals?
Name an animal that eats only plants and one that eats other animals.

rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch2-the-plant-fairy.title: The Plant Fairy
rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch2-the-plant-fairy.subtitle: Leaves, flowers, bark and roots — how to really look at a plant

sections.h: If a fairy turned you into a plant…
sections.md:
Imagine a fairy waves her wand and says, 'Today you will be a plant!' Which plant would you choose? A tall neem tree giving shade to the whole street? A creeper climbing the school wall? A tulsi plant in a pot? A cactus in the desert?

The chapter opens with exactly this game. A plant fairy appears and asks children to *become* plants – to stand tall like a tree, spread out like a creeper, or curl around a pole like a climber. Each child must then tell the class: *Where do I grow? How tall am I? What colour are my flowers? Who visits me?*

This chapter asks you to look at plants as closely as you looked at animals in Chapter 1. Plants are all around us — in parks, on roadsides, in pots on balconies, even growing out of cracks in old walls. Though they cannot walk or talk, they are alive. They grow, they need water and sunlight, and they give us food, shade, air and beauty.

> Did you know? A single big banyan tree can spread so wide that hundreds of people can sit in its shade.

check.q: Which of these is true about plants?
check.why: Plants are living things: they grow and need water, air and sunlight.

sections.md:
Plants come in different kinds:

- **Trees** are tall and strong with a thick, woody trunk — mango, neem, peepal, banyan.
- **Shrubs (bushes)** are smaller, with many woody stems near the ground — rose, hibiscus, tulsi.
- **Herbs** are small and soft — grass, mint, coriander.
- **Creepers** spread along the ground — pumpkin, watermelon.
- **Climbers** need support to climb — money plant, grapevine, bottle gourd on a trellis.

Some plants grow in water, like the lotus. Some grow in very dry places, like the cactus, which stores water in its thick stem.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#f1f8e9'/><rect y='260' width='600' height='60' fill='#a1887f'/><rect x='70' y='120' width='24' height='140' fill='#5d4037'/><circle cx='82' cy='105' r='60' fill='#388e3c'><animate attributeName='r' values='58;62;58' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><text x='50' y='300' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Tree</text><g transform='translate(230,260)'><circle cx='0' cy='-30' r='30' fill='#66bb6a'/><circle cx='-20' cy='-15' r='18' fill='#81c784'/><circle cx='20' cy='-15' r='18' fill='#81c784'/><circle cx='5' cy='-45' r='6' fill='#e53935'/><text x='-25' y='40' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Shrub</text></g><g transform='translate(350,260)'><path d='M-10 0 q-5 -20 -15 -30 M0 0 v-35 M10 0 q5 -20 15 -30' stroke='#7cb342' stroke-width='4' fill='none'/><text x='-20' y='40' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Herb</text></g><g transform='translate(480,260)'><rect x='30' y='-200' width='6' height='200' fill='#8d6e63'/><path d='M33 0 C0 -40 60 -80 33 -120 S0 -180 33 -200' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='5' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='300' stroke-dashoffset='300'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='300;0;0' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><text x='-10' y='40' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Climber</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Tree, shrub, herb and a climber growing up its stick.
fig.alt: Four kinds of plants side by side; the climber's stem draws itself up a pole.

check.q: A money plant climbing up a wall is a…
check.why: Climbers have weak stems and need support like a wall or stick to grow upward.

sections.md:
Walk around your school and look carefully. Plants grow almost everywhere:

- **On old walls and roofs** – a tiny peepal sapling poking out of a crack, green moss on damp bricks.
- **On other trees** – some small plants grow on the branches of big trees.
- **Between paving stones** – grass and little weeds with yellow flowers.
- **In water** – lotus and water hyacinth in ponds.
- **In the desert** – cactus and thorny bushes.

How did they get there? Seeds travel! Birds drop them, wind blows them, water carries them. A seed that lands in a crack with a little soil and rainwater can start to grow.

**Activity:** Make a list of five plants you see on your way to school. Write where each was growing.

**Local names:** Many plants have different names in different languages. Neem is *nimba* in Sanskrit and *vepa* in Telugu; tulsi is also called *holy basil*. Ask your grandparents the names they use.

check.q: How does a peepal plant end up growing on a wall?
options: A seed was dropped by a bird or blown by wind
check.why: Seeds are carried by birds, wind and water, and can sprout wherever they find a little soil and water.

sections.md:
Pick up a few fallen leaves and compare them. You will find that:

- Leaves have **different shapes** — the peepal leaf is heart-shaped with a long tip, the neem leaf is narrow with jagged edges, the banana leaf is huge.
- Leaves have **different colours** — dark green, light green, even red or yellow in some plants.
- Leaves have **edges** that may be smooth, toothed (like a saw) or wavy.
- Leaves have **lines called veins** that carry water.

**Leaf rubbing:** Put a leaf under thin paper and gently rub a crayon over it. The veins appear like magic!

**Leaf art:** Arrange dried leaves to make an animal – a peacock with neem leaves as feathers, a fish from a peepal leaf.

Flowers also differ in colour, smell and size — marigold, jasmine, hibiscus, lotus. Some flowers smell strongly to call bees and butterflies.

The **bark** is the outer skin of a tree trunk. Touch different trees: some barks are smooth, some rough and cracked. Bark protects the tree, like our skin protects us. **Bark rubbing** works just like leaf rubbing!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff8e1'/><g transform='translate(160,150)'><path d='M0 110 C-90 40 -80 -60 0 -110 C80 -60 90 40 0 110Z' fill='#7cb342'/><path d='M0 110 V-120' stroke='#33691e' stroke-width='4'/><g stroke='#33691e' stroke-width='2' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='80' stroke-dashoffset='80'><path d='M0 60 L-45 20 M0 60 L45 20 M0 10 L-50 -30 M0 10 L50 -30 M0 -40 L-35 -75 M0 -40 L35 -75'/><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='80;0;0' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='-40' y='140' font-size='16'>Leaf veins</text></g><g transform='translate(430,150)'><g><circle r='14' fill='#fdd835'/><g fill='#e53935'><ellipse cy='-38' rx='18' ry='26'/><ellipse cy='38' rx='18' ry='26'/><ellipse cx='-38' rx='26' ry='18'/><ellipse cx='38' rx='26' ry='18'/></g><circle r='14' fill='#fdd835'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0' to='360' dur='12s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='-30' y='100' font-size='16'>Flower</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Veins appear across a leaf; a hibiscus-style flower turns slowly.
fig.alt: A leaf with veins drawing in and a red five-petal flower.

check.q: What is the outer covering of a tree trunk called?
check.why: Bark is the tough outer layer that protects the trunk.

sections.md:
Choose one tree near your home or school and make it your **tree friend**. Visit it often and notice:

- Is it tall or short? Can you hug its trunk, or do you need friends to join hands around it?
- Who lives on it? Birds, squirrels, ants, caterpillars?
- Does it have flowers or fruits? In which month?
- How does it change in summer, monsoon and winter?

Draw your tree in a notebook every month. You will be amazed at how it changes. Many trees shed leaves in spring and grow fresh light-green ones soon after.

> Did you know? Plants grow toward light. Keep a pot near a window and watch the stem bend toward the sunshine over a week.

check.q: Why does a plant near a window bend toward it?
check.why: Plants need sunlight to make food, so their stems grow toward the light.

sections.md:
Plants give us so much:

| Plants give us | Examples |
|---|---|
| Food | Rice, wheat, fruits, vegetables, dal |
| Shade | Neem, banyan, peepal trees |
| Wood | Furniture, doors |
| Medicine | Tulsi, neem, haldi plant |
| Homes for animals | Nests, beehives |
| Clean air | All green plants |

So we must care for plants: water them, do not pluck leaves and flowers for no reason, do not carve names on bark, and plant a sapling on your birthday!
keyTerms: Bark — outer skin of a trunk
Vein — thin line in a leaf that carries water
Climber — plant that climbs with support
Creeper — plant that spreads on the ground

check.q: Which is a good way to care for a tree?
check.why: Water helps a tree survive the hot summer, while carving and breaking hurt it.

parts.md: Gudiya's grandfather planted a neem sapling the day she was born. 'You two will grow together,' he said. Every year on her birthday Gudiya stood beside the neem for a photo. At one she was taller than it. At four, it was taller than her. At eight, she couldn't see its top without tipping her head back. Sparrows nested in it, a squirrel raced up its trunk, and in summer the whole family sat under it in the afternoons.

One night Gudiya dreamt a fairy turned her into the neem. She felt her toes become roots drinking from the soil. She felt the sun warm her leaves. She felt the sparrows' tiny feet tickling her branches. When she woke, she ran outside and hugged the trunk. 'Thank you for the shade,' she whispered, and poured a bucket of water at its roots.

summary: The chapter begins with a plant fairy game: pretend to be a plant and describe yourself.
Plants are living things that grow and need water, air and sunlight.
Trees have thick woody trunks; shrubs are bushy; herbs are small and soft.
Climbers need support; creepers spread on the ground.
Plants grow in surprising places – walls, water, deserts – because seeds travel.
Leaves differ in shape, size, colour and edges.
Leaves have veins that carry water; leaf and bark rubbings show patterns.
Bark is the protective outer skin of a tree.
Flowers differ in colour, smell and size.
Plants grow toward light.
Plants give food, shade, wood, medicine and homes for animals.
We should care for plants and plant more trees.
practice: Name two trees, two shrubs and two climbers.
How is a climber different from a creeper?
Name a plant that grows in water and one that grows in a desert.
How can a plant grow on an old wall?
Do a leaf rubbing and paste it in your notebook.
Write three things your tree friend gives to animals.
What is bark? Why does a tree need it?
Name three plants used as food.
Write the names of two plants in your home language.
If you were a plant, which plant would you like to be and why?

rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch3-water-o-water.title: Water O' Water!
rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch3-water-o-water.subtitle: Where water comes from, where it goes, and why every drop counts

sections.md:
Imagine waking up one morning and the tap is dry. No water to brush your teeth. No water to bathe. No water for tea, for cooking rice, for washing clothes, for watering plants. The cow outside moos for a drink. What would you do?

Water is so common that we forget how precious it is. We use it from morning to night. Let us list the ways:

- Drinking and cooking
- Bathing and brushing teeth
- Washing clothes, utensils and floors
- Watering plants and fields
- Giving water to animals
- Cleaning the house, the toilet and the courtyard

Animals and plants need water too. A plant without water droops and dies; an animal without water cannot live long.

> Did you know? Most of your body is made of water — about two out of every three parts!

check.q: Who needs water to live?
check.why: All living things need water to stay alive.

sections.h: How much water does a family use?
sections.md:
Let us count water in **buckets** for one family of four in a day. (Your own family may use more or less – this is just an example.)

| Use | Buckets in a day |
|---|---|
| Drinking | 1 |
| Cooking | 1 |
| Bathing (4 people) | 4 |
| Washing clothes | 3 |
| Washing utensils | 2 |
| Cleaning the house | 1 |
| Toilet | 3 |
| **Total** | **15** |

Check the total: 1 + 1 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 15 buckets.

Now imagine you had to **carry** every one of those buckets from a well a kilometre away! In many villages, people — often women and girls — walk a long way with pots on their heads, sometimes several times a day. When water is far away, families use much less and every drop matters.

**Activity:** Find out who fetches or stores water in your home. Ask how much your family uses, and make your own table.

check.q: In the example, which use took the most buckets?
check.why: Bathing four people took 4 buckets, more than any other single use in the table.

sections.h: Where does our water come from?
sections.md:
Different families get water in different ways:

- **Taps** connected to pipes from a big tank
- **Hand pumps** that pull water from under the ground
- **Wells** — deep holes dug to reach water underground
- **Rivers, ponds and lakes**
- **Tankers** that bring water in trucks
- **Rainwater** collected from rooftops

In some cities, people line up for the water tanker. Ask at home: *where does our water come from?*

All of this water first came from **rain**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='w' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#4fc3f7'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#0277bd'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#e3f2fd'/><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='34' fill='#ffca28'/><g fill='#fff'><ellipse cx='150' cy='60' rx='70' ry='28'/><ellipse cx='200' cy='50' rx='50' ry='26'/></g><g stroke='#0288d1' stroke-width='3'><line x1='120' y1='90' x2='112' y2='110'><animate attributeName='y1' values='90;200' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='y2' values='110;220' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='170' y1='90' x2='162' y2='110'><animate attributeName='y1' values='90;200' dur='1.2s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='y2' values='110;220' dur='1.2s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='220' y1='90' x2='212' y2='110'><animate attributeName='y1' values='90;200' dur='1.2s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='y2' values='110;220' dur='1.2s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g><rect y='230' width='600' height='90' fill='#a1887f'/><path d='M0 230 Q150 210 300 235 T600 228 V260 H0Z' fill='url(#w)'/><g stroke='#90caf9' stroke-width='3' fill='none' opacity='.8'><path d='M380 220 q10 -40 0 -80'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M430 220 q-10 -40 0 -80'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;0' dur='3s' begin='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><rect x='300' y='260' width='20' height='60' fill='#455a64'/><text x='30' y='300' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>River / pond</text><text x='330' y='300' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Underground water (well, pump)</text><text x='70' y='140' font-size='16' fill='#01579b'>Rain</text><text x='390' y='130' font-size='16' fill='#01579b'>Water rises as vapour</text></svg>
fig.caption: Rain fills rivers and soaks underground; the sun lifts water back up to make clouds.
fig.alt: Animated rain falling from a cloud into a river, with vapour rising under the sun.

check.q: Where does all the water in wells and rivers first come from?
check.why: Rainwater fills rivers and ponds and soaks into the ground to fill wells.

sections.md:
The chapter also celebrates the joy of rain. When the first monsoon clouds arrive, children run out to splash in **puddles**, float **paper boats** in the gutters and catch drops on their tongues. The smell of wet earth fills the air. Frogs start croaking; peacocks dance.

**Make a paper boat:** fold a rectangle of paper in half, fold the corners into a triangle, open it into a hat, fold again into a square and pull the sides apart – a boat! Float it in a puddle and watch which way it drifts.

Ask your grandparents about rain songs and games from their childhood. Many Indian languages have songs that call the rain or welcome it.

check.q: What happens to a paper boat after a long time in water?
check.why: Paper soaks up water and becomes heavy and soft, so after a while the boat sinks.

sections.h: What happens to water? Disappearing puddles
sections.md:
After the rain, there are puddles on the road. A few hours of sunshine later — they are gone! Where did the water go?

Some soaks into the ground. The rest is turned by the sun's heat into an invisible gas called **water vapour**. It rises into the air. This is called **evaporation**. Wet clothes dry on the clothesline for the same reason.

High in the sky, the vapour cools and forms tiny droplets — these make **clouds**. When the droplets join and become heavy, they fall as **rain**. Then the rain fills rivers, ponds and wells again. Round and round it goes — the **water cycle**.

**Try it:** Put a wet hanky in the sun and another in the shade. Which dries first? (The sunny one, because heat speeds up evaporation.)

check.q: Why do wet clothes dry faster in the sun?
check.why: Heat from the sun turns the water in clothes into vapour more quickly.

sections.h: What floats, what sinks, what dissolves?
sections.md:
Try these simple tests with a bowl of water:

| Put in water | What happens |
|---|---|
| Leaf, paper boat, cork | Floats |
| Stone, coin, key | Sinks |
| Sugar, salt | Mixes and disappears (dissolves) |
| Sand, chalk powder | Does not dissolve; settles down |
| Oil | Floats as a layer on top |

When sugar dissolves, it is still there — taste the water and it is sweet! Water can mix with many things. That is why dirty water can carry harmful germs we cannot see.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fafafa'/><g transform='translate(160,40)'><path d='M0 0 h200 v200 q0 20 -20 20 h-160 q-20 0 -20 -20Z' fill='#b3e5fc' stroke='#0277bd' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M40 30 h40 l-10 14 h-20Z' fill='#ef6c00'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 4;0 0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><ellipse cx='140' cy='30' rx='22' ry='8' fill='#66bb6a'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -3;0 0' dur='2.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse><circle cx='100' cy='60' r='12' fill='#757575'><animate attributeName='cy' values='40;205;205' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><text x='130' y='290' font-size='16'>Boat and leaf float; the stone sinks.</text></svg>
fig.caption: Some things float, others sink.
fig.alt: A glass of water with a floating boat and leaf and a sinking stone.

check.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
check.why: Sugar mixes completely into water and seems to disappear, but the water tastes sweet.

sections.md:
Only a small part of Earth's water is fresh and safe to drink. So we must not waste it.

- Close the tap while brushing your teeth.
- Use a bucket and mug instead of a running shower.
- Fix leaking taps — a dripping tap can waste many buckets a day.
- Water plants with the water used for washing vegetables.
- Collect rainwater from the roof (**rainwater harvesting**).
- Keep ponds and rivers clean; never throw garbage in them.

Drink only clean water. Boiling or filtering water kills germs and keeps us safe from illness. Keep drinking water covered so dust and flies cannot get in.

> Did you know? In Rajasthan, people built stepwells and underground tanks hundreds of years ago to store precious rainwater.
keyTerms: Evaporation — water turning into vapour
Water vapour — water as an invisible gas
Dissolve — mix completely in water
Rainwater harvesting — collecting rainwater to use later

check.q: Which saves water?
options: Washing a car with a hose daily
check.why: A leaking tap wastes water every minute, so fixing it saves a lot.

parts.md: In Salma's village near Bikaner, summer was long and the well was far. Every morning Ammi and Salma walked with two pots each. One hot May day Salma counted: twelve trips that week. Her legs ached. 'Why can't the water come to us?' she asked.

Her uncle, a mason, had an idea. Before the monsoon he built a small pipe from their flat roof to a covered underground tank, a *tanka*. When the rain came, Salma watched the roof water gurgle down the pipe. 'Our roof is catching rain for us!' she laughed. All through the next winter they used tank water for washing and the garden, and walked to the well far less. Salma painted a sign on the tank: *Every drop counts.*

summary: All living things need water.
We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, cleaning and farming.
A family can use many buckets of water a day.
In many places people carry water from far away, so every drop matters.
Water comes from taps, wells, hand pumps, rivers, ponds and rain.
All our water first comes from rain.
Rain brings fun – puddles, paper boats, the smell of wet earth.
The sun's heat turns water into vapour — evaporation.
Vapour cools to form clouds, which bring rain: the water cycle.
Some things float, some sink, some dissolve in water.
Clean water is precious; we must not waste it.
Boil or filter water and keep it covered to make it safe.
practice: List five ways your family uses water each day.
Make a table of how many buckets your family uses.
Where does your family get water from? Who brings it?
Why do puddles dry up after the rain?
Write how to make a paper boat.
Name two things that float and two that sink.
Does salt dissolve in water? How can you check?
Write three ways to save water at school.
What is rainwater harvesting?
Why should we drink only clean water?

rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch4-our-first-school.title: Our First School
rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch4-our-first-school.subtitle: Before any classroom, there was a family — and a family tree

sections.md:
Who taught you to speak? To walk? To eat with your hand, to say 'thank you', to tie your shoelaces? Not a school teacher — your **family** did. That is why we call the family *our first school*.

In this chapter we look at families: who lives in them, how they are alike and different, how we look like and learn from our family members, and how families change over time.

From grandparents we may learn stories, songs and recipes. From parents we learn to be honest and to help. From older brothers and sisters we learn games and tricks!

> Did you know? Babies learn the language spoken at home just by listening — no textbook needed.

check.q: Why is the family called our first school?
options: We first learn many things at home
check.why: Long before school, we learn to talk, walk, eat and behave from our family.

sections.md:
Make a learning table for your family. Here is one child's example:

| Family member | What I learnt |
|---|---|
| Dadi | to pray, an old lullaby, how to fold rotis |
| Dada | to ride a cycle, to read the newspaper headlines |
| Mummy | to read the clock, to keep my things neat |
| Papa | to fly a kite, to save coins in a gullak |
| Didi | to play ludo, to skip with a rope |
| Baby brother | to be patient! |

Notice: even the *youngest* teaches us something. Learning in a family goes in all directions — sometimes a grandchild teaches a grandparent how to make a video call!

**Activity:** Fill in your own table with at least five people. Then ask: what did *you* teach someone in your family?

check.q: Can a child teach something to a grandparent?
options: Yes, like using a phone for a video call
check.why: Learning in a family goes both ways, and children often help elders with new things like phones.

sections.md:
Every family is different.

- Some families are **small**: a mother, a father and a child.
- Some are **large** or **joint**: grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins all living together.
- Some children live with one parent, or with grandparents.

All of these are real families. What makes a family is people who care for each other.

Make a table of your family members: name, age and relation (mother, grandfather, cousin…). Who is the oldest? Who is the youngest? How many years older is your oldest relative than you?

fig.caption: A family tree grows from grandparents down to the children.
fig.alt: A three-level family tree appearing box by box.

check.q: A family where grandparents, uncles and cousins live together is called a…
check.why: A joint family has many relatives living together in one home.

sections.md:
People often say, 'She has her mother's eyes!' or 'He laughs just like his grandfather!' Family members can look alike — in the shape of the nose, curly or straight hair, height, colour of eyes, or even the way they walk.

**Feature detective:** Look in a mirror, then at your family members, and fill a table:

| Feature | Mine | Who else has it? |
|---|---|---|
| Hair | curly | Papa, Bua |
| Eyes | brown | Mummy |
| Ears | big | Dada |
| Nose | small | Didi |
| Laugh | loud | Nana |

We also share **habits**: the way we speak, the food we enjoy, songs we hum. Some of these we are born with; many we learn by watching.

Look at old family photos — a wedding album is a treasure! Can you find whom you look like? Can you spot your parents when they were young?

check.q: Which of these can we learn by watching family members?
check.why: Habits are learnt from people around us, while things like eye colour come from birth.

sections.md:
A **family tree** is a drawing that shows how family members are related, just like branches grow from a tree trunk. At the top are grandparents. Below them are their children — your parents, uncles and aunts. At the bottom are you, your brothers, sisters and cousins.

In Hindi we have special names for relatives: *Dada-Dadi* (father's parents), *Nana-Nani* (mother's parents), *Chacha* (father's younger brother), *Tau* (father's elder brother), *Mama* (mother's brother), *Bua* (father's sister), *Mausi* (mother's sister). English often uses just 'uncle' and 'aunt' for all of these! Other Indian languages have their own words — in Tamil a grandmother is *paati*, in Bengali *thakuma* (father's mother) or *didima* (mother's mother).

Draw your own family tree. Paste a photo or draw a face in each box.
keyTerms: Family tree — a drawing showing how relatives are connected
Joint family — many relatives living together
Relation — how two people are connected in a family

check.q: Your mother's brother is your…
check.why: In Hindi, the mother's brother is called Mama.

sections.md:
Families change over time. A new baby is born. A cousin gets married and someone new joins. An older brother moves to another city for work. A grandparent may pass away. Sometimes a family moves to a new home.

When things change, we feel happy, sad, or confused. Talking to elders helps. Families also share work: cooking, cleaning, shopping and caring for the old and the young. When everyone helps, the home runs smoothly.

**Who does what at home?**

| Work | Who does it? | Can I help? |
|---|---|---|
| Cooking | | |
| Washing clothes | | |
| Shopping | | |
| Looking after Dadi | | |

Fill it in for your home. Is the work shared fairly between everyone, boys and girls alike?

> Did you know? Ask your grandparents what games they played as children — you might learn a brand-new game!

check.q: Which is a change that can happen in a family?
check.why: The birth of a baby adds a new member and changes the family.

parts.md: Ravi found a torn notebook in Nani's steel trunk. Inside were recipes in three different handwritings. 'This is my mother's writing,' said Nani, pointing to the oldest page. 'This is mine. And this,' she smiled, 'is your Mummy's, when she was your age.' Ravi traced the curly letters of the besan laddoo recipe.

That Diwali, Nani, Mummy and Ravi made laddoos together. Nani showed how to roast the besan till it smelled nutty. Mummy taught him to roll them round. Then Ravi took a pencil and wrote, in his own big letters, on a fresh page: 'Laddoo — by Ravi, age 8.' Now four generations shared one little book. 'This,' said Nani, 'is how a family teaches.'

summary: The family is our first school; we learn to talk, walk and behave there.
We learn different things from different family members – and even teach them.
Families can be small, large, joint, or headed by one parent or grandparents.
What makes a family is care for each other.
Family members can look alike – hair, eyes, ears, nose, laugh – and share habits.
Some features come from birth; many habits are learnt.
Old photos and albums show how families looked long ago.
A family tree shows how relatives are connected.
Hindi and other languages have special names for relatives such as Mama, Chacha, Bua, Mausi.
Families change through births, marriages and moving.
Family members share work at home; it should be shared fairly.
practice: Make a table of your family members with their ages.
Write five things you learnt from different family members.
Draw your family tree up to your grandparents.
Whom do you look like in your family? How?
What did you learn from your grandparents?
Write the Hindi names for your father's sister and mother's sister.
Name two changes that have happened in your family.
Who does which work in your home? How do you help?

rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch4-our-first-school-.title: Our First School (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-a.ch4-our-first-school-.subtitle: Family games, a survey and caring for each other

sections.md:
Your family was your **first school**. Before you came to class, you learnt to talk, walk, eat and share at home.

Ask three friends these questions and fill a table in your notebook:

| Name | People at home | Eldest member | Youngest member |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

Now find out: Whose family is the biggest? Whose is the smallest? Does anyone have grandparents at home? Some children live with one parent, some with grandparents, some with many cousins. Every family is different, and every family is special.

**Did you know?** In many homes in India, grandparents tell stories at bedtime and teach old games like gutte (five stones) and pittu.

check.q: Why is the family called our first school?
options: We learn our first things there
check.why: We learn to speak, walk and share at home before we go to school.

sections.md:
Everyone in a family helps. Who cooks? Who fetches water or milk? Who waters the plants? Who helps the old and the sick?

Things even you can do:
- set the plates before a meal
- fold your clothes
- read the newspaper or a story to a grandparent
- feed the pet or the birds

**Talk about it**: When someone at home is unwell, how does the family take care of them? When a baby is born or someone moves away, how does the family change?

**Draw**: draw your family doing one thing together — eating, playing, or celebrating a festival — and write each person's name.

check.q: Which is a way you can help at home?
check.why: Small jobs like setting plates help the whole family.

summary: The family is our first school.
Families can be big or small, and all are special.
Everyone in a family helps and cares for others.
Families change when people are born, grow up or move.
practice: Name three things you learnt from your family.
Who is the eldest person in your family?
Write two jobs you do at home.
How does your family celebrate a festival?

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch5-chhotus-house.title: Chhotu's House
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch5-chhotus-house.subtitle: What makes a place a home — from a play-house under a table to a palace

sections.h: A house made of a bedsheet
sections.md:
Have you ever made a little 'house' by throwing a bedsheet over two chairs? Chhotu does exactly that. He drapes a sheet over a cot, crawls inside, and suddenly has his own secret house! But soon he finds problems: it gets hot and stuffy, there is no window, and when his mother sweeps, dust blows in.

Chhotu's play-house makes us think: **what does a real house need?**

- A roof to keep out rain and sun
- Walls for safety and privacy
- Doors and windows for light and fresh air
- A clean place to cook, sleep, bathe and store things

> Did you know? Even animals build homes with the right features — a weaver bird's nest has a narrow entrance at the bottom to keep snakes out!

check.q: Why did Chhotu's bedsheet house feel stuffy?
options: It had no windows for air
check.why: Without windows, fresh air cannot come in, so the space gets hot and stuffy.

sections.md:
Here is Chhotu's day, in our own retelling.

**Scene 1 – Building.** Chhotu wants a place that is *only his*. He takes an old bedsheet, ties two corners to the legs of the cot and holds the others down with bricks. He carries in his pillow, his marbles and a picture book.

**Scene 2 – So proud!** He invites his little sister to visit – but only if she knocks first! He feels like a king in his palace.

**Scene 3 – Uninvited guests.** A cat slips in looking for a cool spot. Then a line of ants arrives for the biscuit crumbs he dropped. Chhotu learns that houses need to be clean and closed properly.

**Scene 4 – Too hot.** By noon the sun beats down and the sheet traps the heat. Chhotu is sweating. There is no window for air and no light to read by.

**Scene 5 – Rain!** In the evening a sudden shower soaks the sheet. Water drips on his book. He runs inside the real house, laughing.

**Scene 6 – Thinking.** Sitting dry by the window, Chhotu realises why his parents' house has a strong roof, walls, a door that shuts, and windows. Tomorrow, he decides, his play-house will have a 'window' cut in the side!

check.q: What made Chhotu run back into the real house in the evening?
check.why: A cloth roof cannot keep out rain, so when it rained Chhotu needed the strong roof of a real house.

sections.md:
Let us walk through a house and notice its parts:

| Part | Why we need it |
|---|---|
| Roof | Shelter from rain, sun, cold |
| Walls | Safety and privacy |
| Door | To go in and out, and to lock |
| Windows | Light and fresh air |
| Kitchen | To cook food |
| Toilet and bathroom | To stay clean and healthy |
| Floor | A clean, dry surface to live on |

Some houses have a courtyard (*aangan*), a verandah, a terrace or a balcony. Village houses may have a place for cattle. City flats may be on the tenth floor!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='s' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#90caf9'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#e3f2fd'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='330' fill='url(#s)'/><rect y='280' width='600' height='50' fill='#81c784'/><polygon points='160,140 300,50 440,140' fill='#c62828'/><rect x='180' y='140' width='240' height='140' fill='#ffe0b2' stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='275' y='200' width='50' height='80' fill='#6d4c41'/><rect x='200' y='170' width='50' height='45' fill='#fff59d' stroke='#5d4037' stroke-width='3'><animate attributeName='fill' values='#fff59d;#ffee58;#fff59d' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='350' y='170' width='50' height='45' fill='#fff59d' stroke='#5d4037' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='380' y='70' width='20' height='50' fill='#795548'/><g fill='#bdbdbd' opacity='.8'><circle cx='390' cy='60' r='8'><animate attributeName='cy' values='60;10' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='opacity' values='.8;0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g stroke='#4fc3f7' stroke-width='3'><path d='M60 190 h120'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0,200;120,200' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><g font-size='15' fill='#263238'><text x='275' y='40'>Roof</text><text x='450' y='210'>Wall</text><text x='280' y='300'>Door</text><text x='30' y='180'>Fresh air → window</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: A roof, walls, door and windows — and a chimney puffing smoke from the kitchen.
fig.alt: An animated house with labelled parts and air flowing in through a window.

check.q: Which part of a house lets in light and fresh air?
check.why: Windows let sunlight and fresh air into rooms.

sections.h: Houses are made of many things
sections.md:
Houses are built with materials found nearby and suited to the weather:

- **Bricks, cement and iron** — pucca (strong) houses in towns and cities.
- **Mud, straw and bamboo** — kutcha houses in many villages; they stay cool in summer.
- **Stone** — in hilly areas, where stone is easy to find.
- **Wood** — in places with lots of forests and heavy rain, such as the North-East.
- **Cloth or plastic** — tents for people who move from place to place.

In very rainy places, roofs slope so water slides off. In hot, dry places, roofs are flat and walls are thick.

check.q: Why do houses in rainy places have sloping roofs?
check.why: A sloping roof lets rain flow off quickly instead of collecting on top.

sections.md:
| Home | Where | Special feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Houseboat** | Dal Lake, Srinagar; backwaters of Kerala | a house floating on water |
| **House on stilts** | Assam and other flood areas | raised on poles so floods pass below |
| **Tent** | shepherds, travelling families, soldiers | quick to fold and carry |
| **Flat** | big cities like Mumbai | many homes stacked in one building |
| **Hut** | villages | mud walls, thatched roof, cool inside |
| **Igloo** | icy Arctic lands (not India) | built of snow blocks |

**Survey activity:** Ask five classmates: Is your house pucca or kutcha? How many rooms? Is there a courtyard? Do you live on the ground floor or higher? Make a table and see how different everyone's homes are.

check.q: Why are some houses in Assam built on stilts?
options: So flood water can pass underneath
check.why: Raising the house on poles keeps the living space dry when rivers flood.

sections.md:
Chhotu's house got dusty and the ants came for crumbs. A house must be kept clean to keep us healthy.

- Sweep and mop floors daily.
- Keep the kitchen and toilet clean.
- Put garbage in a covered dustbin.
- Do not let water collect — mosquitoes breed in still water.
- Open windows to let sunlight in; sunlight helps kill germs.

Everyone can help: children can fold clothes, put toys away and water plants. A clean house is a happy house!
keyTerms: Pucca house — strong house of bricks and cement
Kutcha house — house of mud, straw or bamboo
Ventilation — fresh air moving through a room

check.q: Why should we not let water collect near the house?
check.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water and can spread illnesses like malaria and dengue.

sections.md:
Just as we need a house, animals need homes too. A bird builds a nest, a rabbit digs a burrow, bees make a hive, a spider spins a web, ants live in an anthill. Some animals, like the dog and cow, live with people.

And some people do not have a proper house at all. They may sleep on footpaths or in small shelters. We should be kind and respectful to everyone.

> Did you know? A tailorbird stitches leaves together with plant fibre to make its nest — just like a tailor!

check.q: Which animal lives in a hive?
check.why: Honeybees build hives made of wax.

summary: Chhotu builds a bedsheet house that becomes hot, dusty, visited by a cat and ants, and soaked by rain.
A house protects us from rain, sun, cold and danger.
Main parts: roof, walls, floor, doors and windows.
Windows bring in light and fresh air (ventilation).
Houses also need a kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
Pucca houses use bricks and cement; kutcha houses use mud, straw, bamboo.
Houses are built to suit the weather and local materials.
Rainy places have sloping roofs; hot places have thick walls.
Special homes: houseboats, stilt houses, tents, flats, huts.
Keeping the house clean keeps us healthy.
Animals have homes too — nests, burrows, hives, webs.
practice: List the parts of your house.
What problems did Chhotu face in his bedsheet house?
What is the difference between a pucca and a kutcha house?
Why are windows important?
Name a house that floats and a house built on poles.
Survey three friends about their homes and make a table.
Write three ways you help keep your home clean.
Name the homes of a bird, a rabbit and a bee.
Draw your dream house and label its parts.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch5-chhotus-house-2.title: Chhotu's House (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch5-chhotus-house-2.subtitle: Houses through the seasons, sharing space, and building your own model

sections.md:
A good house changes how it helps us as the seasons change.

| Season | How the house helps |
|---|---|
| **Summer** | Thick walls and shady verandahs keep rooms cool; windows let a breeze pass through |
| **Monsoon** | A strong roof keeps us dry; drains carry rainwater away |
| **Winter** | Closed doors and windows keep warm air in; sunny courtyards warm us in the day |

In Ladakh, where winters are freezing, people make thick mud-brick walls and small windows. In Kerala, where it rains a lot, roofs are steep and covered with tiles. People everywhere think carefully about the weather before they build.

> Did you know? Many old houses in Rajasthan have a *jaali* — a stone screen full of little holes — that lets air in but keeps the hot sun out.

check.q: In which season do we most want doors and windows shut to keep warm air in?
check.why: In winter we close doors and windows so the warm air stays inside the house.

sections.md:
Chhotu's real house is shared by his whole family. Sharing a house means sharing space and work.

- Who cooks? Who fetches water? Who cleans? Often many people help.
- Grandparents, parents, brothers and sisters may sleep in the same room in small houses.
- Everyone needs a little space for their things — a shelf, a box or a bag.

**Think and talk:** Do you have a corner of your own like Chhotu wanted? Where do you keep your school bag and toys? Who decides where things go in your house?

A house becomes a **home** when the people in it care for each other.

check.q: What turns a house into a home?
options: People who care for each other
check.why: A home is a house filled with people who love, help and care for one another.

sections.md:
Make your own small house, just like Chhotu did — but better!

1. Take an empty shoe box or carton for the walls.
2. Cut out a door and two windows (ask an adult to help with scissors).
3. Fold a piece of card into a sloping roof and stick it on top.
4. Colour the walls; draw a kitchen and a sleeping corner inside.
5. Pour a spoon of water on the roof. Does it slide off? That is why sloping roofs are good in rainy places!

Show your model to the class and explain each part: roof, walls, door, windows. Compare your house with a friend's model — which one lets in more light?

check.q: In the model, why does water slide off the folded card roof?
check.why: Water flows downhill, so a sloping roof sends rain off its edges.

summary: Houses help us differently in summer, monsoon and winter.
Cold places have thick walls and small windows; rainy places have steep tiled roofs.
Jaalis let in air but keep out harsh sun.
Families share space and housework.
A house becomes a home through care.
A shoe-box model shows why roofs slope.
practice: How does your house keep you cool in summer?
Why do houses in Ladakh have small windows?
Who does which work in your house? Make a list.
Make a model house and label its parts.
What is a jaali and why is it useful?
Write two lines on 'My home'.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch6-foods-we-eat.title: Foods We Eat
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch6-foods-we-eat.subtitle: Why a baby, a grandfather and a cricketer all eat differently

sections.md:
Close your eyes and think of yesterday's dinner. Was it roti and dal? Rice and sambar? Fish curry? Poha? Every family's plate looks a little different, yet all of us eat for the same reason: **food gives us energy to work, play and grow**, and helps us stay healthy.

In this chapter we look at what people eat, how food changes with age, work and place, where food comes from, how it is cooked, and why we should never waste it.

> Did you know? A growing child's body is building new bones and muscles every day — food is the building material.

check.q: Why do we need food?
check.why: Food gives us energy, helps us grow and keeps us healthy.

sections.md:
Keep a food diary for one day. Here is one child's example from Lucknow:

| Meal | What I ate |
|---|---|
| Early morning | a glass of milk |
| Breakfast | poha and a banana |
| Tiffin at school | aloo paratha |
| Evening snack | roasted chana |
| Dinner | rice, arhar dal, bhindi, curd |

Now ask a friend for their diary. Did anyone eat the same thing as you? Did anyone eat something you have never tasted?

**Ask at home:** How many times a day do the grown-ups eat? Who eats first and who eats last? Does everyone eat together? Does anyone keep a fast on some days? Families have many different customs, and all deserve respect.

check.q: What is a food diary?
options: A list of what you ate during the day
check.why: A food diary records each meal of the day so we can see what and how much we eat.

sections.md:
Food changes with **age**:

- A **baby** has only milk at first, then soft foods like mashed banana, dal water and khichdi, because it has no teeth.
- **Children** need lots of food to grow — milk, fruits, vegetables, grains, dal, eggs.
- **Grown-ups** who do hard work, like farmers and labourers, need more food for energy.
- **Old people** often eat soft, light food, as their teeth may be weak.
- A **sick person** is given simple food like khichdi, soup or dalia.

Food also changes with **place**. In Punjab, people often eat makki ki roti and sarson ka saag; in Kerala, rice with coconut curries; in Bengal, rice and fish; in Gujarat, dhokla and thepla; in Rajasthan, dal-baati; in the North-East, rice with bamboo-shoot dishes. People eat what grows well nearby.

fig.caption: A baby, a child, a hard-working farmer and a grandparent need different food.
fig.alt: Four bobbing figures with their typical foods.

check.q: Why is a baby given only milk at first?
options: It has no teeth to chew
check.why: Babies have no teeth, so they need liquid and very soft food.

sections.h: Where does food come from? How is it cooked?
sections.md:
**From plants:** rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruits, sugar, oil, spices, tea.

**From animals:** milk, curd, paneer, ghee, eggs, honey, fish, meat.

**Cooking changes food.** Some foods are eaten **raw** (fruits, cucumber, carrot, sprouts). Others must be cooked:

| Way of cooking | Examples |
|---|---|
| Boiling | rice, dal, eggs |
| Frying | puri, pakora, samosa |
| Roasting | roti, peanuts, corn (bhutta) |
| Steaming | idli, momos, dhokla |
| Baking | bread, cake |

Cooking makes food soft, tasty and easier to chew, and kills many germs. People cook on gas stoves, chulhas with wood or cow-dung cakes, kerosene stoves or electric cookers. Smoke from a chulha can hurt the eyes and lungs, so kitchens need good windows.

check.q: Idli is cooked by…
check.why: Idli batter is cooked in steam, which is why idlis are soft and spongy.

sections.md:
Animals have their own food:

| Animal | Food |
|---|---|
| Cow, goat | Grass, leaves, fodder |
| Cat | Milk, fish, rats |
| Dog | Roti, meat, bones |
| Parrot | Fruits, green chillies, seeds |
| Frog, lizard | Insects |
| Squirrel | Nuts, fruits |
| Honeybee | Nectar from flowers |

Some animals eat plants, some eat other animals and some eat both.

check.q: What does a honeybee feed on?
check.why: Bees suck sweet nectar from flowers and turn it into honey.

sections.md:
Good habits make food work better for us:

- Wash your hands with soap before eating.
- Wash fruits and vegetables before eating or cooking.
- Chew food well and eat slowly.
- Eat a mix of foods — grains, dal, vegetables, fruits, milk.
- Eat fresh food; cover food to keep flies away.
- Do not eat too much junk food like chips and cold drinks.

Many families eat together, sitting on the floor or at a table. Some eat with their hands, some with spoons. In South India, food is often served on a banana leaf! In many homes, food is served in leaf plates (*pattal*) at weddings.
keyTerms: Energy — the power to work and play
Balanced meal — a meal with many kinds of food
Fodder — food given to cattle

check.q: Why should we cover cooked food?
options: To keep flies and dust away
check.why: Flies and dust carry germs that can make us sick.

sections.md:
Many people in our country do not get enough to eat. Farmers work for months to grow the grain in a single roti. So:

- Take only as much food as you can finish.
- Leftover food can be used for the next meal.
- Share extra food with those who need it.

> Did you know? Many gurdwaras run a *langar* — a free community kitchen where anyone, of any background, can sit together and eat. Many schools serve a mid-day meal so that every child gets a hot lunch.

check.q: What is a good way to avoid wasting food?
options: Take a lot and throw the rest
Take only what you can eat
check.why: Taking only what we can finish means no food is thrown away.

parts.md: On the first day at her new school in Pune, Mehak opened her tiffin: aloo paratha. Next to her, Anjali had idli and coconut chutney. Joseph had appam and stew. Faiz had sheer khurma left over from Eid. 'Let's swap one bite each!' said Anjali.

By the end of lunch, Mehak had tasted four states in one recess. 'Everyone's food is different,' she said, 'but everyone's tummy is happy.' The class teacher smiled and made a chart: 'Foods from our homes.' It covered the whole wall.

summary: Food gives us energy, growth and health.
A food diary shows what we eat at each meal.
People eat different food depending on age, work, health and place.
Babies drink milk and eat soft food because they have no teeth.
Hard-working people need more food; old and sick people eat soft, light food.
Different regions of India have different dishes made from local crops.
Food comes from plants and from animals.
Food can be eaten raw or cooked by boiling, frying, roasting, steaming or baking.
Animals eat grass, insects, fruits, nectar or other animals.
Wash hands and food; cover food; eat fresh.
Never waste food; share with those in need.
