Why do babies and old people eat soft food?
Name one dish each from two different states.
Name three foods from plants and three from animals.
Name one food that is boiled, one fried and one steamed.
What does a cow eat? What does a frog eat?
Write three good eating habits.
Why should we not waste food?
What food is given to a sick person in your home?

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch6-foods-we-eat-2.title: Foods We Eat (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch6-foods-we-eat-2.subtitle: Food for babies and grandparents, food across India, and why we never waste a grain

sections.md:
Not everyone in a family eats the same thing.

- **A baby** with no teeth drinks only mother's milk for about six months. Later it eats soft mashed food like dal-rice or banana.
- **Children** need plenty of food to grow and play — milk, dal, vegetables, fruits, roti or rice.
- **Grandparents** whose teeth are weak may like soft foods such as khichdi, porridge or curd.
- **A sick person** is often given light food that is easy to digest.

**Ask at home:** What did you eat when you were a baby? Is there anyone in your house who cannot eat hard food?

check.q: What does a very young baby drink?
check.why: For the first months a baby gets all the food it needs from mother's milk.

sections.md:
India is a huge country, and food changes from place to place, depending on what grows there.

| Region | Common foods |
|---|---|
| Punjab | makki ki roti, sarson ka saag, lassi |
| Tamil Nadu | idli, dosa, sambhar, rice |
| West Bengal | rice, fish curry |
| Gujarat | dhokla, thepla |
| Kashmir | rice, haak saag, kahwa |
| Kerala | puttu, appam, coconut curries |

Where wheat grows well, people eat more rotis; where there is lots of rain and rice grows, people eat more rice. Near the sea, many people eat fish. Festivals bring special food too — sevaiyan at Eid, ladoos at Diwali, plum cake at Christmas, pongal at Pongal.

check.q: Why do people in rainy, rice-growing areas eat a lot of rice?
options: Rice is the only food in India
check.why: People mostly eat what grows easily near them, and rice needs plenty of water.

sections.md: Like us, animals eat different things. A cow eats grass, a cat drinks milk and eats fish or mice, a squirrel nibbles nuts, a crow eats almost anything. Some animals eat plants, some eat other animals, and some eat both.

check.q: Which animal mostly eats grass?
check.why: Cows are plant-eaters and graze on grass.

sections.md:
Many people in the world do not get enough to eat. So every grain is precious.

- Take only as much as you can finish; you can always take a second helping.
- Leftover food can be stored properly and eaten later.
- Peels and scraps can go to a compost pit to feed plants.

**Activity – My food chart:** For one day, draw what you ate at breakfast, lunch, snack time and dinner. Colour fruits and vegetables green. Did you eat something green at every meal?

> Did you know? A farmer works for about four months to grow one crop of rice. Think of that before you leave food on your plate!

check.q: What is the best way to avoid wasting food at a meal?
options: Take a lot and throw the rest
Take only what you can finish
Feed it all to the dustbin
check.why: Taking small helpings and asking for more if needed means nothing is thrown away.

summary: Babies drink mother's milk; later they eat soft food.
Children need plenty of varied food to grow.
Elders and sick people often need soft, light food.
Food differs across India because of local crops and weather.
Festivals have special foods.
Animals eat plants, animals or both.
Never waste food — take small helpings, compost scraps.
practice: What food would you give a baby and a grandparent? Why?
Name two foods from any two states of India.
Why do people near the sea often eat fish?
Name a festival and the special food made for it.
Make a food chart of one day.
Write three ways to avoid wasting food.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch7-saying-without-sp.title: Saying without Speaking
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch7-saying-without-sp.subtitle: Faces, hands, dance and signs — the many ways we talk without words

sections.h: Can you say it without a word?
sections.md:
Here is a challenge: tell your friend 'I am hungry' without speaking. You might rub your tummy and pretend to put food in your mouth. Now try 'Come here!' — you wave your hand toward yourself. Easy, right?

We 'talk' all the time without words. A smile says *I am happy*. A frown says *I am upset*. A finger on the lips says *Be quiet!* This is called **communicating with gestures and expressions**.

In this chapter we will play acting games, read faces, learn hand signs and sign language, look at signs and symbols around us, discover how dancers tell stories, and see how animals 'talk'.

check.q: What does a finger on the lips usually mean?
check.why: Putting a finger on the lips is a common sign asking someone to be silent.

sections.md:
The chapter invites you to play an acting game, like **dumb charades**.

**How to play**
1. Make two teams.
2. One child gets a slip with a word or an action – *climbing a tree*, *flying a kite*, *brushing teeth*, *an elephant*, *rain*.
3. Without making a sound, the child acts it out.
4. The team guesses. No speaking, no pointing at letters!
5. Take turns. The team that guesses most wins.

**Tips:** use your whole body. To show *rain*, wiggle your fingers coming down. To show an *elephant*, swing one arm from your nose like a trunk. To show *reading*, open your palms like a book.

**Try these messages:** *I am sleepy. The baby is crying. It is very cold. My tooth hurts. Let's play cricket!*

Notice how some messages are easy and some very hard. Which ones needed your face more than your hands?

check.q: In dumb charades, how do you give your message?
check.why: In this game the actor must stay silent and use only face and body movements.

sections.md:
Our faces show our feelings, even when we do not want them to:

| Feeling | What the face does |
|---|---|
| Happy | Smile, eyes bright |
| Sad | Lips turn down, eyes droop |
| Angry | Eyebrows pull together, face tight |
| Surprised | Eyes and mouth open wide |
| Scared | Eyes wide, face tense |
| Shy | Looking down, small smile |

Play the **mirror game**: stand before a mirror and make each face. Then ask a friend to guess your feeling.

**Why it matters:** If you notice a friend looking sad, you can ask, *"Are you okay?"* Reading faces helps us be kind.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fce4ec'/><g font-size='15' text-anchor='middle'><g transform='translate(100,110)'><circle r='55' fill='#ffcc80'/><circle cx='-18' cy='-12' r='6'/><circle cx='18' cy='-12' r='6'/><path d='M-25 15 Q0 40 25 15' stroke='#000' stroke-width='4' fill='none'><animate attributeName='d' values='M-25 15 Q0 40 25 15;M-25 15 Q0 48 25 15;M-25 15 Q0 40 25 15' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><text y='90'>Happy</text></g><g transform='translate(240,110)'><circle r='55' fill='#ffcc80'/><circle cx='-18' cy='-12' r='6'/><circle cx='18' cy='-12' r='6'/><path d='M-25 30 Q0 8 25 30' stroke='#000' stroke-width='4' fill='none'/><ellipse cx='-18' cy='5' rx='3' ry='6' fill='#42a5f5'><animate attributeName='cy' values='0;40' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse><text y='90'>Sad</text></g><g transform='translate(380,110)'><circle r='55' fill='#ef9a9a'/><path d='M-30 -28 L-8 -18 M30 -28 L8 -18' stroke='#000' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='-18' cy='-8' r='6'/><circle cx='18' cy='-8' r='6'/><path d='M-20 28 h40' stroke='#000' stroke-width='4'/><text y='90'>Angry</text></g><g transform='translate(520,110)'><circle r='55' fill='#ffcc80'/><circle cx='-18' cy='-12' r='9' fill='#fff' stroke='#000' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='18' cy='-12' r='9' fill='#fff' stroke='#000' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cy='25' rx='10' ry='14'><animate attributeName='ry' values='10;16;10' dur='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse><text y='90'>Surprised</text></g></g></svg>
fig.caption: Four faces, four feelings — no words needed.
fig.alt: Animated faces showing happy, sad, angry and surprised.

check.q: Eyes and mouth wide open usually show…
check.why: When we are surprised, our eyes and mouth open wide.

sections.md:
Our hands are great talkers:

- Thumbs up — *Well done* or *All okay*
- Waving — *Hello* or *Bye*
- Folded hands — *Namaste*
- Nodding the head — *Yes*; shaking it — *No*
- Palm held up facing out — *Stop!*

**Gestures can differ from place to place.** In some parts of South India, a gentle side-to-side tilt of the head can mean *yes* or *okay* – a visitor might think it means *no*! So always watch carefully and ask if unsure.

We also follow **signs without words** in daily life: traffic lights (red — stop, green — go), a picture of a dustbin, a red cross for a hospital, arrows showing the way, a whistle by the sports teacher, the school bell, a policeman's raised hand at a crossing.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#eceff1'/><rect x='80' y='30' width='90' height='220' rx='16' fill='#263238'/><circle cx='125' cy='75' r='28' fill='#e53935'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;1;.2;.2;.2;.2;1' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='125' cy='140' r='28' fill='#fdd835'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='.2;.2;.2;.2;1;.2;.2' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='125' cy='205' r='28' fill='#43a047'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='.2;.2;1;1;.2;.2;.2' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><g font-size='18' fill='#263238'><text x='200' y='82'>Red — STOP</text><text x='200' y='147'>Yellow — Get ready</text><text x='200' y='212'>Green — GO</text></g><g transform='translate(480,140)'><rect x='-40' y='-40' width='80' height='80' rx='10' fill='#fff' stroke='#c62828' stroke-width='4'/><rect x='-10' y='-28' width='20' height='56' fill='#c62828'/><rect x='-28' y='-10' width='56' height='20' fill='#c62828'/><text x='-35' y='65' font-size='15'>Hospital</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: A traffic light cycles through its colours — a message without words.
fig.alt: An animated traffic light and a red-cross hospital sign.

check.q: What does a red traffic light tell us?
check.why: Red is the signal to stop, so everyone at the crossing stays safe.

sections.md:
Some people cannot hear, or cannot speak. Many of them use a full **sign language**, with signs for letters, words and whole sentences. In our country there is **Indian Sign Language (ISL)**. It is a real language, as rich as Hindi or English – people tell jokes, sing songs and give speeches in it!

Sign language uses:
- **hand shapes** (a fist, an open palm, pointing fingers),
- **movement** (where and how the hand moves),
- **face expressions** (raised eyebrows can turn a sentence into a question).

**Be a good friend:** If a classmate signs, look at their face and hands, speak clearly if they lip-read, and learn a few signs – *hello*, *thank you*, *friend*, *play*. Never laugh or stare. Everyone deserves to be understood.

Some TV news channels show a signer in a small box in the corner so that people who cannot hear can follow the news.

check.q: What language do many people who cannot hear use in India?
check.why: Indian Sign Language uses hand shapes, movements and expressions to express words and sentences.

sections.md:
Indian classical dances tell whole stories without speaking! Dancers use **mudras** (special hand positions) and **expressions** to show a deer, a lotus, a bird, a peacock, or feelings like love and anger.

- **Bharatanatyam** — from Tamil Nadu
- **Kathak** — from North India
- **Kathakali** — from Kerala, with colourful painted faces
- **Odissi** — from Odisha
- **Kuchipudi** — from Andhra Pradesh
- **Manipuri** — from Manipur

**Try a mudra:** Put the tips of your thumb and two middle fingers together and lift your little finger and first finger – it looks like a deer's face! Spread your fingers and join both thumbs – a bird flying.

Watch a dancer's eyes and hands closely. You will 'hear' the story.
keyTerms: Gesture — a movement of hands or head that gives a message
Expression — a look on the face that shows a feeling
Mudra — a hand position in Indian dance
Sign language — a language of hand signs

check.q: Kathakali comes from which state?
check.why: Kathakali is a classical dance-drama from Kerala known for painted faces.

sections.md:
Animals communicate without words: a dog wags its tail when happy and growls when angry; a cat purrs or hisses; bees do a 'waggle dance' to tell other bees where flowers are; birds sing to call mates and warn of danger; a peacock spreads its feathers to show off; ants touch feelers to pass messages.

> Did you know? A crow's loud 'caw-caw' can be a warning call that brings other crows rushing to help.

check.q: How does a happy dog often show its feelings?
check.why: A wagging tail is usually a sign of a friendly, happy dog.

parts.md: A new girl, Tara, joined Class 3 in Bhopal. She could not hear. On the first day she sat quietly, watching everyone's faces. At recess Arjun waved, pointed to the ball and raised his eyebrows. Tara grinned and nodded. They played without a single word.

Next day Tara taught the class three signs from Indian Sign Language: *friend*, *play* and *thank you*. Soon the whole class was signing 'thank you' to the canteen didi. 'We thought Tara needed to learn our way of talking,' said the teacher, 'but she taught us hers.'

summary: We can communicate without speaking, using gestures and expressions.
Acting games like dumb charades show how much the body can say.
Our faces show feelings: happy, sad, angry, surprised, scared, shy.
Hands give messages: wave, thumbs up, namaste, nodding, stop.
Gestures can mean different things in different places.
Signs and symbols like traffic lights and hospital crosses give messages.
People who cannot hear may use sign language; India has Indian Sign Language.
Sign language uses hand shapes, movement and face expressions.
Indian classical dances tell stories through mudras and expressions.
Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Manipuri are some dances.
Animals communicate with sounds, movements and tails.
practice: Show 'I am thirsty' without speaking. Describe what you did.
Write the rules of dumb charades.
Draw four faces showing four feelings.
What do the three colours of a traffic light mean?
What is sign language? Who uses it?
How can you be a good friend to someone who uses sign language?
Name three Indian classical dances and their states.
What is a mudra? Show one.
How do bees tell each other where flowers are?
Write two gestures you use every day and their meanings.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch7-saying-without-sp.title: Saying without Speaking (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch7-saying-without-sp.subtitle: Dance that tells stories, signs that help, and animals that 'talk'

sections.md:
In Indian classical dances like **Bharatanatyam**, **Kathak** and **Kathakali**, dancers tell whole stories without saying a word. They use:

- **Mudras** — special hand shapes. One mudra can mean a flower, another a deer, another a bird flying.
- **Facial expressions** — eyes, eyebrows and lips show joy, anger, fear or love.
- **Footwork** — fast steps can show a chase or excitement.

In Kathakali from Kerala, dancers wear bright make-up so the audience can see every movement of the eyes from far away.

**Try it:** Join your thumb and first finger in a circle and keep the other fingers open. Many dancers use a shape like this to show holding a flower.

check.q: What are mudras?
check.why: Mudras are hand gestures that carry meaning in Indian dance.

sections.md:
We see many signs that 'speak' without words:

- A **red** traffic light says *stop*; **green** says *go*.
- A **policeman's raised palm** tells vehicles to halt.
- A picture of a **wheelchair** shows a place people who use wheelchairs can reach.
- A cricket **umpire** raises one finger for *out* and waves an arm for *four*.

People who cannot hear use **sign language**, with hand signs for letters and words. Indian Sign Language has signs for everyday words like *mother*, *water* and *thank you*. Learning a few signs helps us talk with more friends.

check.q: What does an umpire's single raised finger mean?
check.why: In cricket, the umpire raises one finger to show the batter is out.

sections.md:
Animals also send messages:

- A dog **wags its tail** when happy and growls when angry.
- A cat **arches its back** and puffs its fur when scared.
- Bees **dance** in a pattern to show other bees where flowers are.
- A peacock **spreads its feathers** to show off.

**Game – Dumb charades:** In groups, one child acts out a word (like *swimming* or *eating mango*) without speaking. Others guess. Who can guess fastest?

check.q: How do honeybees tell each other where flowers are?
check.why: Honeybees do a waggle dance whose direction and length tell others where the flowers are.

summary: Classical dancers tell stories with mudras, expressions and footwork.
Kathakali make-up makes expressions easy to see.
Traffic lights, umpire signals and symbols speak without words.
Sign language helps people who cannot hear communicate.
Animals communicate by tails, posture, dances and displays.
Dumb charades practises saying without speaking.
practice: Name two Indian classical dances.
Show three feelings using only your face.
What do red and green traffic lights tell us?
What is sign language? Who uses it?
How does a dog show it is happy?
Play dumb charades and write which word was hardest to act.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch8-flying-high.title: Flying High
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch8-flying-high.subtitle: Beaks, feathers, eyes, eggs and nests — the secret lives of birds

sections.md:
Step outside and look up at the sky, the trees, the electric wires. How many birds can you spot in five minutes? Crows, pigeons, sparrows, mynas, parrots, kites circling high above… Birds are everywhere, yet each one is different.

In this chapter we look closely at birds: their size, colour, feathers, beaks, claws, eyes and voices, how they fly, and how they build nests and care for their young.

> Did you know? The **peacock** is India's national bird, and the female is called a **peahen**.

check.q: What is India's national bird?
check.why: The peacock is the national bird of India.

sections.md:
Bird-watching is a wonderful hobby. India's most famous bird scientist, **Dr Salim Ali**, began as a boy curious about a sparrow – and spent his whole life studying birds. He is often called the 'Birdman of India'.

**How to watch birds:**
1. Go out early in the morning – birds are busiest then.
2. Sit still and quiet. Wear dull-coloured clothes.
3. Watch: size (bigger or smaller than a crow?), colour, beak, tail, how it moves, what it eats.
4. Listen to its call.
5. Write it in a **bird diary** with the date and place.

| Bird | Where seen | Colour | What it was doing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Myna | school ground | brown, yellow beak | walking, pecking insects |
| Pigeon | balcony | grey | cooing, eating grains |
| Kite | sky | brown | gliding in circles |

**Bird sounds:** crow – *caw caw*; koel – *koo-oo* (loudest in summer); pigeon – *gutur-goo*; parrot – a sharp screech; sparrow – *chee-chee*. Can you copy them? Some birds even copy *other* sounds – mynas and parrots can learn words!

check.q: When is the best time to watch birds?
check.why: Birds are most active early in the morning, looking for food and calling to each other.

sections.md:
Birds come in all sizes and colours:

| Size | Examples |
|---|---|
| Small | Sparrow, sunbird, tailorbird |
| Medium | Pigeon, crow, myna, parrot |
| Large | Peacock, kite, eagle, vulture, ostrich |

Parrots are green with red beaks, kingfishers flash blue, crows are black, and the male peacock has a dazzling tail of blue-green feathers with 'eye' spots.

All birds have **feathers**, **two legs**, **two wings** and a **beak**. Feathers keep them warm and help them fly.

**Feather activity:** Find a fallen feather. Run your finger along it one way – smooth; the other way – the parts separate! Now stroke it smooth again; the tiny parts hook back together. Birds clean and 'zip up' their feathers with their beaks every day.

check.q: Which feature do ALL birds have?
check.why: Feathers are found only in birds, and every bird has them.

sections.md:
Most birds fly by flapping their wings up and down. Their bodies are light, and many bones are hollow. Big birds like the **kite** and **eagle** can **glide** — they spread their wings and float on warm air without flapping, circling high in the sky.

Some birds cannot fly at all: the **ostrich** is too heavy but can run very fast; the **penguin** uses its wings like flippers to swim. Hens can fly only a little.

**Make a paper bird:** fold a sheet into a paper plane, or cut a bird shape and tie it to a thread. Swing it gently – see how wide wings help it float.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='sk' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#4fc3f7'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#e1f5fe'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='url(#sk)'/><g><g><ellipse rx='22' ry='9' fill='#37474f'/><circle cx='20' cy='-4' r='7' fill='#37474f'/><path d='M26 -4 l8 2 -8 2Z' fill='#ffb300'/><path d='M-5 0 Q-10 -30 -30 -40' stroke='#37474f' stroke-width='6' fill='none'><animate attributeName='d' values='M-5 0 Q-10 -30 -30 -40;M-5 0 Q-10 25 -30 35;M-5 0 Q-10 -30 -30 -40' dur='0.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><animateMotion dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M-50 200 Q150 120 300 180 T650 150'/></g><g transform='translate(300,80)'><g><path d='M-60 0 Q-30 -12 0 0 Q30 -12 60 0' stroke='#5d4037' stroke-width='6' fill='none'/><ellipse rx='10' ry='5' fill='#5d4037'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 0 40' to='360 0 40' dur='10s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g></g><text x='20' y='280' font-size='16' fill='#01579b'>Small bird flaps its wings</text><text x='380' y='30' font-size='16' fill='#01579b'>Kite glides in circles</text></svg>
fig.caption: A small bird flaps; a kite glides in wide circles on warm air.
fig.alt: One bird flapping across the sky and a kite circling.

check.q: Which bird cannot fly but runs very fast?
check.why: The ostrich is too heavy to fly, but it is one of the fastest runners.

sections.md:
Look at a pigeon's face. Its eyes are on the **sides** of its head! It can see a wide area around it – useful for spotting a cat sneaking up. Most birds that eat grains have eyes like this.

Now look at a picture of an **owl**. Its big eyes are in the **front**, like ours. Owls hunt at night and need to judge exactly how far away a mouse is. But an owl cannot roll its eyes – instead it can **turn its head** a very long way round, almost to look behind itself!

| Eyes on the sides | Eyes in front |
|---|---|
| pigeon, sparrow, parrot, hen | owl, eagle (more forward) |
| see a wide area | judge distance well |

**Try it:** close one eye and try to touch two pencil tips together. Hard! Two eyes looking forward help judge distance.

check.q: How does an owl look to the side if it cannot move its eyes?
options: It turns its head far round
check.why: An owl's neck lets it turn its head a long way, making up for eyes that stay fixed.

sections.h: Beaks and claws tell what birds eat
sections.md:
A bird's **beak** fits its food:

- **Parrot** — strong, curved beak to crack nuts and cut fruits.
- **Sparrow, pigeon** — short, cone-shaped beak to pick up grains.
- **Kingfisher, heron** — long, pointed beak to catch fish.
- **Woodpecker** — strong, sharp beak to drill holes in bark for insects.
- **Eagle, kite** — hooked beak to tear meat.
- **Sunbird** — thin, long beak to suck nectar from flowers.

Claws also differ: eagles have sharp curved claws to grip prey; ducks have webbed feet for swimming; sparrows have claws that grip branches when perching.

head: Bird
Beak
Food
fig.caption: Match the beak to the meal.

check.q: Why does a kingfisher have a long pointed beak?
check.why: A long, pointed beak helps it spear and grab slippery fish.

sections.md:
Birds lay **eggs**. To keep eggs safe, most birds build **nests** with twigs, grass, leaves, feathers or mud. Different birds build different nests:

- **Weaver bird** — hanging nest woven from grass.
- **Tailorbird** — stitches two leaves together.
- **Crow** — rough nest of twigs (and sometimes wires!).
- **Woodpecker** — a hole in a tree trunk.
- The **koel** does not build a nest at all; it lays eggs in a crow's nest!

The parent birds sit on the eggs to keep them warm. After some days, chicks hatch. Parents feed them until they can fly.

**Be kind:** never touch or disturb a nest. Put out water and grain for birds in summer.
keyTerms: Feathers — soft covering of a bird
Beak — hard mouth of a bird
Glide — fly without flapping
Hatch — come out of an egg

check.q: Which bird lays its eggs in a crow's nest?
check.why: The koel does not build a nest and leaves its eggs for crows to hatch.

parts.md: One scorching May afternoon in Jaipur, Kabir saw a sparrow panting on the railing, beak open. He filled a clay bowl with water and placed it in the shade. For an hour nothing happened. Then – *flutter!* – the sparrow hopped in and splashed.

By the end of summer, Kabir's bird diary listed eleven visitors: sparrows, a bulbul with a red patch, mynas, pigeons, even a shy purple sunbird. 'I didn't know so many birds lived near us,' he told his class. 'You just have to give them a reason to come – and sit quietly enough to see them.'

summary: Birds have feathers, two wings, two legs and a beak.
Bird-watching needs quiet, patience and a diary; Salim Ali was India's famous birdman.
Birds have different calls; some, like mynas, can copy sounds.
Birds differ in size, colour and voice.
Most birds fly by flapping; kites and eagles also glide.
Ostrich and penguin cannot fly.
Pigeons have eyes on the sides; owls have eyes in front and turn their heads.
Beak shape matches the food a bird eats.
Claws and feet match how a bird lives — gripping, swimming, perching.
Birds lay eggs and many build nests.
The koel lays eggs in a crow's nest.
We should never disturb nests.

Write the calls of three birds.
Who was Salim Ali?

Why does an owl turn its head so much?
How does a tailorbird make its nest?
Draw the beaks of a sparrow and an eagle.

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch8-flying-high-2.title: Flying High (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch8-flying-high-2.subtitle: Beaks, claws, nests and a bird-watching diary

sections.h: Beaks and claws for different jobs
sections.md:
A bird's beak and feet tell us how it eats and lives.

| Bird | Beak / feet | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Parrot | short, curved, strong beak | cracking nuts and fruits |
| Eagle, kite | sharp hooked beak, curved claws | catching and tearing prey |
| Woodpecker | long, sharp beak | drilling into tree bark for insects |
| Duck | flat beak, webbed feet | straining food from water, swimming |
| Sunbird | thin, long beak | sipping nectar from flowers |

Birds that perch, like sparrows, have toes that wrap tightly round a branch so they do not fall even while sleeping.

check.q: Which bird has webbed feet for swimming?
check.why: Skin between a duck's toes works like a paddle in water.

sections.h: Birds that cannot fly, and birds that travel far
sections.md:
Not all birds fly. The **ostrich** is too heavy to fly but runs very fast. The **penguin** cannot fly but swims beautifully. Hens can only flutter a short way.

Other birds fly amazing distances. Every winter, birds such as the **Siberian crane** and many ducks fly thousands of kilometres to lakes in India, like Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Chilika in Odisha, where it is warmer. This journey is called **migration**.

check.q: What is the seasonal long journey of birds called?
check.why: Migration is when birds travel far to warmer places for the season.

sections.md:
Sit quietly near a tree, park or your balcony for 15 minutes, morning or evening.

1. Count how many different birds you see.
2. Note each bird's colour, size (smaller than a sparrow? bigger than a crow?) and beak shape.
3. Listen: does it chirp, caw, coo or whistle?
4. Where is it — on the ground, a branch, a wire, in the sky?

Put out a bowl of water in summer; you may get many visitors! Never disturb a nest or touch eggs — the parents may leave.

check.q: Why should we not touch a bird's nest or eggs?
options: The parent birds may abandon them
check.why: Disturbing a nest can frighten parent birds away so the eggs or chicks are not cared for.

summary: Beak shapes match food: nuts, prey, insects, nectar, water food.
Feet differ: claws for gripping, webbed feet for swimming, perching toes.
Ostrich, penguin and hen cannot really fly.
Migratory birds come to Indian lakes in winter.
Keep a bird diary; give water; never disturb nests.
practice: Match beaks to food for parrot, eagle and sunbird.
Why does a woodpecker need a strong beak?
Name two birds that cannot fly.
What is migration? Name one place in India migratory birds visit.
Keep a bird diary for a week.
How can you help birds in summer?

rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch9-its-raining.title: It's Raining
rd-school-c3-evs-b.ch9-its-raining.subtitle: Dark clouds, the smell of wet earth, and what rain means to everyone

sections.md:
The afternoon is hot and sticky. Suddenly the sky turns dark grey, a cool wind blows, dust swirls on the road — and then *plip, plop*, the first fat drops fall. Soon there is the wonderful smell of wet earth. Children run out to dance; mothers rush to pull clothes off the line.

What do *you* do when it rains? In this chapter we see what happens when it rains, how people and animals feel, what we use to stay dry, how much it rains, and why rain is so important — and sometimes troublesome.

> Did you know? The smell of the earth after the first rain has a name: **petrichor**. In Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh, people even make a perfume called *mitti attar* that smells like it!

check.q: Which sign often tells us rain is coming?
check.why: Dark heavy clouds and a cool breeze usually come just before rain.

sections.md:
The sun heats water in seas, rivers and ponds. The water turns into invisible **vapour** and rises up. High above, it cools and forms tiny droplets that make **clouds**. When the droplets join and grow heavy, they fall as **rain**. Rain fills rivers and ponds, and the cycle begins again.

In India most rain comes in the **monsoon** season, roughly June to September. The monsoon usually reaches Kerala first, around the start of June, and then spreads north across the country. Farmers wait eagerly for it to sow crops like rice.

**Thunder and lightning:** In a storm, a bright flash of **lightning** jumps between clouds or to the ground. The loud **thunder** is the sound it makes. We see the flash first and hear the thunder later, because light travels much faster than sound.

fig.caption: Heavy clouds, lightning, falling rain and a puddle that keeps growing.
fig.alt: Animated thunderstorm with rain and lightning.

check.q: In which season does India get most of its rain?
check.why: The monsoon brings most of India's yearly rain, mainly from June to September.

sections.md:
Rain makes different people feel different things:

- **Children** love jumping in puddles and floating paper boats.
- **Farmers** are happy because crops need water.
- **A shopkeeper** selling umbrellas has more customers!
- **A labourer** working outdoors may lose a day's work.
- **A vegetable seller** on the footpath must cover her basket.
- **People with leaking roofs** worry about water coming inside.

Too little rain brings **drought** — fields dry up, there is no drinking water. Too much rain brings **floods** — rivers overflow, homes and roads go under water. So rain must come in the right amount.

**Rain fun:** Many Indian languages have rain songs and rhymes. Children sing them while making paper boats and racing them in the gutters. Ask your grandparents to teach you one!

check.q: What happens when there is too little rain for a long time?
check.why: A drought is a long period without enough rain, so land and wells dry up.

sections.h: What we use in the rain
sections.md:
| Thing | How it helps |
|---|---|
| Umbrella (*chhata*) | keeps head and body dry |
| Raincoat | covers the whole body, hands free for cycling |
| Gumboots / plastic chappals | keep feet dry, don't spoil in water |
| Plastic sheet | covers a cycle, a cart, a shop or a roof |
| *Ghongi* or *kambal* hood | some farmers fold a jute sack or blanket into a hood |
| Palm-leaf or bamboo hats | used by farmers in paddy fields in many states |

Notice: things for the rain are made of materials that **water cannot pass through** – plastic, rubber, waxed cloth, tightly woven leaves. A cotton hanky soaks water; a plastic bag does not.

**Test it:** pour a spoon of water on cotton cloth, paper, plastic and a leaf. Which ones let water through? Which would make a good umbrella?

check.q: Why are raincoats made of plastic or rubber-coated cloth?
check.why: Waterproof materials stop rain from soaking through to our clothes and skin.

sections.md:
Scientists measure rain with a **rain gauge**. You can make a simple one.

**Make a rain gauge**
1. Take a clear plastic bottle with straight sides. Cut off the top part.
2. Turn the top upside down and fit it into the bottle like a funnel.
3. Stick a paper strip with a ruler scale (in centimetres) on the side.
4. Keep it in an open place, away from trees and roofs.
5. Check it at the same time every day and write how many centimetres of water collected. Empty it after reading.

| Day | Rain (cm) |
|---|---|
| Monday | 1 |
| Tuesday | 3 |
| Wednesday | 0 |

Total for these three days: 1 + 3 + 0 = 4 cm.

> Did you know? Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya are among the rainiest places on Earth, while parts of Rajasthan's Thar Desert get very little rain.

check.q: What does a rain gauge measure?
check.why: A rain gauge collects rain so we can read how much fell, in centimetres or millimetres.

sections.h: Animals and plants in the rain
sections.md:
After rain, nature wakes up:

- **Frogs** croak loudly from ponds.
- **Earthworms** come out of the soggy soil.
- **Peacocks** dance with their tails spread wide.
- **Snails** crawl out; **mosquitoes** breed in still water.
- Dry grass turns green; seeds sprout; trees look washed and shiny.

Animals also hide from heavy rain — birds sit in nests, dogs shelter under parked cars, cows stand under trees.

**Rainbows:** When sun shines while it is still drizzling, look away from the sun — you may see a rainbow with seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.

fig.caption: A rainbow draws itself across the sky — red on the outside, violet inside.
fig.alt: An animated seven-coloured rainbow arc.

keyTerms: Monsoon — the rainy season
Drought — a long time with too little rain
Flood — too much water covering land
Petrichor — smell of earth after rain

check.q: Which colour is on the outer edge of a rainbow?
check.why: In a rainbow, red is on the outside and violet on the inside.

sections.md:
**In the rain:** carry an umbrella or raincoat; dry yourself quickly; don't stand under trees or touch electric poles during lightning; keep away from open drains and flooded roads.

**After the rain:** empty water from old tyres, pots and coolers so mosquitoes cannot breed.

**Save rainwater:** many homes and schools collect rain from rooftops in tanks or let it soak into the ground through pits. This is called **rainwater harvesting**. It refills wells for the dry months.

check.q: Where should you NOT stand during lightning?
check.why: Lightning often strikes tall objects like trees, so standing under one is dangerous.

parts.md: All through May, Salim Chacha's little umbrella shop near the Pune bus stand was empty. He sat fanning himself, watching the dry sky. 'When will the rain come?' asked his niece Zoya, swinging her legs on the counter.

One June afternoon the clouds rolled in, the wind smelled of wet earth, and – *dhadaam!* – thunder. Within minutes a crowd squeezed under the shop's awning. Black umbrellas, flowered ones, tiny ones for children – all sold by evening. Across the road the chaiwala covered his stove with a plastic sheet, and a farmer on the bus grinned at the drumming on the roof. 'Same rain,' Zoya thought, 'but a different story for everyone.'

summary: Before rain, clouds darken and a cool wind blows.
Sun heats water into vapour; vapour forms clouds; clouds give rain.
India gets most rain in the monsoon, June to September, starting in Kerala.
We see lightning before we hear thunder because light is faster than sound.
Rain makes some people happy and causes problems for others.
Too little rain causes drought; too much causes floods.
Umbrellas, raincoats and plastic sheets are made of waterproof materials.
A rain gauge measures how much rain falls.
After rain, frogs croak, peacocks dance and plants turn green.
A rainbow has seven colours, red outside and violet inside.
Stay safe: avoid trees and electric poles in lightning.
Rainwater harvesting saves rain for later.
practice: What do you see, hear and smell just before it rains?
How are clouds formed?
Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
Why are farmers happy when it rains? Who might be unhappy?
What is a drought? What is a flood?
Name four things people use in the rain and what they are made of.
Write the steps to make a rain gauge.
Name three animals you see after rain.
Write the seven colours of a rainbow.
How can a school save rainwater?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch10-what-is-cooking.title: What is Cooking
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch10-what-is-cooking.subtitle: Raw or cooked, boiled or fried — and the utensils, fuels and people behind every meal

sections.md:
Stand at the kitchen door at dinnertime. Can you hear the *chhhh* of the tadka? The whistle of the pressure cooker? Can you smell hot rotis puffing up on the tawa? Close your eyes and you can almost guess the whole meal just from the sounds and smells!

Cooking is one of the oldest skills humans have. Long, long ago, people ate everything raw — fruits, roots, leaves. Then they learnt to make fire, and they found that food held over fire became soft and tasty. Cooking was born.

But even today, **not all food needs cooking**. Some food we eat **raw**, some only **cooked**, and some both ways. In this chapter we will:

- sort foods into raw and cooked,
- learn the different ways of cooking,
- look at the utensils in a kitchen, old and new,
- find out about the fuels that give heat,
- and ask an important question: *who cooks in your home?*

check.q: Which of these can we eat raw?
check.why: Cucumber is eaten raw in salads, while rice, dal and flour must be cooked first.

sections.md:
Think of everything you ate yesterday. Now sort it!

| Eaten raw | Eaten cooked | Raw or cooked |
|---|---|---|
| Banana, apple, guava | Rice, dal, potato | Tomato, carrot |
| Cucumber, mango | Roti, rajma | Onion, peas |
| Sprouts, coconut | Brinjal, egg | Spinach, radish |
| Jamun, papaya | Chicken, fish | Gram (chana) |

**Why do we cook food?**

1. Cooking makes food **soft**, so it is easy to chew and digest.
2. Cooking gives food a **better taste and smell**.
3. Cooking **kills germs** that could make us sick.
4. Some foods, like rice grains or rajma, simply **cannot be eaten raw**.

But be careful: **overcooking** can destroy some of the goodness in vegetables. That is why salads of raw cucumber, carrot and tomato are so healthy. Always **wash** fruits and vegetables well before eating them raw.

**Activity:** Make a list of food items eaten raw in your home and another list of food items that are cooked. Which list is longer?

check.q: Why do we cook food?
options: To make it soft, tasty and germ-free
check.why: Cooking softens food, improves its taste and kills harmful germs.

sections.md:
There are many ways to cook food. Each gives a different taste.

- **Boiling** — cooking in hot bubbling water: rice, eggs, potatoes, dal.
- **Steaming** — cooking over steam from boiling water: idli, dhokla, momos, puttu.
- **Frying** — cooking in hot oil: puri, pakora, samosa, jalebi.
- **Roasting** — cooking directly on fire or a hot tawa: roti, papad, bhutta (corn), peanuts.
- **Baking** — cooking in an oven or tandoor: bread, cake, naan.
- **Pressure cooking** — cooking in a closed cooker: dal, rajma and chana cook fast.

One food can be cooked in many ways! A potato can be **boiled** (aloo chaat), **fried** (chips), **roasted** in the fire, or **baked**. Rice can be boiled (plain rice), cooked with vegetables (pulao), made into kheer with milk, or soaked, ground and steamed into idli.

**Find out:** Ask your family how many different dishes they can make with rice. Write their names.

fig.caption: Steam rising from a boiling pot, and a roti puffing up on a hot tawa.
fig.alt: Animated pot with rising steam and a puffing roti over flames.

check.q: Idli is cooked by…
check.why: Idli batter is cooked in the steam that rises from boiling water.

sections.md:
**Utensils** are the vessels and tools we cook and eat with. Look around your kitchen:

| Utensil | Use |
|---|---|
| Tawa | roasting rotis, dosas |
| Kadhai | frying puris, pakoras |
| Patila / degchi | boiling rice, milk |
| Pressure cooker | cooking dal quickly |
| Belan and chakla | rolling dough |
| Chimta | turning rotis on fire |
| Sil-batta / mixer | grinding chutney and masala |
| Karchhi (ladle) | stirring and serving |

Utensils are made of many materials: **steel, aluminium, iron, copper, brass, clay, glass** and **non-stick** coated metal.

**Then and now:** Ask your grandparents what utensils they used as children. Many will say **clay pots**, brass lotas, copper handis, iron kadhais and stone grinders (sil-batta, chakki). Today many homes use pressure cookers, mixers and non-stick pans. Clay pots are still loved for curd and for the special taste of food cooked slowly in them!
keyTerms: Utensil — a vessel or tool used for cooking or eating
Sil-batta — a flat stone and a roller used for grinding
Tandoor — a clay oven for baking naan

check.q: Which utensil is used to roll out rotis?
check.why: The belan (rolling pin) rolls dough flat on the chakla to make rotis.

sections.md:
To cook, we need heat. **Fuels** are things we burn or use to get that heat.

- **LPG** cooking gas in a cylinder or piped gas
- **Electricity** — induction cooktop, microwave, electric oven
- **Kerosene** stove
- **Wood, coal, dung cakes** burnt in a clay **chulha** or angithi
- **Biogas** made from cow dung and waste
- **Sunlight** in a **solar cooker**!

Smoke from wood and dung chulhas hurts the eyes and lungs of the person cooking, so cleaner fuels like LPG and biogas are better for health. A **solar cooker** burns nothing at all — it is a box with a shiny lid that traps the sun's heat. It is slow but free and clean.

**Safety rules:** Never play near the stove. Turn the gas knob off after cooking. Keep matches away from small children. Handle hot pans with a cloth or holder.

**Ask at home:** Which fuel does your family use? What did your grandparents use?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#e3f2fd'/><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='35' fill='#ffca28'><animate attributeName='r' values='32;38;32' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><g stroke='#ffb300' stroke-width='4'><line x1='490' y1='90' x2='360' y2='160'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;.2;1' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='500' y1='95' x2='400' y2='160'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='.2;1;.2' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g><rect x='300' y='160' width='160' height='60' fill='#212121'/><polygon points='300,160 460,160 430,110 300,110' fill='#b0bec5' opacity='.8'/><text x='310' y='245' font-size='16'>Solar cooker</text><rect x='60' y='150' width='60' height='80' rx='12' fill='#e53935'/><text x='70' y='245' font-size='16'>LPG</text><path d='M180 230 h100 v-30 h-100Z' fill='#8d6e63'/><path d='M215 200 q10 -30 15 0Z' fill='#ff7043'><animate attributeName='d' values='M215 200 q10 -30 15 0Z;M215 200 q10 -45 15 0Z;M215 200 q10 -30 15 0Z' dur='.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><text x='195' y='250' font-size='16'>Chulha</text></svg>

fig.alt: LPG cylinder, flickering chulha and sun rays striking a solar cooker.

check.q: Which fuel uses sunlight?
check.why: A solar cooker traps the sun's heat to cook food without burning anything.

sections.md:
In many homes, mothers and grandmothers do most of the cooking. They wake up early and cook three meals a day — that is a lot of work! But cooking is a skill **everyone** can learn: boys and girls, fathers and grandfathers. Many famous chefs in big hotels are men, and many are women. In langars at gurudwaras, hundreds of volunteers cook together for everyone.

Children can help safely:

- wash vegetables and fruits,
- pick stones from dal and rice,
- knead dough, shell peas,
- set the plates and fill water,
- clean up after the meal.

Stay away from hot oil and sharp knives unless an adult is with you.

> Did you know? A pressure cooker cooks faster because the trapped steam makes the water boil at a higher temperature than in an open pot. It also saves fuel!

check.q: Who should learn to cook?
check.why: Cooking is a life skill that every boy and girl can learn and share at home.

sections.md:
Here is a fun game to play with friends. One person says a cooking word and the next person names a dish!

- *Boiled* → egg
- *Fried* → pakora
- *Roasted* → bhutta
- *Steamed* → idli
- *Baked* → cake
- *Raw* → cucumber

Now try a harder round: name a dish that uses **both** boiling and frying (aloo tikki — boiled potatoes, then fried!).

Also talk about **food from different places**: in Punjab people love makki ki roti; in Kerala, appam and puttu; in Gujarat, dhokla; in Bengal, fish curry and rice; in Rajasthan, dal-baati. Every region cooks in its own way with what grows nearby.

check.q: Aloo tikki uses which two ways of cooking?
check.why: Potatoes are boiled and mashed first, then the tikkis are fried in oil.

summary: Some foods are eaten raw, some cooked, some both ways.
Wash fruits and vegetables before eating them raw.
Cooking makes food soft, tasty and free of germs.
Ways of cooking: boiling, steaming, frying, roasting, baking, pressure cooking.
One food, like potato or rice, can be cooked in many ways.
Utensils include tawa, kadhai, patila, pressure cooker, belan, chimta.
Utensils are made of steel, iron, aluminium, clay, copper and brass.
Old kitchens used clay pots and stone grinders; new ones use cookers and mixers.
Fuels: LPG, electricity, kerosene, wood, coal, dung cakes, biogas, sunlight.
Smoky chulhas harm health; cleaner fuels are better.
Always follow safety rules near the stove.
Everyone can learn to cook and share kitchen work.
practice: Name three foods eaten raw and three eaten only cooked.
Why do we cook food? Give two reasons.
Name one food each that is boiled, fried, roasted and steamed.
Write the names of three dishes made from rice.
Name four utensils in your kitchen and their uses.
What utensils did your grandparents use? Ask and write.
Which fuel is used in your home for cooking?
Why is a solar cooker good for the environment?
Write two safety rules for the kitchen.
How do you help in the kitchen?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch11-from-here-to-the.title: From Here to There
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch11-from-here-to-the.subtitle: Feet, bullock carts, trains, boats and planes — how people and things travel

sections.md:
Meet Kiran. Her grandmother lives in a village far away. To reach her, Kiran's family first takes an **auto-rickshaw** to the railway station, then rides a **train** all night, then a **bus**, and at last walks the dusty path to the village, where a **bullock cart** carries their heavy bags. Phew! Four kinds of transport in one trip!

Every day, people and goods move **from here to there**. A milkman cycles to your door. Vegetables come in trucks from farms. Letters fly in planes. Fish come to the market in boats.

**Think:** How do you come to school? On foot, by cycle, by bus, by van, by auto, or on your father's scooter? Make a class chart and count how many children use each.

check.q: How many kinds of transport did Kiran's family use in the story?
check.why: They used an auto, a train, a bus and a bullock cart — four kinds — plus walking.

sections.h: On land, on water, in the air
sections.md:
We can sort all transport into three groups by **where** it moves.

| Land | Water | Air |
|---|---|---|
| bicycle, scooter, car | boat, canoe | aeroplane |
| bus, truck, train | ship, ferry | helicopter |
| bullock cart, tonga | raft, houseboat | hot-air balloon |
| auto-rickshaw, metro | steamer | rocket (space!) |

Some places need special transport. In the **Sundarbans** and **Kerala backwaters**, people go to school and market by boat. On **snowy mountains**, people use yaks and mules. In the **desert** of Rajasthan, the camel is called the *ship of the desert* because it walks easily on sand. Islands like the Andamans are reached by ship or plane.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#bbdefb'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='100' fill='#81c784'/><rect x='0' y='240' width='600' height='60' fill='#4fc3f7'/><g><g fill='#e53935'><rect x='0' y='175' width='90' height='25' rx='4'/><rect x='95' y='175' width='70' height='25' rx='4'/></g><circle cx='20' cy='202' r='6'/><circle cx='70' cy='202' r='6'/><circle cx='120' cy='202' r='6'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-180 0;620 0' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g><path d='M0 250 h70 l-12 15 h-46Z' fill='#6d4c41'/><polygon points='35,250 35,215 60,248' fill='#fff'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='620 0;-80 0' dur='9s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g fill='#eceff1'><path d='M0 60 h80 l15 -8 v16 h-95Z'/><path d='M30 60 l20 -20 h10 l-10 20Z'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-100 20;640 -10' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='20' y='30' font-size='16'>Air</text><text x='20' y='190' font-size='16'>Land</text><text x='20' y='290' font-size='16'>Water</text></svg>
fig.caption: A plane in the sky, a train on land and a sailing boat on water.
fig.alt: Animated plane, train and boat moving across sky, land and river.

check.q: Which animal is called the ship of the desert?
check.why: The camel walks easily on hot sand for long distances, so it is called the ship of the desert.

sections.md:
Long before engines, people used **animals** to carry them and their goods. Many still do!

- **Bullocks** pull carts and ploughs in villages.
- **Horses** pull tongas in some towns.
- **Camels** carry loads in the desert.
- **Donkeys and mules** carry bricks and goods up hills.
- **Elephants** carried kings and logs in forests.
- **Yaks** carry loads high in the Himalayas.

These animals work hard. They need good food, water, rest and kindness. We must never overload them or hurt them.

> Did you know? Before cars, a journey from Delhi to Agra took about a week by bullock cart. Today an express train does it in under two hours!

check.q: Which animal carries loads in the high Himalayas?
check.why: The yak has thick hair and strong lungs, so it can carry loads in the cold, high mountains.

sections.md:
Ask your grandparents how they travelled when they were young. Many will say they **walked** long distances, rode **bicycles**, or took a **bullock cart** or **tonga**. Trains then ran on **steam engines** that puffed black smoke — chhuk-chhuk!

Today we have:

- fast **electric trains** and the **metro** in big cities,
- buses, cars, scooters and auto-rickshaws,
- **aeroplanes** that cross India in two or three hours.

The **wheel** was one of the most important inventions ever. Without it there would be no carts, cycles, cars or trains. Look around — how many things with wheels can you count?

**Activity:** Draw a vehicle from your grandparents' time and one from today. What is different?

check.q: Which invention made carts, cycles and cars possible?
check.why: Every cart, cycle, car and train rolls on wheels, one of the greatest inventions.

sections.h: Fuel and the air we breathe
sections.md:
Most vehicles need **fuel** to move. Cars and scooters use **petrol**; buses and trucks often use **diesel**; some use **CNG** (a cleaner gas). Electric trains, the metro and e-rickshaws use **electricity**. A cycle uses only **your legs**!

Burning petrol and diesel makes **smoke**. Too much smoke makes the air dirty and makes people cough. That is called **air pollution**.

We can help:

- walk or cycle for short trips,
- share a ride or use a bus or metro,
- switch off the engine at red lights,
- keep vehicles well serviced.

Petrol and diesel come from deep under the ground and will not last forever, so we should not waste them.

check.q: Which of these does NOT need fuel?
check.why: A bicycle moves only with the push of our legs, so it makes no smoke.

sections.h: Signs and safety on the road
sections.md:
Roads are busy, so we follow rules.

- **Traffic light:** red means **stop**, yellow means **get ready**, green means **go**.
- Cross the road at a **zebra crossing**, after looking right, left and right again.
- Walk on the **footpath** or on the side of the road.
- Wear a **helmet** on two-wheelers and a **seat belt** in cars.
- Never put your hand or head out of a bus window.
- At railway crossings, wait until the train has passed and the gate opens.

There are also **signs** with pictures — a school sign, a hospital sign, a no-horn sign. Look out for them on your way to school!

check.q: What does the red traffic light mean?
check.why: Red means all vehicles and people must stop and wait.

sections.md:
Transport carries **goods** too, not just people. Rice from Punjab reaches Tamil Nadu in **goods trains**. Apples from Kashmir reach Mumbai in **trucks**. Big ships bring and take goods across the sea at ports like Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

In villages, a woman may carry water pots on her head, and a farmer may carry grain on a cycle. A child carries a school bag on the back! Even this is moving things from here to there.

**Fun fact:** Indian Railways is one of the biggest railway networks in the world, carrying crores of passengers every single day.

check.q: How do apples from Kashmir usually reach faraway cities?
check.why: Goods like apples travel long distances by road in trucks and by goods trains.

summary: People and goods travel from place to place every day.
Transport moves on land, on water and in the air.
Boats are used in the Sundarbans and Kerala backwaters; camels in deserts; yaks in mountains.
Animals like bullocks, horses, camels, donkeys and yaks carry people and loads.
Working animals need food, water, rest and kindness.
Old travel: walking, carts, tongas, steam trains; new: metro, cars, planes.
The wheel is one of the most important inventions.
Most vehicles use petrol, diesel, CNG or electricity; cycles need no fuel.
Smoke from vehicles pollutes the air; walking, cycling and buses help.
Follow traffic lights, zebra crossings, helmets and seat belts.
Trucks, trains and ships carry goods across the country and the world.
practice: How do you come to school? Draw it.
Name three vehicles each for land, water and air.
Why is the camel called the ship of the desert?
Name two animals used for transport and say what they carry.
How did your grandparents travel? Ask and write.
Which vehicles do not need fuel?
Write three ways to reduce smoke from vehicles.
What do the three colours of a traffic light mean?
Where in India do people use boats to go to school?
Why is the wheel an important invention?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch11-from-here-to-the.title: From Here to There (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch11-from-here-to-the.subtitle: Transport on land, water and air — then and now — and staying safe on the road

sections.md:
We can sort ways of travel into three groups:

| Land | Water | Air |
|---|---|---|
| bicycle, bus, car, train, auto-rickshaw, bullock cart, camel | boat, ship, ferry, houseboat | aeroplane, helicopter |

Some need fuel (petrol, diesel, CNG), some need electricity (metro trains), and some need muscle power (cycle, rickshaw, cart pulled by animals). Animals like horses, camels, elephants and yaks still carry people and goods in some places — camels in deserts, yaks in the high mountains.

check.q: Which of these travels on water?
check.why: A ferry is a boat that carries people and vehicles across water.

sections.md:
Long ago people walked or used animals. A journey from one city to another could take weeks. Then came the steam railway, and later cars, buses and aeroplanes.

**Ask your grandparents:** How did they go to school? Did they ride a bicycle, walk, or take a bullock cart? How long did it take to visit relatives? Today, a flight from Delhi to Chennai takes under three hours!

Faster travel is useful, but vehicles burn fuel and make the air dirty. Walking, cycling and using buses and metro trains keep the air cleaner.

check.q: Which choice keeps the air cleanest for a short trip?
check.why: Walking and cycling burn no fuel, so they produce no smoke.

sections.md:
- Cross the road only at a **zebra crossing** or when the walking signal is green.
- **Look right, look left, then right again** before crossing.
- Walk on the footpath; if there is none, walk facing the traffic.
- Wear a **helmet** on a cycle or two-wheeler and a **seat belt** in a car.
- Never lean out of a bus window or play on the road.

check.q: Where should we cross a road?
check.why: Zebra crossings are marked so drivers expect people there and slow down.

sections.md: Not only people travel — messages do! Long ago, letters went by runners and pigeons. Then came the post office, the telegram and the telephone. Now a mobile phone sends a message across India in a second. **Activity:** write a postcard to a relative and post it; find out how many days it takes to arrive.

summary: Transport is by land, water and air.
Vehicles run on fuel, electricity or muscle power.
Camels, yaks and horses still carry loads in some areas.
Travel has become much faster over the years.
Walking, cycling and public transport keep the air cleaner.
Follow road safety: zebra crossing, look both ways, helmet, seat belt.
Messages travel by post, phone and internet.
practice: Make a table of land, water and air transport.
How did your grandparents travel to school?
Name an animal used for transport in deserts.
Write four road safety rules.
Why are buses better for the air than many cars?
How do messages travel today and long ago?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch12-work-we-do.title: Work We Do
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch12-work-we-do.subtitle: Jobs outside, chores at home, and why every kind of work deserves respect

sections.md:
It is six o'clock. The milkman's cycle bell rings. The newspaper lands on the doorstep. Somewhere a baker is pulling hot pav from an oven. A bus driver starts the first bus. A farmer is already in the field. A nurse is finishing a night shift at the hospital.

Before you even brush your teeth, dozens of people have **worked** to make your day possible! In this chapter we look at:

- the many kinds of work people do,
- the tools they use,
- the work done **at home**,
- how family members share work,
- and why children should be in school, not at work.

check.q: Who brings milk to many homes in the morning?
check.why: The milkman delivers fresh milk to homes early every morning.

sections.md:
| Worker | Work | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| Farmer | grows crops | plough, sickle, spade |
| Carpenter | makes furniture | saw, hammer, chisel |
| Tailor | stitches clothes | needle, scissors, sewing machine |
| Potter | makes pots | wheel, clay |
| Doctor / nurse | treats the sick | stethoscope, thermometer |
| Teacher | teaches | books, board, chalk |
| Cobbler | mends shoes | awl, thread, last |
| Driver | drives vehicles | steering wheel, vehicle |
| Electrician | fixes wiring | tester, pliers |
| Sweeper | keeps streets clean | broom, cart |
| Police officer | keeps us safe | whistle, wireless |
| Shopkeeper | sells things | weighing scale |

Some people work in **offices**, some in **fields**, some in **factories**, some on **roads**, some in **hospitals** and some at **home**.

**Activity:** Act out a worker without speaking. Can your friends guess who you are?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fffde7'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='60' fill='#a5d6a7'/><g transform='translate(120,190)'><line x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='-70' stroke='#795548' stroke-width='6'/><path d='M0 -70 q40 -10 50 20' fill='none' stroke='#9e9e9e' stroke-width='6'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' values='0 120 190;-25 120 190;0 120 190' dur='1.2s' additive='sum' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='70' y='240' font-size='16'>Farmer: sickle</text><g transform='translate(300,150)'><circle r='40' fill='#8d6e63'/><path d='M-20 -10 q20 -30 40 0 v20 h-40Z' fill='#d7a86e'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 300 150' to='360 300 150' dur='3s' additive='sum' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='255' y='240' font-size='16'>Potter: wheel</text><g><rect x='460' y='150' width='90' height='10' fill='#6d4c41'/><rect x='490' y='110' width='14' height='40' fill='#9e9e9e'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -20;0 0' dur='.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><text x='445' y='240' font-size='16'>Carpenter: hammer</text></svg>
fig.caption: Workers and their tools: a farmer's sickle, a potter's spinning wheel and a carpenter's hammer.
fig.alt: Animated sickle swinging, potter's wheel spinning and hammer tapping.

check.q: Which tool does a tailor use?
check.why: A tailor stitches clothes using a needle, scissors and a sewing machine.

sections.md:
Some of the most important work happens **at home**: cooking, cleaning, washing clothes, fetching water, looking after babies and old people, shopping for vegetables, mending things and keeping the house tidy.

This work is **not paid**, but without it no family could manage. Think how tired someone gets doing it every single day!

**Make a chart:** Who does what in your home?

| Work | Who does it? |
|---|---|
| Cooking | |
| Washing clothes | |
| Buying vegetables | |
| Cleaning the house | |
| Helping with homework | |
| Looking after grandparents | |

Is most of the work done by one person? Can it be shared more fairly?

check.q: Which is true about housework?
options: It is important work, though often unpaid
check.why: Cooking, cleaning and caring are real, important work even when no one is paid for them.

sections.md:
In one family, the mother cooks and also goes to work in an office. The father washes the dishes and drops the children to school. Grandfather waters the plants and buys milk. The children fold clothes, lay the table and keep their books neat. When everyone helps, no one is too tired, and there is more time to play and talk together!

Work has **no boy-work or girl-work**. Boys can cook and sweep; girls can fix a cycle and drive a bus. Women are pilots, doctors, scientists and farmers. Men are nurses, cooks and teachers.

**Discuss:** Which work do you do at home? Which new job could you start helping with this week?

check.q: Which statement is fair?
options: Boys and girls can both do any work
Children should never help at home
check.why: Any work can be done by anyone, and sharing it makes the family happier.

sections.md:
Some children cannot go to school because they have to work — in shops, tea stalls, fields, factories or other people's homes. Imagine a girl of your age washing dishes all day, with no time to read or play. She may be tired, hungry and sad.

**Children have a right to study and play.** In India, the law says every child from 6 to 14 years must get free schooling, and young children must not be made to do paid work. Helping a little at home is fine, but school comes first.

**Think:** If you see a child working instead of studying, how do you feel? What could grown-ups do to help?

check.q: What do children have a right to?
check.why: Every child has the right to go to school and to have time to play.

sections.md:
Some people think some jobs are 'big' and others are 'small'. But think: who keeps our streets clean? Who grows our rice? Who mends our shoes? Who carries our letters? If the sweepers stopped working for one week, the whole town would smell!

Every job helps others, so **every worker deserves respect**. Say *thank you* to the guard at the gate, the bus driver, the cleaner in your school and the vegetable seller.

**Interview:** Talk to one worker near your home. Ask: What work do you do? When do you start and finish? What tools do you use? What do you like about your work? Write what you learnt.

> Did you know? Farmers in India grow food for more than 140 crore people. That is why India celebrates them with sayings like 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan'.

check.q: Which job is important for the town to stay healthy?
check.why: All jobs help others; sweepers keep the town clean and safe from disease.

summary: Many people work every day to make our lives possible.
Workers include farmers, tailors, potters, carpenters, doctors, teachers, drivers and sweepers.
Each worker uses special tools for the job.
People work in fields, offices, factories, hospitals, shops, roads and homes.
Housework — cooking, cleaning, caring — is real, important work, usually unpaid.
Family members should share housework fairly.
There is no boy-work or girl-work; anyone can do any job.
Children should study and play, not do paid work.
Every child aged 6–14 has a right to free schooling in India.
Every worker deserves respect and thanks.
practice: Name five workers and the tools they use.
What work is done at home? Who does it in your family?
Make a chart of work in your home and who does it.
Why should housework be shared?
Can a girl be a pilot? Can a boy be a cook? Explain.
Why should children not work in shops or factories?
Interview a worker near your home and write three things you learnt.
Why does every worker deserve respect?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch12-work-we-do-2.title: Work We Do (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch12-work-we-do-2.subtitle: Work at home, work for money, tools of the trade, and respect for every job

sections.md:
A lot of work happens inside every home: cooking, washing clothes and utensils, sweeping, fetching water, shopping, caring for babies and grandparents, helping children with homework. This work is not paid with money, but without it a family could not live.

**Survey:** Make a table with the names of everyone in your house and tick who does each job.

| Work | Mother | Father | Grandparent | Me |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cooking | | | | |
| Washing clothes | | | | |
| Buying vegetables | | | | |
| Watering plants | | | | |

Is the work shared fairly? Can boys and girls both do every job? Yes — every job at home can be done by anyone.

check.q: Can both boys and girls help with cooking and cleaning?
check.why: Housework is for everyone; any family member can learn and share it.

sections.md:
Many adults go out to work and earn money to buy food, clothes and other things. Some work in fields (farmers), some in shops (shopkeepers), some build (masons, carpenters), some heal (doctors, nurses), some teach, some drive (bus and auto drivers), some keep us safe (police, soldiers, firefighters).

Some people work from home — a tailor stitching clothes, a potter making pots, a weaver at a loom.

check.q: Who makes pots from clay?
check.why: A potter shapes clay on a wheel and bakes it to make pots.

sections.md:
| Worker | Tools |
|---|---|
| Farmer | plough, sickle, spade |
| Carpenter | saw, hammer, chisel |
| Tailor | needle, scissors, sewing machine, measuring tape |
| Doctor | stethoscope, thermometer |
| Cobbler | awl, thread, hammer |
| Mason | trowel, spirit level |

**Game:** One child names a tool; others shout out the worker who uses it.

check.q: Which worker uses a stethoscope?
check.why: A doctor listens to the heartbeat and breathing with a stethoscope.

sections.md:
The sweeper who cleans our street, the person who collects garbage, the washerman, the vegetable seller — all make our lives easier. We should greet them politely and say thank you.

Children's main work is to **study, play and help a little at home**. Children should not be made to do hard work for money; they have the right to go to school.

> Did you know? When we use dustbins and do not litter, we make the work of sanitation workers easier and safer.

summary: Housework is real work, though unpaid.
Housework should be shared by everyone.
Adults work for money in many jobs.
Some people work from home: tailors, potters, weavers.
Each job has its own tools.
Every worker deserves respect and thanks.
Children's work is to study, play and help a little.
practice: Make a table of who does which work at your home.
Name four jobs and the tools used in each.
Name two people who work from home.
Why should we respect sanitation workers?
Why should children not do paid hard work?
What would you like to be when you grow up? Why?

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch13-sharing-our-feel.title: Sharing Our Feelings
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch13-sharing-our-feel.subtitle: Happy, sad, left out, brave — understanding feelings and including everyone

sections.md:
Some days you wake up feeling like singing. Some days a small thing makes you cry. Sometimes you feel angry, scared, shy, proud or lonely — all in one day!

These are **feelings**, and **everyone** has them: children, parents, teachers, grandparents. Feelings are not good or bad; they are messages from inside us. What matters is how we **share** them and how we treat other people's feelings.

In this chapter we will:

- name different feelings,
- hear a story about a child who felt left out,
- learn how children who cannot see, hear or walk do their work in their own way,
- and think about how to make **everyone** feel included.

fig.alt: Animated faces showing happy, sad with a tear, angry turning red, and scared.

keyTerms: Feeling — what we sense inside, like joy or fear
Included — being made part of the group

check.q: Who has feelings?
check.why: Every person, of any age, feels happy, sad, angry or scared at times.

sections.md:
*This is our own retelling of the kind of story in the chapter; read the original in your NCERT book.*

Bhanu loved cricket. He knew every player's name and every score. But Bhanu used a **wheelchair**, because his legs could not walk.

One afternoon the class went out to play. Everyone ran to the ground shouting. Nobody asked Bhanu to come. He sat alone near the classroom door and watched. His throat felt tight. He wanted to say, *'I can play too!'* but he did not know how.

His friend Meena noticed him. She walked back. 'Why are you sitting here?' she asked.

'Nobody wanted me,' said Bhanu quietly.

Meena thought for a moment. Then she ran to the others. 'Bhanu knows more about cricket than all of us. He can be our **scorer** and **umpire**! And he can bowl from his chair.'

That day Bhanu kept the score, made fair decisions, and even bowled out the class champion! Everyone cheered. On the way home Bhanu was smiling the widest smile.

**Think:** How did Bhanu feel when he was left out? How did he feel at the end? What did Meena do that was kind?

check.q: What changed Bhanu's feeling in the story?
options: A friend found a way to include him
check.why: Meena noticed Bhanu was left out and found a role for him, so he felt included and happy.

sections.h: Have you ever felt left out?
sections.md:
Maybe you were not chosen for a team. Maybe friends spoke in a language you did not know. Maybe you were new in school. Feeling left out hurts.

When you feel this way:

- **say it** to a friend, teacher or parent — 'I feel sad because…'
- take a deep breath and count to five if you are angry,
- draw or write about it,
- remember: it will pass.

When you see someone else alone:

- go and say hello,
- ask them to join your game,
- listen when they talk,
- never laugh at someone or call them names.

**Role play:** In pairs, act out one child sitting alone and another inviting them to play. Swap roles.

check.q: What is a good thing to do when you feel angry?
options: Breathe deeply and talk about it
check.why: Calming down and putting the feeling into words helps us and does not hurt others.

sections.md:
Some children cannot see, hear, speak or walk the way most of us do. They are as clever, funny and curious as anyone. They just do some things **in a different way**.

| Challenge | How they manage |
|---|---|
| Cannot see | read **Braille** — raised dots felt with fingers; use a white cane; recognise people by voice |
| Cannot hear | use **sign language** with hands; lip reading; hearing aids |
| Cannot speak | use signs, writing, pictures |
| Cannot walk | use a wheelchair, crutches, ramps |

The **Braille** script was invented by **Louis Braille** in France, who lost his sight as a small boy. He made a system of six dots so that blind people could read and write.

**Activity:** Close your eyes and let a friend lead you around the classroom. Then try to identify objects only by touch. How did it feel? What helped you?

**Activity:** Try telling your friend 'I am hungry' without speaking. You have just used signs!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='200' fill='#ede7f6'/><g fill='#5e35b1'><circle cx='150' cy='60' r='14'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='150' cy='140' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='190' cy='60' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='190' cy='100' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='190' cy='140' r='14' opacity='.2'/></g><text x='130' y='190' font-size='16'>Braille: a</text><g fill='#5e35b1'><circle cx='330' cy='60' r='14'/><circle cx='330' cy='100' r='14'/><circle cx='330' cy='140' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='370' cy='60' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='370' cy='100' r='14' opacity='.2'/><circle cx='370' cy='140' r='14' opacity='.2'/></g><text x='310' y='190' font-size='16'>Braille: b</text><circle cx='470' cy='100' r='18' fill='#ffcc80'><animate attributeName='cx' values='450;520;450' dur='2.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='cy' values='60;140;60' dur='2.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><text x='440' y='190' font-size='16'>finger reading</text></svg>
