fig.alt: Two Braille cells for a and b with a moving fingertip.

check.q: Braille is read using…
check.why: Braille uses raised dots that are felt with the fingertips.

sections.md:
A school or town can be made friendly for everyone:

- **ramps** next to steps for wheelchairs,
- **Braille** books and talking computers,
- teachers who know **sign language**,
- toilets and buses that everyone can use,
- games where every child has a role.

Helping is good — but **ask first**. Say 'Would you like help?' instead of grabbing someone's wheelchair or hand. Treat everyone as a friend, not as someone to pity.

> Did you know? Many famous people have a disability. Helen Keller, who could neither see nor hear, learnt to read, write and speak, and travelled the world. India's Paralympic athletes have won many medals for the country.

check.q: What should you do before helping someone in a wheelchair?
check.why: Asking first respects the person and lets them decide what help they need.

sections.md:
The more words we know for feelings, the easier it is to share them. Try using these:

*happy, excited, proud, calm, surprised, shy, nervous, worried, sad, lonely, angry, jealous, grateful, brave.*

Play **Feelings Charades**: one child acts a feeling with face and body; others guess. Then say when you felt that way.

Finish these sentences in your notebook:

- I feel happy when …
- I feel scared when …
- I feel proud when …
- I can make a friend happy by …

check.q: Which word means feeling thankful?
check.why: Grateful means feeling thankful for something someone did or gave.

summary: Everyone has feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared, proud, lonely and more.
Feelings are messages; sharing them in words helps.
Being left out hurts; inviting others in makes them happy.
In the story, a friend included Bhanu as scorer, umpire and bowler.
Calm down by breathing and counting before talking about anger.
Children who cannot see, hear, speak or walk do things in different ways.
Braille, invented by Louis Braille, uses raised dots read by touch.
Sign language uses hand movements to talk.
Ramps, Braille books and sign language make places friendly for all.
Always ask before helping, and treat everyone as an equal friend.
practice: Name five feelings. When did you feel each one?
How did Bhanu feel at the start and at the end of the story?
What would you do if a classmate was sitting alone?
How does a child who cannot see read?
What is sign language?
Name two changes that make a school friendly for a child in a wheelchair.
Why should we ask before helping someone?
Write about a time you felt left out and what helped you.

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch13-sharing-our-feel.title: Sharing Our Feelings (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch13-sharing-our-feel.subtitle: Naming feelings, being a good friend, and including everyone

sections.md:
We all feel many things in a day: **happy, sad, angry, scared, proud, shy, jealous, excited**. All feelings are normal. What matters is what we do with them.

| Feeling | What might help |
|---|---|
| Angry | stop, take five slow breaths, count to ten |
| Sad | talk to a parent, teacher or friend |
| Scared | hold someone's hand, ask for help |
| Happy | share the joy! |

**Activity – feelings faces:** Draw four faces showing four feelings. Under each, write one time you felt that way.

check.q: What is a good first step when you feel very angry?
check.why: Slow breathing calms the body so we can think before we act.

sections.md:
A good friend listens, takes turns, shares and says sorry when wrong. If a classmate is teased, a good friend does not laugh but helps and tells a teacher.

Sometimes a child cannot walk, see or hear well, or speaks a different language. Such children like playing and learning just as much as anyone. We can include them: choose games everyone can play, speak clearly, offer help *if they want it*, and never make fun.

check.q: A new child at school uses a wheelchair. What should you do?
options: Invite them to a game everyone can play
check.why: Including everyone kindly — and asking before helping — makes a friend feel welcome.

sections.md: Your body belongs to you. If anyone makes you feel uncomfortable or scared, say **No**, move away, and **tell a trusted adult** — a parent, grandparent or teacher. Keeping such things secret is never needed. In India you can also call the free Childline number **1098**.

check.q: If someone makes you feel unsafe, what should you do?
options: Say no and tell a trusted adult
check.why: Telling a trusted adult gets you help; it is never your fault.

summary: All feelings are normal; we choose how we act on them.
Calm anger with slow breaths and counting.
Talk about sad or scared feelings with someone you trust.
Good friends listen, share, take turns and say sorry.
Include children with disabilities and new classmates kindly.
Say no, move away and tell an adult if you feel unsafe; Childline is 1098.
practice: Name six feelings.
What do you do when you feel sad?
Write about a time a friend helped you.
How can you include a classmate who cannot see well?
What should you do if someone makes you feel unsafe?
Draw a feelings face for 'proud'.

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch14-the-story-of-foo.title: The Story of Food
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch14-the-story-of-foo.subtitle: Eating together, food then and now, mid-day meals, and never wasting a grain

sections.md:
*An original story to begin.*

Anu's family of seven sits on a mat for dinner. Grandmother serves hot rotis, Father pours dal, little Chintu spills his water and everybody laughs. Grandfather tells how, when he was a boy, the whole joint family of twenty people ate together in the courtyard, and the women ate last after serving everyone.

'Today,' says Mother, 'we all eat together. Nobody waits hungry.'

Anu thinks: food is not just something we eat. It has a **story** — where it grows, who cooks it, how we share it, and how it has changed over time. That is what this chapter is about.

check.q: In Grandfather's childhood, who often ate last?
check.why: In many old joint families, women served everyone first and ate last.

sections.md:
Think about your own home.

- Do all of you eat together, or at different times?
- Who cooks? Who serves?
- Does anyone eat after everyone else?
- Do you sit on the floor, at a table, or in front of the TV?

In some homes, the person who cooks eats last and may get the leftover food. That is not fair. Everyone in the family should get **enough good food** and a chance to eat with others.

**Eating together** is a happy time to talk, laugh and share the day's stories.

**Activity:** Make a table for your family: name, who cooks, who serves, who eats when.

check.q: Why is eating together good?
check.why: Mealtimes together help families talk, share and make sure everyone gets fed.

sections.md:
Ask your grandparents what they ate as children. You may be surprised!

| Then | Now |
|---|---|
| bajra, jowar, ragi rotis | mostly wheat and rice |
| food from the farm and garden | packets from shops |
| cooked on chulha in clay pots | gas, cooker, microwave |
| buttermilk, lassi, sherbet | soft drinks and juices |
| home-made snacks — chana, laddoo | chips, noodles, biscuits |
| seasonal fruits | fruits all year |

Some changes are good: more variety, cleaner fuel, food reaches far places. But packaged junk food has too much salt, sugar and oil. **Millets** like ragi and bajra, which grandparents ate, are very healthy — and now people are eating them again!

check.q: Which grain did many grandparents eat that is very healthy?
check.why: Millets like ragi and bajra are full of goodness and were common food in earlier times.

sections.md:
In many government schools in India, children get a **hot cooked lunch** every school day. It is called the **mid-day meal** (now PM-POSHAN). It may be rice and dal, khichdi, roti and sabzi, sometimes with an egg, fruit or milk.

Why is it important?

- Some children come to school hungry. A good meal helps them learn and grow.
- More children come to school.
- Children of all families sit and eat **together**, as friends.

Rules for a happy mid-day meal: wash hands with soap, sit in a line, take only what you can eat, and help keep the place clean.

**Find out:** Does your school serve a meal? What is the menu this week?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#fff8e1'/><rect y='180' width='600' height='60' fill='#bcaaa4'/><g id='k'><circle cx='0' cy='120' r='18' fill='#8d6e63'/><rect x='-16' y='138' width='32' height='40' rx='8' fill='#42a5f5'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='188' rx='26' ry='7' fill='#cfd8dc'/></g><use href='#k' x='120'/><use href='#k' x='240'/><use href='#k' x='360'/><use href='#k' x='480'/><g><ellipse cx='0' cy='184' rx='14' ry='5' fill='#ffd54f'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='120 -80;120 0' dur='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g><ellipse cx='0' cy='184' rx='14' ry='5' fill='#ffd54f'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='360 -80;360 0' dur='1.5s' begin='.7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='190' y='40' font-size='20'>Mid-day meal: eat together</text></svg>
fig.caption: Children sitting in a row as hot khichdi is served on their plates.
fig.alt: Row of children with plates, food dropping onto them.

check.q: What is the mid-day meal?
options: A hot lunch given to children in school
check.why: The mid-day meal is a free cooked lunch served to children in many government schools.

sections.md:
Every festival has its special food: **sewaiyan** on Eid, **gujiya** on Holi, **pongal** at Pongal, **til-gud** on Makar Sankranti, **cake** at Christmas, **karah prasad** at the gurudwara, **modak** on Ganesh Chaturthi, **pitha** in Assam during Bihu.

Every region also has its own food, because different crops grow there:

- Punjab: makki ki roti, sarson ka saag
- Kerala: appam, fish curry, coconut
- Gujarat: dhokla, thepla
- West Bengal: rice, fish, mishti doi
- Rajasthan: dal-baati-churma
- Northeast: bamboo shoot dishes, rice

**Activity:** Bring a recipe from home and make a class recipe book!

check.q: Which sweet is linked with Ganesh Chaturthi?
check.why: Modak, a sweet dumpling, is traditionally made on Ganesh Chaturthi.

sections.md:
A single grain of rice reaches your plate after the hard work of the **farmer**, the transporter, the shopkeeper and the cook. Yet a lot of food gets thrown away at weddings, parties and even at home.

At the same time, many people in the world **do not get enough to eat**. Some children sleep hungry.

What can we do?

- Take **small helpings**; you can always take more.
- Finish what is on your plate.
- Store food properly so it does not spoil.
- Leftover good food can be shared or eaten next meal.
- Some groups collect extra food from parties and give it to people who need it.

> Did you know? Many Indian families teach children to touch their forehead with respect if a roti falls — a sign that food is precious.

check.q: What is the best way to avoid wasting food?
options: Take small helpings and finish them
check.why: Taking small helpings and finishing them means nothing goes in the dustbin.

sections.md:
- **Wash hands** with soap before and after eating.
- Eat **fresh**, home-cooked food more than packets.
- Eat **many colours**: green leaves, yellow dal, red tomatoes, white curd.
- Drink clean water.
- Chew slowly and do not talk with a full mouth.
- Do not run or play right after a heavy meal.
- Say thank you to the person who cooked!

check.q: When should we wash our hands?
check.why: Washing hands before and after meals keeps germs away from our food and mouth.

summary: Food has a story: who grows, cooks, serves and eats it.
Families eat in different ways; everyone deserves enough good food.
Eating together is a time to share and talk.
Food habits have changed from grandparents' time to now.
Millets like ragi and bajra are healthy traditional grains.
Junk food has too much salt, sugar and oil.
The mid-day meal gives children a free hot lunch at school.
Festivals and regions have special foods.
Food is precious; many people go hungry, so we should not waste it.
Wash hands, eat fresh, colourful food and thank the cook.
practice: Who cooks and serves food in your home? Who eats last?
Write three foods your grandparents ate that you rarely eat.
What is the mid-day meal? Why is it useful?
Name the special food of two festivals.
Name a dish from two different states of India.
Why should we not waste food? Give two ways to save food.
Write four good food habits.
Draw your favourite healthy plate.

rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch14-the-story-of-foo.title: The Story of Food (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-c.ch14-the-story-of-foo.subtitle: Who grows, cooks and serves our food — and how we keep it safe and fair

sections.md:
A roti on your plate has a long story:

1. A **farmer** ploughs the field and sows wheat seeds.
2. Rain or canal water helps the plants grow; the farmer removes weeds.
3. The crop is **harvested** and the grain separated from the stalks.
4. A truck takes the grain to a **market (mandi)**, then to a shop.
5. It is ground into **atta** at a flour mill (*chakki*).
6. Someone at home kneads the dough and cooks the roti.

Many hands — farmers, drivers, shopkeepers, millers and cooks — help bring us every meal.

check.q: Where is wheat ground into atta?
check.why: A chakki or flour mill grinds wheat grains into flour.

sections.md:
Who cooks in your house? Who serves? Who eats first? In many families, everyone now eats together and helps clear up. Ways of eating differ too: some people eat with hands from a banana leaf, some with spoons from steel plates, some sitting on the floor, some at a table. All are fine ways.

In some families and schools there is a **community kitchen** — like a langar at a gurdwara or the **mid-day meal** in schools — where many people eat the same food together.

check.q: What is the meal served to children in many government schools called?
check.why: The mid-day meal scheme gives children a cooked lunch at school.

sections.md:
- Wash hands with soap before eating and cooking.
- Wash fruits and vegetables before use.
- Keep food **covered** so flies cannot sit on it.
- Do not eat stale or bad-smelling food.
- Drink clean, boiled or filtered water.

> Did you know? Pickles, papad and dried mango (aamchur) are old Indian ways to make food last for months — salt, oil and sun-drying stop germs from growing.

check.q: Why should food be kept covered?
options: So flies and dust cannot spoil it
check.why: Flies and dust carry germs that can make food unsafe.

sections.md: Some families do not get enough food. Government ration shops give grains at low prices, and many people donate food. We can help by not wasting food and by sharing. **Activity:** trace the story of one food you ate today — rice, an egg, or milk — and draw each step from where it came from to your plate.

summary: Food passes from farmer to market to mill/shop to kitchen.
Many workers help bring us each meal.
Families eat in different ways — all are fine.
Langars and mid-day meals feed many people together.
Wash hands, wash vegetables, cover food, drink clean water.
Pickling and sun-drying help food last.
Share food and never waste it.
practice: Write the steps by which wheat becomes a roti.
Name three workers who help bring food to us.
What is a mid-day meal?
Write four rules for keeping food safe.
Name two Indian ways of storing food for a long time.
Draw the story of milk from cow to glass.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch15-making-pots.title: Making Pots
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch15-making-pots.subtitle: From wet clay to a cool matka — the potter's craft, old and new

sections.h: A pot that keeps water cool
sections.md:
On a hot May afternoon, Grandmother pours water from the **matka** in the corner. It is cool and sweet — without any fridge! How?

A clay pot has tiny holes, too small to see. A little water seeps out and **evaporates** from the outside, and this takes heat away, so the water inside stays cool.

People have made pots from clay for **thousands of years**. In this chapter we will:

- look at the many containers in our homes,
- learn how a potter makes a pot,
- find out about very old pots found by digging,
- and make a little pot ourselves!

check.q: Why does water stay cool in a matka?
options: Water seeping out evaporates and takes heat away
It is kept in the sun
check.why: Tiny pores let a little water reach the surface, and its evaporation cools the pot.

sections.md:
Look around your kitchen. What do we keep things in?

| Container | Made of | Stores |
|---|---|---|
| Matka, surahi | clay | drinking water |
| Dabba, steel tin | steel | flour, dal, sugar |
| Bottle, jar | glass or plastic | pickle, oil, water |
| Basket | bamboo, cane | vegetables, fruits |
| Bori (sack) | jute | grain |
| Handi, kulhad | clay | curd, tea |
| Gagar, lota | brass, copper | water |

In villages, large **clay bins** called *kothi* are used to store grain for months.

Plastic is cheap and light, but it does not rot and fills our land and rivers with waste. Clay, jute, bamboo and metal containers are better for the earth — and clay pots simply return to soil when broken.

**Activity:** List ten containers in your home and what each is made of.

check.q: Which container material simply returns to the soil when broken?
check.why: Clay comes from soil, so broken clay pots crumble back into earth.

sections.h: How a potter makes a pot
sections.md:
Visit a **potter** (kumhar) if you can. Here are the steps:

1. **Collect clay** from a pond or riverbank.
2. **Clean it** — remove stones, roots and grass.
3. **Soak and knead** the clay with water, pressing it with feet and hands until it is soft and smooth, like dough.
4. Put a lump on the **potter's wheel** and spin it fast.
5. With wet hands, press the centre and pull the sides up — a pot rises like magic!
6. Cut it off the wheel with a thread and **dry** it in the shade, then in the sun.
7. **Bake** (fire) the dry pots in a hot **kiln** (bhatti). This makes them hard and red.
8. **Paint and decorate** them.

The whole family often helps: someone kneads clay, someone shapes pots, someone paints. Potters also make **diyas** for Diwali, **kulhads** for tea, **gamlas** (flower pots), toys and idols.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='c' x1='0' x2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#a1887f'/><stop offset='.5' stop-color='#d7a86e'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#a1887f'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff3e0'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='240' rx='150' ry='24' fill='#5d4037'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='232' rx='150' ry='24' fill='#795548'/><g><line x1='160' y1='232' x2='440' y2='232' stroke='#4e342e' stroke-width='3'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='scale' values='1 1;-1 1;1 1' dur='1s' additive='sum' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><path d='M250 230 q-20 -50 20 -90 h60 q40 40 20 90Z' fill='url(#c)'><animate attributeName='d' values='M260 230 q-10 -20 10 -30 h60 q20 10 10 30Z;M250 230 q-30 -50 20 -90 h60 q50 40 20 90Z;M250 230 q-30 -50 20 -90 h60 q50 40 20 90Z' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M200 150 q30 10 50 40' stroke='#ffcc80' stroke-width='16' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M400 150 q-30 10 -50 40' stroke='#ffcc80' stroke-width='16' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='200' y='290' font-size='18'>A pot rises on the spinning wheel</text></svg>
fig.caption: On a spinning potter's wheel, a lump of clay is pulled up into a pot.
fig.alt: Animated wheel with clay growing into a pot between two hands.

keyTerms: Potter (kumhar) — a person who makes pots
Kiln (bhatti) — a very hot oven for baking pots
Knead — press and fold to make soft

check.q: Why are pots baked in a kiln?
options: To make them hard and strong
check.why: Firing in a hot kiln turns dried clay hard and strong so it does not melt in water.

sections.md:
When people dig at very old places, they often find **broken pieces of pots**. These tell us how people lived long ago.

About **4,500 years ago**, people of the **Harappan civilisation** (cities like Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Lothal and Dholavira) made beautiful red pots with black painted designs — fish, leaves, circles and lines. They also made clay toys: carts with wheels, animals and whistles!

Clay pots do not rust or rot, so they last for thousands of years under the ground. That is why they are like a **diary from the past**.

> Did you know? The museum at Delhi and many state museums show Harappan pots. If you visit, look at their designs and compare them with pots today.

items.what: Harappan people make painted red pots and clay toys
Kings' kitchens store grain and oil in huge clay jars
Matkas, handis and clay chulhas in most homes

fig.caption: Clay pots through time.

check.q: What do old pots found by digging tell us?
check.why: Old pots show what people ate, stored and liked to draw, so they teach us about the past.

sections.md:
**You need:** some clay or mud, water, a plank, a small stick.

1. Mix clay with a little water and knead it till smooth.
2. Roll a ball. Press your thumb in the middle to make a hollow — a **pinch pot**.
3. Or roll long 'snakes' of clay and coil them round and round to build a pot — a **coil pot**.
4. Smooth it with wet fingers.
5. Scratch designs with the stick.
6. Dry it in the shade for two or three days.
7. Paint it!

Your pot is not baked, so do not fill it with water — use it for pencils or dry flowers.

**Discuss:** What was difficult? Why do potters need so much skill and practice?

check.q: Why should you not fill your unbaked clay pot with water?
check.why: Unbaked clay gets soft again when wet, so the pot would lose its shape.

sections.md:
Many potters today find life hard, because people buy cheap plastic and steel instead. Yet clay pots are healthy and earth-friendly.

We can help by:

- buying clay diyas at Diwali instead of plastic lights,
- using a matka in summer,
- drinking tea in kulhads,
- using clay gamlas for plants.

Craft, like pottery, weaving and carpentry, is a skill passed from parents to children over many years. It needs patience, strength and an artist's eye.

check.q: Which is an earth-friendly choice?
check.why: Kulhads are made of clay and return to soil, so they do not pollute like plastic.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch15-making-pots-2.title: Making Pots (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch15-making-pots-2.subtitle: Pots for every need, pots through history, and pots you can make

sections.md:
Look closely and you will see that pots come in many **shapes and sizes**, and each shape has a reason.

- A **surahi** has a long, thin neck. Water pours out slowly and dust cannot get in easily.
- A **matka** is round and wide, so it holds a lot of water.
- A **kulhad** is a small cup for tea or lassi. After use it can be thrown away — it simply goes back to the soil.
- A **diya** is a tiny flat lamp for Diwali.
- A **handi** is a cooking pot with a wide mouth, used to cook dal or set curd.
- A **gamla** is a flower pot with a hole at the bottom so extra water can drain out.

In different parts of India, potters make their own special pots. Khurja in Uttar Pradesh is famous for glazed pottery, Manipur has pots shaped by hand without a wheel, and in Bengal clay figures are made for festivals.

**Think:** Why does a flower pot need a hole but a water matka must not have one?

check.q: Why does a gamla (flower pot) have a hole at the bottom?
options: So extra water can drain out
check.why: Too much water rots plant roots, so the hole lets the extra water drain away.

sections.h: Pots tell us about the past
sections.md:
Long, long ago — about **4,500 years ago** — people lived in big cities like **Harappa** and **Mohenjodaro**. When people dig the ground at such places today, they find **broken pieces of pots**.

These pots were red with black designs painted on them: circles, fish scales, leaves and lines. Because clay pots do not rot when baked, they last for thousands of years under the ground.

From such pots we learn:

- what people stored (grain, oil, water),
- how skilled their potters were,
- what designs they liked.

Today we keep such old pots safely in **museums**. If you visit a museum, look for the pottery section!

**Did you know?** Pieces of broken pots are called *potsherds*, and they help history detectives tell how old a place is.

check.q: Why do old baked clay pots last thousands of years under the ground?
options: Baked clay becomes hard and does not rot
check.why: Firing in a kiln makes clay hard like stone, so it survives long after wood or cloth have rotted away.

sections.h: Let us make our own pot
sections.md:
You can be a little potter at home or school.

**Clay pot:** Take some soft clay (or wet soil mixed well with a little water). Knead it until smooth. Make a ball, press your thumb in the middle and pinch the sides upward to make a small bowl. Or roll thin clay snakes and coil them round and round, one on top of another, then smooth the sides. Let it dry in the shade, then paint it.

**Paper pot (papier-mâché):** Tear old newspaper into small pieces and soak them in water overnight. Squeeze out the water, mix the pulp with a little flour glue (maida + water). Spread the pulp over an upturned bowl, let it dry for two days, take it off and paint it.

Wash your hands afterwards and clean up the mess — every potter keeps the workplace tidy!

**Talk about it:** Which was harder — the clay pot or the paper pot? What could you keep in your pot?

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch16-games-we-play.title: Games We Play
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch16-games-we-play.subtitle: Kho-kho, gilli-danda, ludo and cricket — rules, teams, fair play and games of long ago

sections.md:
*Tring!* The recess bell rings and the playground explodes with noise. One group is playing **kho-kho**, another is drawing boxes for **stapu** (hopscotch), a few boys and girls are arguing about who is out in **cricket**, and two friends sit under the neem tree with a **ludo** board.

Games make us happy, make our bodies strong, and teach us to play with others. In this chapter we will look at:

- games played **indoors** and **outdoors**,
- games needing **things** and games needing nothing,
- **rules** and **teams**,
- games our **grandparents** played,
- and why **fair play** matters.

check.q: Which game is usually played indoors on a board?
check.why: Ludo is played with a board, dice and counters, often sitting indoors.

sections.md:
| Outdoor games | Indoor games |
|---|---|
| kho-kho, kabaddi | ludo, snakes and ladders |
| cricket, football | carrom, chess |
| gilli-danda, pithoo (lagori) | cards, antakshari |
| stapu, skipping rope | puzzles, five stones (gitte) |
| hide and seek, chor-police | pallanguzhi (Kerala/Tamil Nadu) |

Outdoor games make us run, jump and breathe fresh air. Indoor games make us think, count and plan. Both are good!

Some games need **things**: a bat and ball, a rope, marbles (kanche), a carrom board. Others need **nothing** — just friends and space, like kho-kho, kabaddi, hide and seek and *poshampa*.

**Survey:** Ask ten friends their favourite game. Make a tally chart. Which is the class favourite?

check.q: Which game needs no equipment at all?
check.why: Kabaddi needs only players and a marked ground, no bat, ball or board.

sections.md:
Imagine cricket where the bowler can throw the ball from anywhere and the batter never gets out. Chaos! **Rules** make a game fair and fun.

**Kho-kho rules (simple):**

- Two teams. One team sits in a line, each player facing the opposite way from the next.
- One player chases; one runner from the other team runs.
- The chaser cannot cross the line between sitting players. To pass the chase, she touches a sitting teammate's back and says **'kho!'** — that player gets up and chases.
- When a runner is touched, she is out.
- After a fixed time, teams change places. The team that catches more runners in less time wins.

**Gilli-danda:** A small pointed stick (gilli) is hit with a long stick (danda) to make it jump up, then struck far. Fielders try to catch it.

**Play and decide:** Make up a new game with your friends. Write down its rules.

check.q: In kho-kho, what does the chaser say to pass the chase?
check.why: The chaser touches a sitting teammate and says 'kho', and that teammate becomes the chaser.

sections.md:
Many games are played in **teams**: kabaddi, kho-kho, cricket, football, tug of war. In a team, everyone has a job. In cricket there are batters, bowlers, a wicketkeeper and fielders. The **captain** plans and encourages the team.

Good team players:

- pass the ball instead of keeping it,
- cheer when a teammate does well,
- do not blame anyone when the team loses,
- listen to the captain,
- shake hands with the other team at the end.

**How do we choose teams?** Some groups pick by *eeny-meeny* rhymes, some by tossing a coin, some by the two captains choosing turns. Make sure nobody is always left for last — mix teams so that everyone gets a fair chance.

check.q: What does a good team player do when the team loses?
check.why: Good team players accept losses calmly, encourage others and try again next time.

sections.md:
Is it fun if someone cheats? No! **Fair play** means:

- following the rules,
- accepting the umpire's or referee's decision,
- not hurting anyone on purpose,
- letting boys and girls, younger and older children, and children with disabilities play too,
- winning without boasting and losing without sulking.

There is no 'boys' game' or 'girls' game'. India has great women cricketers, wrestlers, badminton players, boxers and kabaddi players, and boys enjoy skipping and stapu too!

check.q: Which is fair play?
check.why: Accepting the umpire's decision keeps the game fair and friendly for everyone.

sections.md:
Ask your grandparents what they played. You may hear about:

- **gilli-danda** and **kanche** (marbles),
- **pithoo / lagori** — knock down a pile of seven stones with a ball, then rebuild it while dodging,
- **chaupar / pachisi** — an old board game played with cowrie shells,
- **pallanguzhi / ali guli mane** — a board with pits and seeds,
- **gutte / five stones** — toss and catch small stones,
- flying **kites** on rooftops.

Many of these needed no money — just stones, sticks, seeds or a cloth ball. **Snakes and ladders** itself began in India long ago as a game called *moksha patam*.

> Did you know? Kabaddi and kho-kho are Indian games now played in leagues watched on TV, and chess is believed to have grown from an old Indian game called *chaturanga*.

check.why: Snakes and ladders grew from the old Indian game moksha patam.

Some games need equipment; others, like kabaddi and kho-kho, need none.

Team games need cooperation, a captain and team spirit.
Fair play means following rules, accepting decisions and including everyone.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch16-games-we-play-2.title: Games We Play (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch16-games-we-play-2.subtitle: Rules, teams, games of long ago, and making up your own game

sections.md:
Imagine playing **kho-kho** where anyone can run anywhere, or cricket where the batter never gets out. It would be confusing and no fun!

**Rules** tell everyone:

- how to start the game,
- what each player may and may not do,
- how to win or lose,
- what happens if someone breaks a rule.

When everyone follows the same rules, the game is **fair**. A good player plays by the rules even when no one is watching.

Sometimes children change the rules a little — for example, in gully cricket, "hitting the wall is a four" or "one-tip-one-hand is out". That is fine, as long as **everyone agrees before** the game begins.

**Activity:** Pick one game you play. Write three of its rules.

check.q: When is it fine to change the rules of a game?
options: When everyone agrees before the game starts
check.why: A rule change is fair only when all the players agree to it before playing.

sections.md:
Some games are played **alone** — like hopscotch (stapu), or a puzzle. Some need **two players** — like carrom, chess or ludo with a friend. Others are played in **teams** — kabaddi, kho-kho, football, cricket and hockey.

In a team game:

- Players help each other, pass the ball and plan together.
- A **captain** leads the team.
- Everyone wins or loses together — so we do not blame one player.

When two teams are chosen, it is kind to make them **equal**, so the game is exciting for both sides. Including a child who is new, younger or cannot run fast makes the game better for everyone.

**Did you know?** Kabaddi and kho-kho began in India, and kabaddi is now played in many countries.

check.q: Which of these is a team game?
check.why: Kabaddi is played by two teams, each with several players working together.

sections.h: Games of long ago and games we make
sections.md:
Ask your grandparents what they played as children. You may hear of **gilli-danda**, **pithoo** (seven stones / lagori), **kanche** (marbles), **gutte** (five stones), **pachisi** and **chaupar**. Most of these need no money — just sticks, stones, seeds or a cloth ball.

Games also differ by place: children near rivers swim and row, hill children play in snow, and in deserts children play with sand and sticks.

Today many children play on mobile phones and computers. These can be fun, but too much screen time hurts the eyes and keeps us indoors. **Outdoor games** make our bodies strong and help us make friends.

**Make your own game:** With your friends, invent a new game. Decide its name, what you need, how many players, the rules and how someone wins. Play it and see if the rules need fixing!

**Talk about it:** Is there a game boys and girls do not play together in your area? Why? Should everyone be allowed to play every game?

Rules may be changed only if all players agree before playing.
Some games are played alone, some by two, some in teams.
Team games teach working together, leadership and sharing wins and losses.
Kabaddi and kho-kho began in India.
Elders played gilli-danda, pithoo, kanche and gutte with simple things.
Outdoor play keeps us healthy; too much screen time is harmful.
Everyone, boys and girls, can play every game.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch17-here-comes-a-let.title: Here Comes a Letter
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch17-here-comes-a-let.subtitle: Postcards, PIN codes, post offices and phones — how messages travel

sections.md:
*An original story to begin.*

The postman's cycle bell rings — *tring tring!* 'Dak aayi!' calls Raju, racing to the gate. It is a **postcard** from his cousin Meera in Guwahati. She writes that she has a new puppy named Bijli, and that it rained so hard the school closed for a day. Raju reads it three times and keeps it under his pillow.

How did this little card travel more than a thousand kilometres to Raju's house in Jaipur? Who carried it? How did it know where to go? Let us follow its journey.

check.q: Who brings letters to our homes?
check.why: The postman collects letters from the post office and delivers them to each address.

sections.md:
At a **post office** you can buy:

- **Postcard** — a cheap card; the message is open, anyone can read it. Write on one side; address on the other.
- **Inland letter** — a blue sheet that you write on, fold and seal. Your message is hidden.
- **Envelope** — put your letter inside, stick stamps, and write the address on the front.
- **Registered post / Speed Post** — for important things; reaches fast and you get a receipt.
- **Parcel** — to send packets and gifts.
- **Money order** — to send money to someone (older way, still used in some places).

A **stamp** shows that you have paid for the letter's journey. Stamps have pictures of great people, birds, animals, monuments and festivals. Many children collect stamps — this hobby is called **philately**.

fig.alt: Postcard layout and an animated letter dropping into a red letter box.

check.q: Which can anyone read on the way?
check.why: A postcard is open, so its message can be seen by anyone who handles it.

sections.md:
For a letter to reach the right house, the **address** must be clear and complete:

> Name
> House number, street
> Area / village
> City / district, State
> **PIN code**

The **PIN code** (Postal Index Number) is a **six-digit number** for each area in India. The first digit tells the region of India; the rest narrow it down to a single post office. It helps workers sort letters quickly.

Also write **your own address** (the sender's address) on the back or top-left, so the letter can come back if it cannot be delivered.

**Activity:** Write your full home address with PIN code. Find out your school's PIN code too.

check.q: How many digits are in an Indian PIN code?
check.why: Every Indian PIN code has six digits that point to one post office area.

sections.md:
1. Meera writes the postcard and **drops it in the red post box**.
2. A postman **collects** letters from the box at fixed times.
3. At the post office, letters are **stamped with a date seal** so they cannot be reused, and **sorted** by PIN code.
4. Bags of letters go by **van, bus, train or aeroplane** to the far city. (Some trains even had special mail coaches!)
5. At Raju's local post office, letters are sorted again by street.
6. The postman **delivers** the card to Raju's door.

In hilly and remote places, postmen walk for hours, cross rivers and climb mountains to deliver mail. In the old days there were runners called **harkaras** who ran with mail bags, ringing bells! India's post office network is one of the biggest in the world, with a post office even in the high mountains of Ladakh and Himachal.

items.what: Date-stamped and sorted by PIN code
Travels by van, train or plane

fig.caption: How a letter travels from sender to receiver.

check.q: Why is a letter stamped with a date seal?
options: So the stamp cannot be used again
check.why: The seal marks the stamp as used and shows the date the letter was posted.

sections.md:
Visit a post office with a grown-up. You will see:

- counters to buy stamps, postcards and envelopes,
- a **weighing scale** for parcels (heavier parcels cost more),
- people sorting letters into pigeonholes,
- a counter for savings accounts — many people save money in the post office too,
- big sacks of mail.

**Interview the postman:** What time do you start? How many letters do you deliver in a day? What is hardest about your job? What do you do in rain?

Say thank you to your postman — in sun, rain and cold, they bring our news!

check.q: Why does a post office have a weighing scale?
options: To find the cost of sending parcels
check.why: The cost of sending a parcel depends on its weight, so it is weighed first.

sections.md:
Letters take a few days. Today we have faster ways:

- **Telephone and mobile phones** — talk at once, anywhere.
- **SMS and chat messages** on phones.
- **Email** — letters sent on a computer in seconds.
- **Video calls** — see the person while you talk.

In earlier times, people sent messages through **pigeons**, drum beats, smoke signals, and the **telegram** — short messages sent through wires, very costly, so people used few words like 'ARRIVING MONDAY'.

Yet a handwritten letter is special — you can keep it for years and read it again. Grandparents treasure old letters!

**Activity:** Write a postcard or letter to a friend or grandparent and post it. Wait and see how many days it takes to arrive.

check.q: Which is the fastest way to send a written message today?
check.why: Email and SMS reach in seconds over the phone or internet network.

summary: Letters carry news between people far apart.
Post offices sell postcards, inland letters, envelopes, stamps; send parcels and Speed Post.
A postcard is open; an inland letter and envelope keep the message private.
A stamp shows the cost of sending is paid; collecting stamps is philately.
A full address includes name, house, area, city, state and PIN code.
The PIN code has six digits and helps sort letters.
Letters are collected, date-stamped, sorted, carried by road, rail or air, and delivered.
Postmen work in all weather and even reach remote mountain villages.
Parcels are weighed to decide the cost.
Phones, SMS, email and video calls are faster ways to send messages.
Long ago people used pigeons, runners, drums and telegrams.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch17-here-comes-a-let.title: Here Comes a Letter (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch17-here-comes-a-let.subtitle: Writing an address, the postcard and inland letter, and other ways to send news

sections.md:
A letter can only reach the right person if the **address** is complete and clear. Write it in this order:

1. Name of the person
2. House number, street or lane
3. Area or village, post office
4. City or district, state
5. **PIN code** — six numbers

For example:

> Ms Meena Sharma
> 12, Gandhi Gali, Ram Nagar
> Jaipur, Rajasthan — 302001

The **PIN code** (Postal Index Number) tells the post office exactly which area the letter must go to. Without it, sorting takes longer.

Also write **your own address** (the sender's address), so the letter can come back if it cannot be delivered.

**Activity:** Write your complete home address with your PIN code.

check.q: How many digits does an Indian PIN code have?
check.why: An Indian PIN code has six digits that point to one particular post office area.

sections.md:
At the post office you can buy different things to send your message:

| Item | What it is | Who can read it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Postcard** | A single card, stamp already printed | Anyone who handles it — it is open |
| **Inland letter** | A blue sheet that folds and sticks shut | Only the receiver |
| **Envelope** | A cover; you put your letter inside and stick a stamp | Only the receiver |

A postcard is the cheapest. If your message is private, use an inland letter or an envelope.

A **stamp** shows that you have paid for the letter's journey. The postman puts a **postmark** (a round seal with the date and place) on it so the stamp cannot be used again.

**Did you know?** Some letters are sent by **speed post** or **registered post** so they reach faster or safely with a receipt.

check.q: Which should you use to send a private message?
check.why: An envelope or inland letter is closed, so only the receiver reads the message.

sections.md:
Long ago, before post offices, people sent messages through **messengers** on foot or horseback, by **drum beats**, by **smoke signals** and even with trained **pigeons**!

Today we also send messages by:

- **telephone** and mobile phone calls,
- **SMS** and chat messages,
- **email** on a computer,
- **video calls**, where we can see the person.

These are very fast. But a handwritten letter is special — it can be kept for years, read again and again, and shows that someone took time for you.

**Write a letter:** Write a short letter to a grandparent, friend or cousin. Start with the date and a greeting ("Dear Nani,"), share your news, ask how they are, and end with "Your loving …" and your name. Then fold it, write the address and post it!

**Talk about it:** Who brings letters to your house? Have you ever thanked the postman?

summary: An address has name, house, street, area, city, state and PIN code.
The PIN code has six digits and helps sorting.
Always write the sender's address too.
A postcard is open; an inland letter or envelope keeps a message private.
A stamp pays for the letter; a postmark stops the stamp being reused.
Speed post and registered post are faster or safer services.
Long ago messengers, drums, smoke and pigeons carried news.
Today phones, SMS, email and video calls are fast ways to send messages.

What is the difference between a postcard and an inland letter?
Why is a postmark put on a stamp?
Name three old ways and three new ways of sending messages.
Write a short letter to a friend telling about your school.
Why should the sender's address be written on a letter?

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch18-a-house-like-thi.title: A House Like This
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch18-a-house-like-thi.subtitle: Igloos, houseboats, stilt houses and flats — why homes look so different

sections.h: Why do we need a house?
sections.md:
Imagine sleeping outside on a rainy monsoon night, or on a freezing winter night in Ladakh, or under the burning sun in Rajasthan. Not nice!

A **house** protects us from **rain, sun, cold, wind** and wild animals. It keeps our things safe. It is where the family eats, sleeps, talks and celebrates.

But houses across India — and the world — look very different. Some are tall, some are on water, some are made of snow! In this chapter we will find out:

- the different kinds of houses,
- what they are made of,
- why houses are built differently in different places,
- and what is special about our own home.

check.q: Which is NOT a reason we need a house?
check.why: Houses protect us from weather and keep things safe; they do not change the weather.

sections.md:
| House | Made of | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Kutcha house (hut) | mud, straw, bamboo, leaves | many villages |
| Pucca house | bricks, cement, iron, stone | towns and villages |
| Flats / apartments | cement, iron, bricks; many floors | big cities |
| Tent | cloth, plastic, poles | for travellers, shepherds, camps |
| Houseboat | wood, on water | Dal Lake, Kashmir; Kerala backwaters |
| Stilt house | bamboo and wood, on poles | Assam and northeast, near rivers |
| Igloo | blocks of snow and ice | very cold Arctic lands |
| Caravan | a home on wheels | travelling families |

A **kutcha** house is made of materials like mud and straw; it is cool, but needs repairs after rain. A **pucca** house is strong and lasts many years.

**Activity:** Look at houses on your way to school. Which kinds do you see? Draw two.

check.q: Which house floats on water?
check.why: A houseboat is a home built on a boat, as on Dal Lake in Kashmir.

sections.md:
Why don't all houses look the same? Because people build homes to suit the **weather** and the **materials** found nearby.

- **Lots of rain (Assam, Kerala, Northeast):** steep **sloping roofs** so rain slides off; **stilt houses** raised on poles so floodwater and snakes stay below.
- **Hot deserts (Rajasthan):** thick mud walls and small windows keep homes cool; flat roofs to sleep on at night; round huts called *jhonpas*.
- **Snowy mountains (Ladakh, Himachal):** thick stone and wood walls, sloping roofs so snow slides off; small windows to keep warmth in.
- **Very cold Arctic:** the **Inuit** people once built **igloos** from snow blocks — snow traps warmth inside!
- **Big crowded cities:** land is costly, so people build **tall buildings with many flats**, one on top of another.

fig.alt: Three animated scenes showing rain and rising water, hot sun, and snowfall.

check.q: Why do houses in rainy places have sloping roofs?
check.why: A slope lets rainwater (and snow) run off instead of collecting and leaking in.

sections.md:
Most houses have spaces for different work:

- a **kitchen** for cooking,
- a place to **sleep**,
- a place to **sit and talk**,
- a **bathroom and toilet**,
- a **courtyard, balcony or verandah** in many homes,
- a place to store water, grain and things.

In a one-room house, the same room may be for cooking, eating and sleeping. In a big house, each has a separate room. Every house — big or small — is a **home** when a family lives there with love.

**Draw and label:** Draw a plan of your home. Mark the kitchen, where you sleep, the door and windows. Where does light and fresh air come in?

check.q: Why are windows important in a house?
check.why: Windows let in sunlight and fresh air, keeping the home healthy.

sections.md:
Humans are not the only builders!

| Animal | Home |
|---|---|
| Bird | nest |
| Rabbit, rat | burrow (hole in ground) |
| Bee | hive |
| Spider | web |
| Ant, termite | anthill / mound |
| Lion | den |
| Horse | stable |
| Cow | shed (gaushala) |
| Hen | coop |
| Dog | kennel |

The weaver bird stitches a hanging nest of grass with its beak — a real engineer!

> Did you know? A termite mound can be taller than a grown-up, and it has tunnels that keep it cool inside even in hot weather.

check.q: Where does a rabbit live?
check.why: Rabbits dig burrows, which are tunnels and holes in the ground.

sections.h: Keeping our home clean and safe
sections.md:
A good home is clean and safe:

- sweep and mop the floor; keep things in place,
- throw garbage in a covered dustbin,
- do not let water collect — mosquitoes breed in it,
- keep medicines and sharp things out of small children's reach,
- switch off fans and lights when leaving a room,
- open windows for fresh air.

Some people have no house at all. They sleep on footpaths or under bridges. Others lose their homes in floods or earthquakes. We should be kind and help them when we can.

check.q: Why should we not let water collect near our home?
check.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and they spread diseases like malaria and dengue.

summary: Houses protect us from rain, sun, cold, wind and animals.
Kutcha houses use mud, straw and bamboo; pucca houses use bricks, cement and stone.
Other homes: flats, tents, houseboats, stilt houses, igloos and caravans.
Houses are built to suit the weather and local materials.
Rainy and snowy places have sloping roofs; flood areas have stilt houses.
Deserts have thick mud walls and small windows to stay cool.
Cities have tall buildings with many flats because land is costly.
A home has spaces for cooking, sleeping, sitting and bathing.
Animals have homes too: nest, burrow, hive, web, den, stable.
Keep the home clean; do not let water collect.
practice: Why do we need a house?
What is the difference between a kutcha and a pucca house?
Name four different kinds of houses and where they are found.
Why do houses in Assam stand on poles?
Why do desert houses have thick walls?
Draw a plan of your home and label its parts.
Match these animals to their homes: bee, lion, bird, spider.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch18-a-house-like-thi.title: A House Like This (part 2)
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch18-a-house-like-thi.subtitle: Houses that suit the weather, building materials, and keeping a home clean

sections.md:
People build houses to protect themselves from **sun, rain, cold and wind**. So houses look different in different places.

| Place | Weather | Kind of house |
|---|---|---|
| Hills (Himachal, Sikkim) | Cold, snow, heavy rain | Sloping roofs so snow and rain slide off; thick walls of wood and stone |
| Desert (Rajasthan) | Very hot days, cold nights | Thick mud walls, small windows, flat roofs |
| Assam, Kerala (lots of rain) | Rain and floods | Houses on **stilts** (bamboo poles) above the ground |
| Ladakh | Very cold | Thick stone and mud walls, flat roofs |
| Kashmir lakes | Water all around | **Houseboats** |
| Cities | Crowded | Tall buildings with many **flats** |

Some people move from place to place with their animals and live in **tents**. Some people have no house at all and live on footpaths — they need our kindness and help.

check.q: Why do houses in the hills have sloping roofs?
options: So rain and snow slide off
check.why: A sloping roof lets rain and snow slide down instead of collecting and damaging the house.

sections.md:
Houses are built with things found nearby:

- **Mud, straw and cow dung** — cool in summer, cheap, used in villages.
- **Bamboo and wood** — light and strong, used in hills and the north-east.
- **Stone** — strong, used in hilly and rocky places.
- **Bricks, cement, sand and iron rods** — used for pucca houses in towns.
- **Ice blocks** — the igloos of very cold lands far away.
- **Cloth, plastic sheets** — for tents.

A **kutcha house** is made of mud, straw or bamboo. A **pucca house** is made of bricks, cement and stone.

Many people help to build a house: the **mason** (raj mistri), **labourers**, **carpenter**, **plumber**, **electrician** and **painter**.

**Did you know?** Birds, bees and ants build homes too — a weaver bird stitches a nest from grass!

check.q: A house made of bricks and cement is called a —
check.why: Brick-and-cement houses are strong and long-lasting, so they are called pucca houses.

sections.md:
A good home is not just walls and a roof. It should be **clean, airy and full of light**.

- Open windows let in fresh air and sunlight.
- Sweep and mop the floor every day.
- Keep a **dustbin** with a lid; throw garbage in it.
- Do not let water collect — mosquitoes breed in it.
- Use a toilet, and keep it clean.

Everyone in the family can help — folding clothes, putting away toys, watering plants.

In festivals like Diwali, Pongal and Christmas, people clean and decorate their houses with rangoli, lights and flowers.

**Activity:** Draw your house. Show its doors, windows, roof and the things around it. What is it made of?

**Talk about it:** If you could build your dream house, what would it look like?

summary: Houses protect us from sun, rain, cold and wind.
Houses differ by weather: sloping roofs in hills, thick mud walls in deserts, stilt houses in rainy areas.
Houseboats, tents, flats and igloos are other kinds of homes.
Houses are made of mud, bamboo, wood, stone, bricks and cement.
Kutcha houses: mud, straw, bamboo. Pucca houses: bricks, cement, stone.
Masons, carpenters, plumbers, electricians and painters help build a house.
A home should be clean, airy and bright; stagnant water breeds mosquitoes.

Why are some houses built on bamboo stilts?
Write two differences between a kutcha and a pucca house.
Name four people who help build a house.
Write three ways to keep your house clean.
Draw and describe your dream house.

rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch19-our-friends-anim.title: Our Friends – Animals
rd-school-c3-evs-d.ch19-our-friends-anim.subtitle: Pets, farm animals and street dogs — what animals need and how we care for them

sections.md:
*An original story to begin.*

It was pouring. Under the school gate, a tiny brown puppy shivered and whimpered. Some children walked past. Then Salma stopped. She wrapped the puppy in her old dupatta and carried it to the guard's cabin. The guard gave a little warm milk in a bowl. The puppy licked Salma's fingers and wagged its tail so hard its whole body wobbled.

The next day the whole class named it **Laddoo**. Laddoo now sleeps near the gate, and barks at strangers at night. 'He's our watchman!' laughs the guard.

Animals are our **friends**. They help us, and they need us to care for them.

check.q: How did Salma help the puppy?
options: Wrapped it up and gave it shelter and milk
check.why: She gave the cold puppy warmth, shelter and food — exactly what it needed.

sections.md:
Look around your home and street. Which animals do you see?

- **Pets** live with us: dogs, cats, parrots, fish, rabbits.
- **Farm / domestic animals** help us: cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, hens, horses, camels, donkeys, bullocks.
- **Street animals** live around us: dogs, cats, cows, pigeons, crows, squirrels.
- **Wild animals** live in forests: tigers, elephants, deer, monkeys.

**Activity:** Make a list of animals you see in one day. Which ones live with people? Which ones live on their own?

check.q: Which is a domestic animal that gives us milk?
check.why: Cows are domestic animals kept by people, and they give us milk.

sections.md:
| Animal | How it helps |
|---|---|
| Cow, buffalo, goat | milk (and dung for fuel and manure) |
| Hen | eggs |
| Sheep | wool for sweaters and shawls |
| Bullock | pulls carts and ploughs |
| Horse, camel, donkey | carry people and loads |
| Dog | guards the house, helps police find things by smell |
| Cat | catches rats |
| Bees | honey, and they help flowers make fruits |
| Silkworm | silk |
| Earthworm | makes soil soft and rich for farmers |

Some specially trained dogs help **people who cannot see** to walk safely. Police dogs sniff out lost people and things.

check.q: Which animal gives us wool?
check.why: Sheep grow thick wool, which is cut and spun into yarn for warm clothes.

sections.md:
Animals need many of the same things we do:

- **Food** — the right kind! Cows eat grass and fodder; cats eat fish, meat and milk; parrots eat fruits and seeds.
- **Clean water** — especially in hot summers. Keep a bowl of water outside for birds and street animals.
- **Shelter** — a shed, nest, kennel or a dry corner away from rain, sun and cold.
- **Care when ill** — an animal doctor is called a **veterinary doctor (vet)**.
- **Love and kindness** — gentle touch, no teasing.

**Taking care of a pet** means: feed it on time, give fresh water, keep it and its place clean, take a dog for walks, get vaccinations from the vet, and never leave it alone for long.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff3e0'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='60' fill='#c5e1a5'/><g transform='translate(220,150)'><ellipse cx='0' cy='20' rx='60' ry='32' fill='#a1887f'/><circle cx='60' cy='-10' r='26' fill='#a1887f'/><ellipse cx='74' cy='-30' rx='8' ry='16' fill='#6d4c41'/><circle cx='68' cy='-14' r='4'/><circle cx='84' cy='-4' r='4' fill='#3e2723'/><rect x='-40' y='40' width='12' height='26' fill='#a1887f'/><rect x='30' y='40' width='12' height='26' fill='#a1887f'/><path d='M-58 10 q-30 -20 -20 -40' stroke='#a1887f' stroke-width='10' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' values='-15 -58 10;20 -58 10;-15 -58 10' dur='.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><ellipse cx='350' cy='205' rx='40' ry='10' fill='#1e88e5'/><ellipse cx='350' cy='201' rx='32' ry='6' fill='#90caf9'><animate attributeName='rx' values='32;28;32' dur='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse><text x='325' y='240' font-size='14'>Water</text><path d='M430 200 v-50 l40 -30 l40 30 v50Z' fill='#8d6e63'/><path d='M455 200 v-30 h30 v30Z' fill='#3e2723'/><text x='440' y='240' font-size='14'>Shelter</text><text x='170' y='240' font-size='14'>Happy, wagging Laddoo</text></svg>
fig.caption: A happy dog wagging its tail, with fresh water and a dry kennel — what every animal needs.
fig.alt: Animated dog wagging tail next to a water bowl and a kennel.

keyTerms: Pet — an animal kept at home with love
Domestic animal — an animal kept by people for help or food
Vet — a doctor for animals
Fodder — food for cattle

check.q: Who treats sick animals?
check.why: A veterinary doctor, or vet, is trained to treat animals.

sections.md:
**Kindness:**

- Never throw stones at, tease or tie up animals cruelly.
- Don't overload donkeys, horses or bullocks.
- Don't feed animals plastic bags or junk — cows on streets often swallow plastic and fall sick.
- Don't keep birds locked in tiny cages; they love to fly.

**Safety:**

- Do not touch or pull the tail of a strange dog, especially one with puppies or one that is eating.
- Do not run suddenly in front of animals.
- Wash hands after touching animals.
- If an animal bites or scratches, tell an adult at once and see a doctor.

> Did you know? Many Indian festivals honour animals — Pongal's Mattu Pongal thanks cattle, and Nag Panchami is linked to snakes. In Nepal and parts of India, Kukur Tihar honours dogs.

check.q: Why should we not throw plastic bags where cows graze?
options: Cows may swallow them and fall sick
check.why: Swallowed plastic cannot be digested and can make cows very ill.

sections.md:
Watch a dog when its family comes home — it jumps and wags with joy. A cow calls out for its calf. A cat purrs when stroked and hisses when scared. Animals feel **happiness, fear, pain and love**.

Animals also make **sounds** to 'talk': a dog barks, a cat mews, a cow moos, a goat bleats, a lion roars, a hen clucks, a crow caws, a horse neighs, a donkey brays.

**Activity:** Observe an animal near your home for ten minutes. What does it eat? Where does it rest? What sounds does it make? How does it show it is happy or scared? Write your notes.

check.q: What sound does a horse make?
check.why: A horse neighs; a donkey brays and a goat bleats.

summary: Animals are our friends; they help us and need our care.
Pets live with us; domestic animals help us; some animals live on streets; wild animals live in forests.
Animals give us milk, eggs, wool, honey and silk, and carry loads.
Dogs guard homes and help police and people who cannot see.
Animals need food, clean water, shelter, care and kindness.
A vet treats sick animals.
Caring for a pet means feeding, cleaning, walking and vaccinating it.
Never tease, hurt or overload animals, or feed them plastic.
Stay safe: don't disturb strange dogs; wash hands after touching animals.
Animals have feelings and make different sounds.

Write two ways each in which a cow, sheep and dog help us.
What does an animal need to stay healthy?
How would you look after a pet dog?
Who is a vet?
Why should we not give plastic to cows?
Write four safety rules with street animals.
Match animals with their sounds: cow, goat, crow, donkey.
